The mim in ﴿from a sulalah﴾ is for the beginning of the source (ibtida'iyyah), attached to khalaqna (We created). The mim in ﴿from clay﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah), attached to an omitted element, and it occurs as a qualifier of sulalah, meaning: existing from clay. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, first created the essence of man from clay, because the origin is Adam, who was from pure clay, and his descendants are from clay and sperm.

It was said: the sulalah is clay, which, when you squeeze it, slips out from between your fingers, so what comes out is the sulalah. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Then ﴿We made him﴾, that is, the genus, by considering its individuals who are the children of Adam, or ﴿We made his offspring﴾, with an omitted noun, if by "man" Adam is meant: ﴿a drop (nutfah)﴾. The explanation of the nutfah has already been given in Surat al-Hajj, and likewise the explanation of the clinging clot (alaqah) and the lump (mudghah).

By the firm abode (al-qarar al-makin) is meant the womb, and it is expressed by "abode" (qarar), which is a verbal noun, for emphasis.

The meaning of ﴿Then We made the drop a clinging clot﴾ is that He, glorified is He, transformed the white drop into a red clot. ﴿Then We made the clot a lump﴾, that is, a piece of flesh not yet shaped. ﴿Then We made the lump bones﴾, that is, Allah, glorified is He, made them hard so that they would be a backbone for the body, in specific shapes. ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾, that is, Allah, glorified is He, caused flesh to grow over every bone in the amount that suits it and befits it. ﴿Then We brought him into being as another creation﴾, that is, We breathed into him the spirit after he had been an inanimate thing. It was said: We brought him out into the world. It was said: it is the growth of hair. It was said: it is the emergence of teeth. It was said: it is the completion of the powers created in him. There is no obstacle to intending all of these. The use of thumma (then) indicates the great difference between the two creations. ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, that is, He deserves glorification and praise.

It was said: it is derived from barakah (blessing), that is, His good and blessing are abundant. Al-khalq in the language means measurement (taqdir). It is said: "I measured (khalaqtu) the hide" when you measure it in order to cut a piece from it. So the meaning of "the best of creators" is: the most skilful of makers who measure. From this is the words of the poet:
"Indeed you cut what you measure, and some people measure and then do not cut."

﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die.﴾ The reference in His words "after that" is to the preceding matters, that is: then indeed you, after those matters, are surely those who will go to death without doubt.

﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised﴾ from your graves to the place of gathering (al-mahshar) for the reckoning and the punishment.

The lam in ﴿And We had certainly created above you seven paths﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and the sentence is independent, containing an explanation of the creation of what they need after the explanation of their own creation. The tara'iq (paths) are the heavens.

Al-Khalili, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: they were called tara'iq because some of them were layered (tuwriqa) above others, like the layers of a shoe sole (mutarraqat al-na'l).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "I layered (tarraqtu) the thing," meaning I made some of it above others, and the Arabs call everything above something else a tariqah.

It was said: because they are the paths of the angels. It was said: because they are the paths of the stars.

﴿And We were not unaware of the creation﴾. Here "creation" means the created things, that is: We were not unaware of these seven paths and their keeping from falling onto the earth.

Most of the exegetes said: what is meant is that We are not unaware of all creation; rather, We preserved the heavens from falling, and We preserved those on the earth from the sky falling on them and destroying them, or the earth shaking with them, or them perishing by some cause that would uproot them. It is permissible that what is intended is the negation of heedlessness regarding the maintenance of their interests and what they live by, and the negation of heedlessness regarding their protection.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water﴾. This is among the blessings with which Allah, glorified is He, favoured His creatures. What is meant by water is rainwater, for by it is the life of the earth and of the animals in it. Among that is the water of the rivers that descend from the sky, and of the springs and wells that are extracted from the earth, for their origin is from the water of the sky.

It was said: by this verse He, glorified is He, intended the four rivers: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile. But there is no basis for this specification.

It was said: what is meant is sweet water. But there is no basis for that either, for there is no water on earth except that it is from the sky. The meaning of "in a measure" (bi-qadar) is by a measure from Us, or in an amount by which there is the welfare of crops and fruits, for if it were abundant it would bring about the destruction of that. Similar to it is His words, glorified is He: ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾. The meaning of ﴿then We caused it to settle in the earth﴾ is We made it lodged in it, so that they benefit from it at the time of their need for it, like the water that remains in pools and puddles and the like. ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾, that is, just as We were able to send it down, so We are able to take it away in some manner. The indefinite form here has a beautiful effect that is not hidden. In this is a severe threat, because of what it indicates of His power, glorified is He, to remove it and sink it deep, until people perish of thirst and their livestock perish. Similar to it is His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾

Then He, glorified is He, explained what results from the sending down of water, saying: ﴿So We produced for you therewith gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾, that is, We brought into being with that water gardens of the two kinds mentioned, for you, ﴿in them there are abundant fruits﴾ with which you enjoy yourselves and of which you eat.

It was said: the meaning is: from these gardens are the sources of your sustenance and livelihood, like His words: "So-and-so eats from such-and-such a trade." This is far-fetched. He, glorified is He, limited the mention to palms and grapes because they are the ones found in al-Ta'if and al-Madinah and what is connected to them.

Thus said Ibn Jarir. It was also said: because they are the noblest of trees in fruit, and the best of them in benefit, taste and pleasure.

It was said that what is meant by His words ﴿for you in them are fruits﴾ is that for you in these gardens are fruits other than grapes and palms.

It was said: the meaning is that for you in these two kinds in particular are fruits, because in them are varieties differing in taste and colour.

The jurists have differed greatly over what the word "fruit" (fakihah) applies to. The best of what has been said is that it applies to the fruits that people eat, which are not a staple for them, nor food, nor condiment. Disagreement arose over whether vegetables (buqul) enter into fruit or not.

As for the accusative of shajarah (tree), it is in coordination with jannat (gardens). Al-Farra' permitted the nominative on the assumption: "and there is a tree," so it is raised as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted and estimated before it, which is the mentioned adverbial phrase.

Al-Wahidi said: all the exegetes say that what is meant by this tree is the olive tree. It was singled out for mention because no one tends it with irrigation, and it is the one from which oil is extracted. Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it as a favour upon His servants; and because it is the most noble of trees, the most widely beneficial, and the most abundant in blessing.

Then He, glorified is He, described this tree as ﴿coming forth from Mount Sinai﴾, which is a mountain in Bayt al-Maqdis. In the speech of the Arabs al-tur means mountain. It was said: it is "the blessed." The majority held that it is the name of a mountain, as you say "Mount Uhud." It was said: Sayna' is a particular stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it exists near it. It was said: it is every mountain that bears fruit.

The Kufans read Sayna' with a fatha on the sin, and the rest read it with a kasra on the sin. It is not declined (la yusrafa) because it became the name of a place. Al-Akhfash claimed that it is non-Arabic.

The majority read ﴿grows with the oil﴾ with a fatha on the first letter and a damma on the ba' (tanbutu). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the first letter and a kasra on the ba' (tunbitu).

The meaning according to the first reading is: it grows by itself, accompanied by the oil. According to the second reading the ba' is in the sense of ma'a (with), so it is for accompaniment. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi said: the estimate is: its branches grow and the oil is with it. It was said: the ba' is superfluous. This was said by Abu 'Ubaydah, and similar to it is the words of the poet:
"They are free women, not mothers of asses, black-eyed, who do not recite the suwar."
Another said:
"We strike with the sword and hope for relief (bil-faraj)."

Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: nabata and anbata have the same meaning. Al-Asma'i denies anbata and rejects this with the words of Zuhayr:
"You saw those in need around their homes, a settled community for them, until the herbage grew (anbata)."
That is, grew (nabata). Al-Zuhri, al-Hasan and al-A'raj read tunbatu with a damma on the first letter and a fatha on the ba'. Al-Zajjaj and Ibn Jinni said: that is, it grows and the oil is with it. Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿comes forth with the oil﴾. Zirr ibn Hubaysh read ﴿grows the oil﴾ by dropping the preposition.

Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik and al-Ashhab read ﴿with the dihan﴾ (dihan being a variant of the word for oil), and ﴿and a condiment (sibgh) for the eaters﴾ is coordinated with al-duhn (oil), that is: it grows with the thing that combines being an oil with which one anoints, and being a condiment with which one eats with bread.

The majority read sibgh, and a group read sibagh, like libs and libas. Every relish with which one eats bread is sibgh and sibagh. The original meaning of sibgh is what a garment is dyed with, and the relish was likened to it because bread with relish is like something dyed with it.

﴿And indeed in the cattle there is surely a lesson﴾. This is among the blessings with which Allah favoured them, and the explanation of al-an'am (the cattle) has already been given in Surat al-Nahl.

Al-Naysaburi said in his tafsir: Perhaps what is intended by al-an'am here is specifically camels, because they are what is ridden in the customary way, and because He paired them with the ship (al-fulk), which are the ships of the land, just as the ship is the ship of the sea. He, glorified is He, explained that they are a lesson, because they are among the things by whose creation and actions one is guided to the immensity of divine power. Then He, glorified is He, detailed what there is in these cattle of blessings after mentioning the lesson in them for the servants, saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾. He means: the milk formed in their bellies and channelled to their udders. Indeed, in the transformation of what they eat of fodder into this delicious nourishment and this precious drink there is the greatest lesson for those who take heed and the greatest admonition for those who are admonished.

It was read nusqikum with the nun, on the basis that the agent is Allah, glorified is He. It was read with the upper ta' (tusqikum), on the basis that the agent is the cattle. Then He mentioned their benefits in general, saying: ﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾, that is, in their backs, their milk, their offspring, their wool and their hair. Then He mentioned a particular benefit, saying: ﴿and from them you eat﴾, because of the great benefit of eating for them.

Likewise He mentioned riding upon them because of its great benefit, saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾. That is: and upon the cattle. If by al-an'am is meant camels, cattle and sheep, then the meaning is: and upon some of the cattle, which are camels specifically. If by al-an'am is meant camels specifically, the meaning is clear.

Then, since the cattle are the most common thing one rides on in the land, He added to them what one rides on in the sea, saying: ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾, as a completion of the blessing and a perfecting of the favour.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim transmitted from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: al-sulalah is the pure essence of the thin water from which the child is produced.

(p-980) … (p-981)

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn Mas'ud that he said: "When the drop (nutfah) falls into the womb, it spreads into hair and nails, and it remains there for forty days. Then it slides down into the womb and becomes a clinging clot ('alaqah)."

The Successors (al-Tabi'un) had various opinions on the interpretation of *al-sulalah*, and we have already pointed out those views.

Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ that he said: "The hair and the teeth."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from him concerning ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ that he said: "He breathed the spirit into him." Mujahid, 'Ikrimah, al-Sha'bi, al-Hasan, Abu al-'Aliyah, al-Rabi' (from Anas), al-Suddi, al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said the same, and Ibn Jarir chose this view.

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Mujahid concerning ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾ that he said: "When youth came to him in full."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Salih Abi al-Khalil, who said: "When this verse was revealed to the Prophet (ﷺ), up to His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, 'Umar said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. He (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand my soul is, it has been concluded with what you have just said, O 'Umar.'"

al-Tayalisi, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn 'Asakir related from Anas, who said: 'Umar said: "I agreed with my Lord in four matters. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only we prayed behind the Station (of Ibrahim)!' Then Allah revealed ﴿And take from the Station of Ibrahim a place of prayer﴾. I said: 'O Messenger of Allah, if only you would place a veil over your wives, for the good and the wicked enter upon you.' So Allah revealed ﴿And when you ask them for something, ask them from behind a veil﴾. And I said to the wives of the Prophet (ﷺ): 'You must desist, or Allah will replace him with wives better than you.' So there was revealed ﴿It may be that his Lord, if he divorces you, will substitute for him wives better than you﴾, the verse. And there was revealed ﴿And We created man from an extract of clay﴾, up to His words ﴿Then We produced him as another creation﴾, so I said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾."

Ibn Rahawayh, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani in al-Awsat and Ibn Mardawayh related from Zayd ibn Thabit, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) dictated this verse, ﴿And We created man﴾, up to His words ﴿another creation﴾. Mu'adh ibn Jabal then said: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) laughed, and Mu'adh said to him: 'What are you laughing at, O Messenger of Allah?' He said: 'With it, it was concluded: ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾.'" In its chain is Jabir al-Ju'fi, who is extremely weak.

Ibn Kathir said: "In this report there is a severe strangeness, because this surah is Meccan, while Zayd ibn Thabit only wrote down revelation in Medina, and likewise Mu'adh ibn Jabal's conversion took place in Medina. And Allah knows best."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Khatib (al-Suyuti said, with a weak chain) related from Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Allah sent down five rivers from Paradise to the earth: Sayhun, which is the river of India; Jayhun, which is the river of Balkh; the Tigris and the Euphrates, which are the two rivers of Iraq; and the Nile, which is the river of Egypt. He sent them down from one spring among the springs of Paradise, from the lowest level of its levels, upon the two wings of Jibril. He entrusted them to the mountains and made them flow on the earth, and made them benefits for people in the kinds of their livelihoods. This is His saying: ﴿And We sent down water from the sky in measure, and We made it settle in the earth﴾. When Gog and Magog come out, Allah will send Jibril, and he will lift from the earth the Qur'an and knowledge, the Black Stone from the corner of the House, the Station of Ibrahim, the Ark of Musa with what is in it, and these five rivers. He will raise all of that to the sky. This is His saying: ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾. When these things are lifted from the earth, its people have lost the good of this world and the Hereafter."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: "Tur Sinin is the mountain from which Musa was called."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him concerning His saying ﴿growing with oil﴾ that he said: "It is the olive oil, which is eaten and used as an ointment."

Then He mentioned their benefits in general, saying: ﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾, that is, in their backs, their milk, their offspring, their wool and their hair. Then He mentioned a particular benefit, saying: ﴿and from them you eat﴾, because of the great benefit of eating for them.

Likewise He mentioned riding upon them because of its great benefit, saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾. That is: and upon the cattle. If by al-an'am is meant camels, cattle and sheep, then the meaning is: and upon some of the cattle, which are camels specifically. If by al-an'am is meant camels specifically, the meaning is clear.

Then, since the cattle are the most common thing one rides on in the land, He added to them what one rides on in the sea, saying: ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾, as a completion of the blessing and a perfecting of the favour.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 12–41 (part 1 of 2):

.
When He, glorified is He, urged His servants to worship and promised them Paradise (al-Firdaws) for doing it, He returned to establishing the origin (al-mabda') and the return (al-ma'ad), so that this would take firm root in the souls of the responsible (al-mukallafin). So He said: ﴿And We had certainly created man﴾ to the end of the verse. The lam is the answer to an omitted oath (qasam), and the sentence is independent (mubtada'ah). It was also said that it is coordinated (ma'tufah) with what precedes it. By "man" is meant the genus (al-jins), because they were created within the creation of their father Adam. It was also said that what is meant is Adam.

Al-sulalah is on the pattern fu'alah, from al-sall, which is extracting one thing from another. It is said: "I drew (salaltu) a hair from the dough" and "the sword from its scabbard, so it slid out (fansalla)." So the semen-drop (al-nutfah) is a sulalah, and the child is a salil, and also a sulalah. From this is the words of the poet:
"She brought him forth, a sharp-edged, lion-like one, the offspring (sulalah) of a womb that was not secure."
And the words of another:
"Is Hind anything but an Arab mare, the offspring (sulalah) of mares whom a mule has mated with?"

The mim in ﴿from a sulalah﴾ is for the beginning of the source (ibtida'iyyah), attached to khalaqna (We created). The mim in ﴿from clay﴾ is explanatory (bayaniyyah), attached to an omitted element, and it occurs as a qualifier of sulalah, meaning: existing from clay. The meaning is that He, glorified is He, first created the essence of man from clay, because the origin is Adam, who was from pure clay, and his descendants are from clay and sperm.

It was said: the sulalah is clay, which, when you squeeze it, slips out from between your fingers, so what comes out is the sulalah. This was said by al-Kalbi.

Then ﴿We made him﴾, that is, the genus, by considering its individuals who are the children of Adam, or ﴿We made his offspring﴾, with an omitted noun, if by "man" Adam is meant: ﴿a drop (nutfah)﴾. The explanation of the nutfah has already been given in Surat al-Hajj, and likewise the explanation of the clinging clot (alaqah) and the lump (mudghah).

By the firm abode (al-qarar al-makin) is meant the womb, and it is expressed by "abode" (qarar), which is a verbal noun, for emphasis.

The meaning of ﴿Then We made the drop a clinging clot﴾ is that He, glorified is He, transformed the white drop into a red clot. ﴿Then We made the clot a lump﴾, that is, a piece of flesh not yet shaped. ﴿Then We made the lump bones﴾, that is, Allah, glorified is He, made them hard so that they would be a backbone for the body, in specific shapes. ﴿Then We clothed the bones with flesh﴾, that is, Allah, glorified is He, caused flesh to grow over every bone in the amount that suits it and befits it. ﴿Then We brought him into being as another creation﴾, that is, We breathed into him the spirit after he had been an inanimate thing. It was said: We brought him out into the world. It was said: it is the growth of hair. It was said: it is the emergence of teeth. It was said: it is the completion of the powers created in him. There is no obstacle to intending all of these. The use of thumma (then) indicates the great difference between the two creations. ﴿So blessed is Allah, the best of creators﴾, that is, He deserves glorification and praise.

It was said: it is derived from barakah (blessing), that is, His good and blessing are abundant. Al-khalq in the language means measurement (taqdir). It is said: "I measured (khalaqtu) the hide" when you measure it in order to cut a piece from it. So the meaning of "the best of creators" is: the most skilful of makers who measure. From this is the words of the poet:
"Indeed you cut what you measure, and some people measure and then do not cut."

﴿Then indeed you, after that, will surely die.﴾ The reference in His words "after that" is to the preceding matters, that is: then indeed you, after those matters, are surely those who will go to death without doubt.

﴿Then indeed you, on the Day of Resurrection, will be raised﴾ from your graves to the place of gathering (al-mahshar) for the reckoning and the punishment.

The lam in ﴿And We had certainly created above you seven paths﴾ is the answer to an omitted oath, and the sentence is independent, containing an explanation of the creation of what they need after the explanation of their own creation. The tara'iq (paths) are the heavens.

Al-Khalili, al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: they were called tara'iq because some of them were layered (tuwriqa) above others, like the layers of a shoe sole (mutarraqat al-na'l).

Abu 'Ubaydah said: "I layered (tarraqtu) the thing," meaning I made some of it above others, and the Arabs call everything above something else a tariqah.

It was said: because they are the paths of the angels. It was said: because they are the paths of the stars.

﴿And We were not unaware of the creation﴾. Here "creation" means the created things, that is: We were not unaware of these seven paths and their keeping from falling onto the earth.

Most of the exegetes said: what is meant is that We are not unaware of all creation; rather, We preserved the heavens from falling, and We preserved those on the earth from the sky falling on them and destroying them, or the earth shaking with them, or them perishing by some cause that would uproot them. It is permissible that what is intended is the negation of heedlessness regarding the maintenance of their interests and what they live by, and the negation of heedlessness regarding their protection.

﴿And We sent down from the sky water﴾. This is among the blessings with which Allah, glorified is He, favoured His creatures. What is meant by water is rainwater, for by it is the life of the earth and of the animals in it. Among that is the water of the rivers that descend from the sky, and of the springs and wells that are extracted from the earth, for their origin is from the water of the sky.

It was said: by this verse He, glorified is He, intended the four rivers: Sayhan, Jayhan, the Euphrates and the Nile. But there is no basis for this specification.

It was said: what is meant is sweet water. But there is no basis for that either, for there is no water on earth except that it is from the sky. The meaning of "in a measure" (bi-qadar) is by a measure from Us, or in an amount by which there is the welfare of crops and fruits, for if it were abundant it would bring about the destruction of that. Similar to it is His words, glorified is He: ﴿And there is nothing but that its treasuries are with Us, and We send it down only in a known measure﴾. The meaning of ﴿then We caused it to settle in the earth﴾ is We made it lodged in it, so that they benefit from it at the time of their need for it, like the water that remains in pools and puddles and the like. ﴿And indeed We are able to take it away﴾, that is, just as We were able to send it down, so We are able to take it away in some manner. The indefinite form here has a beautiful effect that is not hidden. In this is a severe threat, because of what it indicates of His power, glorified is He, to remove it and sink it deep, until people perish of thirst and their livestock perish. Similar to it is His words: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if your water should become sunken, who would bring you clear water?﴾

Then He, glorified is He, explained what results from the sending down of water, saying: ﴿So We produced for you therewith gardens of palm trees and grapevines﴾, that is, We brought into being with that water gardens of the two kinds mentioned, for you, ﴿in them there are abundant fruits﴾ with which you enjoy yourselves and of which you eat.

It was said: the meaning is: from these gardens are the sources of your sustenance and livelihood, like His words: "So-and-so eats from such-and-such a trade." This is far-fetched. He, glorified is He, limited the mention to palms and grapes because they are the ones found in al-Ta'if and al-Madinah and what is connected to them.

Thus said Ibn Jarir. It was also said: because they are the noblest of trees in fruit, and the best of them in benefit, taste and pleasure.

It was said that what is meant by His words ﴿for you in them are fruits﴾ is that for you in these gardens are fruits other than grapes and palms.

It was said: the meaning is that for you in these two kinds in particular are fruits, because in them are varieties differing in taste and colour.

The jurists have differed greatly over what the word "fruit" (fakihah) applies to. The best of what has been said is that it applies to the fruits that people eat, which are not a staple for them, nor food, nor condiment. Disagreement arose over whether vegetables (buqul) enter into fruit or not.

As for the accusative of shajarah (tree), it is in coordination with jannat (gardens). Al-Farra' permitted the nominative on the assumption: "and there is a tree," so it is raised as a subject (mubtada') whose predicate is omitted and estimated before it, which is the mentioned adverbial phrase.

Al-Wahidi said: all the exegetes say that what is meant by this tree is the olive tree. It was singled out for mention because no one tends it with irrigation, and it is the one from which oil is extracted. Allah, glorified is He, mentioned it as a favour upon His servants; and because it is the most noble of trees, the most widely beneficial, and the most abundant in blessing.

Then He, glorified is He, described this tree as ﴿coming forth from Mount Sinai﴾, which is a mountain in Bayt al-Maqdis. In the speech of the Arabs al-tur means mountain. It was said: it is "the blessed." The majority held that it is the name of a mountain, as you say "Mount Uhud." It was said: Sayna' is a particular stone, and the mountain was attributed to it because it exists near it. It was said: it is every mountain that bears fruit.

The Kufans read Sayna' with a fatha on the sin, and the rest read it with a kasra on the sin. It is not declined (la yusrafa) because it became the name of a place. Al-Akhfash claimed that it is non-Arabic.

The majority read ﴿grows with the oil﴾ with a fatha on the first letter and a damma on the ba' (tanbutu). Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with a damma on the first letter and a kasra on the ba' (tunbitu).

The meaning according to the first reading is: it grows by itself, accompanied by the oil. According to the second reading the ba' is in the sense of ma'a (with), so it is for accompaniment. "They are free women, not mothers of asses, black-eyed, who do not recite the suwar."

Sulayman ibn 'Abd al-Malik and al-Ashhab read ﴿with the dihan﴾ (dihan being a variant of the word for oil), and ﴿and a condiment (sibgh) for the eaters﴾ is coordinated with al-duhn (oil), that is: it grows with the thing that combines being an oil with which one anoints, and being a condiment with which one eats with bread.

Al-Naysaburi said in his tafsir: Perhaps what is intended by al-an'am here is specifically camels, because they are what is ridden in the customary way, and because He paired them with the ship (al-fulk), which are the ships of the land, just as the ship is the ship of the sea. He, glorified is He, explained that they are a lesson, because they are among the things by whose creation and actions one is guided to the immensity of divine power. Then He, glorified is He, detailed what there is in these cattle of blessings after mentioning the lesson in them for the servants, saying: ﴿We give you to drink from what is in their bellies﴾. He means: the milk formed in their bellies and channelled to their udders. Indeed, in the transformation of what they eat of fodder into this delicious nourishment and this precious drink there is the greatest lesson for those who take heed and the greatest admonition for those who are admonished.

It was read nusqikum with the nun, on the basis that the agent is Allah, glorified is He. It was read with the upper ta' (tusqikum), on the basis that the agent is the cattle. Then He mentioned their benefits in general, saying: ﴿And for you in them are many benefits﴾, that is, in their backs, their milk, their offspring, their wool and their hair. Then He mentioned a particular benefit, saying: ﴿and from them you eat﴾, because of the great benefit of eating for them.

Likewise He mentioned riding upon them because of its great benefit, saying: ﴿And upon them and upon the ships you are carried﴾. That is: and upon the cattle. If by al-an'am is meant camels, cattle and sheep, then the meaning is: and upon some of the cattle, which are camels specifically. If by al-an'am is meant camels specifically, the meaning is clear.

Then, since the cattle are the most common thing one rides on in the land, He added to them what one rides on in the sea, saying: ﴿and upon the ships you are carried﴾, as a completion of the blessing and a perfecting of the favour.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." It is also said that the pronoun in *la'allahum* (perhaps they) refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but this is an error, because Musa was not given the Torah except after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43].

(p-985)
Then Glorified is He alluded briefly to the story of 'Isa, saying: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾, meaning a sign indicating the greatness of Our power and the wondrous nature of Our making. The discussion of this has already been presented at the end of Surat al-Anbiya' in the exegesis of His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is said that it is the land of Damascus, and this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. It is also said that it is the land of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi. ﴿A place of settlement﴾, meaning a place of stability upon which its inhabitants settle, ﴿and running water (*ma'in*)﴾, meaning flowing water.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is water flowing in springs, so the *mim* in this case is an augmentative, like its augmentation in *manba'* (source)." It is also said that *ma'in* is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: "The meaning of water when it flows is *ma'in* and *mamun*." Ibn al-A'rabi said likewise. It is also said that it is derived from *ma'un* (help, benefit), which is benefit, and Al-Farra' said the same as al-Zajjaj.

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "This address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the plural indicates that all the messengers were commanded likewise." It is also said that this address was made to every prophet, because this is their way, which they should follow, so the meaning is: "And We said, O messengers," addressing each one individually, due to the difference of their times. Ibn Jarir said that the address was to 'Isa.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like saying to one man, 'Stop from us.'" The *tayyibat* (good things) are what is found agreeable and pleasant. It is also said that they are the lawful, and it is also said that they are what combines the two descriptions mentioned.

Then, after commanding them to eat of the good things, He commanded them to do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a righteous deed, which is what conforms to the Law. Then He gave the reason for this command by His words: ﴿Indeed I am All-Knowing of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Me, and I will recompense you according to your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾. This is part of what was addressed to the prophets. The meaning is: this is your religion and your law, O messengers, a single religion and a unified law, comprising one principle, which is the greatest thing God sent His prophets with and revealed His books concerning: calling all the prophets to the worship of God, without partner.

It is also said that the meaning is: this which has been mentioned is your religion and your creed, so adhere to it, taking *ummah* here to mean religion, as in His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers following a religion (*ummah*)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:
"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah read yusāriʿu with the yāʾ (third person), its subject being what is indicated by amdadnā, namely the provision (al-imdād). It may also mean: God hastens for them. The rest read nusāriʿu with the nūn. Al-Thaʿlabī said: This reading is the correct one because of His saying numiddu-hum (We provide them).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

Wakīʿ, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated. Al-Suyūṭī said, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿to a high ground﴾, he said: "We were told that it is Damascus."

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām the like of it, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated it from him. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Umāmah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Murrah al-Nahzī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The rabwah is al-Ramlah."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Mandah, Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from al-Aqraʿ ibn Shufayy al-ʿAkkī, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Aḥmad, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, God is good and accepts only what is good, and God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 51], or He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]." Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

Ibn Jarir said that the address was to 'Isa.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like saying to one man, 'Stop from us.'" The *tayyibat* (good things) are what is found agreeable and pleasant. It is also said that they are the lawful, and it is also said that they are what combines the two descriptions mentioned.

Then, after commanding them to eat of the good things, He commanded them to do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a righteous deed, which is what conforms to the Law. Then He gave the reason for this command by His words: ﴿Indeed I am All-Knowing of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Me, and I will recompense you according to your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾. This is part of what was addressed to the prophets. The meaning is: this is your religion and your law, O messengers, a single religion and a unified law, comprising one principle, which is the greatest thing God sent His prophets with and revealed His books concerning: calling all the prophets to the worship of God, without partner.

It is also said that the meaning is: this which has been mentioned is your religion and your creed, so adhere to it, taking *ummah* here to mean religion, as in His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers following a religion (*ummah*)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:
"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah read yusāriʿu with the yāʾ (third person), its subject being what is indicated by amdadnā, namely the provision (al-imdād). It may also mean: God hastens for them. The rest read nusāriʿu with the nūn. Al-Thaʿlabī said: This reading is the correct one because of His saying numiddu-hum (We provide them).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

Wakīʿ, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated. Al-Suyūṭī said, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿to a high ground﴾, he said: "We were told that it is Damascus."

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām the like of it, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated it from him. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Umāmah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Murrah al-Nahzī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The rabwah is al-Ramlah."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Mandah, Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from al-Aqraʿ ibn Shufayy al-ʿAkkī, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Aḥmad, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, God is good and accepts only what is good, and God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 51], or He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]." Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." It is also said that the pronoun in *la'allahum* (perhaps they) refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but this is an error, because Musa was not given the Torah except after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43].

(p-985)

The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine."
