"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah read yusāriʿu with the yāʾ (third person), its subject being what is indicated by amdadnā, namely the provision (al-imdād). It may also mean: God hastens for them. The rest read nusāriʿu with the nūn. Al-Thaʿlabī said: This reading is the correct one because of His saying numiddu-hum (We provide them).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

Wakīʿ, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated. Al-Suyūṭī said, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿to a high ground﴾, he said: "We were told that it is Damascus."

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām the like of it, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated it from him. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Umāmah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Murrah al-Nahzī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The rabwah is al-Ramlah."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Mandah, Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from al-Aqraʿ ibn Shufayy al-ʿAkkī, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Aḥmad, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, God is good and accepts only what is good, and God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 51], or He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]." Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." It is also said that the pronoun in *la'allahum* (perhaps they) refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but this is an error, because Musa was not given the Torah except after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43].

The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is said that it is the land of Damascus, and this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. It is also said that it is the land of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi. ﴿A place of settlement﴾, meaning a place of stability upon which its inhabitants settle, ﴿and running water (*ma'in*)﴾, meaning flowing water.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is water flowing in springs, so the *mim* in this case is an augmentative, like its augmentation in *manba'* (source)." Ibn al-A'rabi said likewise. It is also said that it is derived from *ma'un* (help, benefit), which is benefit, and Al-Farra' said the same as al-Zajjaj.

Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." It is also said that the pronoun in *la'allahum* (perhaps they) refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but this is an error, because Musa was not given the Torah except after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43].

(p-985)
Then Glorified is He alluded briefly to the story of 'Isa, saying: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾, meaning a sign indicating the greatness of Our power and the wondrous nature of Our making. The discussion of this has already been presented at the end of Surat al-Anbiya' in the exegesis of His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is said that it is the land of Damascus, and this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. It is also said that it is the land of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi. ﴿A place of settlement﴾, meaning a place of stability upon which its inhabitants settle, ﴿and running water (*ma'in*)﴾, meaning flowing water.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is water flowing in springs, so the *mim* in this case is an augmentative, like its augmentation in *manba'* (source)." It is also said that *ma'in* is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: "The meaning of water when it flows is *ma'in* and *mamun*." Ibn al-A'rabi said likewise. It is also said that it is derived from *ma'un* (help, benefit), which is benefit, and Al-Farra' said the same as al-Zajjaj.

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "This address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the plural indicates that all the messengers were commanded likewise." It is also said that this address was made to every prophet, because this is their way, which they should follow, so the meaning is: "And We said, O messengers," addressing each one individually, due to the difference of their times. Ibn Jarir said that the address was to 'Isa.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like saying to one man, 'Stop from us.'" The *tayyibat* (good things) are what is found agreeable and pleasant. It is also said that they are the lawful, and it is also said that they are what combines the two descriptions mentioned.

Then, after commanding them to eat of the good things, He commanded them to do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a righteous deed, which is what conforms to the Law. Then He gave the reason for this command by His words: ﴿Indeed I am All-Knowing of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Me, and I will recompense you according to your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾. This is part of what was addressed to the prophets. The meaning is: this is your religion and your law, O messengers, a single religion and a unified law, comprising one principle, which is the greatest thing God sent His prophets with and revealed His books concerning: calling all the prophets to the worship of God, without partner.

It is also said that the meaning is: this which has been mentioned is your religion and your creed, so adhere to it, taking *ummah* here to mean religion, as in His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers following a religion (*ummah*)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:
"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah read yusāriʿu with the yāʾ (third person), its subject being what is indicated by amdadnā, namely the provision (al-imdād). It may also mean: God hastens for them. The rest read nusāriʿu with the nūn. Al-Thaʿlabī said: This reading is the correct one because of His saying numiddu-hum (We provide them).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

Wakīʿ, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated. Al-Suyūṭī said, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿to a high ground﴾, he said: "We were told that it is Damascus."

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām the like of it, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated it from him. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Umāmah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Murrah al-Nahzī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The rabwah is al-Ramlah."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then Glorified is He alluded briefly to the story of 'Isa, saying: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾, meaning a sign indicating the greatness of Our power and the wondrous nature of Our making. The discussion of this has already been presented at the end of Surat al-Anbiya' in the exegesis of His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is said that it is the land of Damascus, and this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. It is also said that it is the land of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi. ﴿A place of settlement﴾, meaning a place of stability upon which its inhabitants settle, ﴿and running water (*ma'in*)﴾, meaning flowing water.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is water flowing in springs, so the *mim* in this case is an augmentative, like its augmentation in *manba'* (source)." It is also said that *ma'in* is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: "The meaning of water when it flows is *ma'in* and *mamun*." Ibn al-A'rabi said likewise. It is also said that it is derived from *ma'un* (help, benefit), which is benefit, and Al-Farra' said the same as al-Zajjaj.

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "This address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the plural indicates that all the messengers were commanded likewise." It is also said that this address was made to every prophet, because this is their way, which they should follow, so the meaning is: "And We said, O messengers," addressing each one individually, due to the difference of their times. Ibn Jarir said that the address was to 'Isa.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like saying to one man, 'Stop from us.'" The *tayyibat* (good things) are what is found agreeable and pleasant. It is also said that they are the lawful, and it is also said that they are what combines the two descriptions mentioned.

Then, after commanding them to eat of the good things, He commanded them to do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a righteous deed, which is what conforms to the Law. Then He gave the reason for this command by His words: ﴿Indeed I am All-Knowing of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Me, and I will recompense you according to your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾. This is part of what was addressed to the prophets. The meaning is: this is your religion and your law, O messengers, a single religion and a unified law, comprising one principle, which is the greatest thing God sent His prophets with and revealed His books concerning: calling all the prophets to the worship of God, without partner.

It is also said that the meaning is: this which has been mentioned is your religion and your creed, so adhere to it, taking *ummah* here to mean religion, as in His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers following a religion (*ummah*)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:
"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).

Abū ʿAbd al-Raḥmān al-Sulamī and ʿAbd al-Raḥmān ibn Abī Bakrah read yusāriʿu with the yāʾ (third person), its subject being what is indicated by amdadnā, namely the provision (al-imdād). It may also mean: God hastens for them. The rest read nusāriʿu with the nūn. Al-Thaʿlabī said: This reading is the correct one because of His saying numiddu-hum (We provide them).

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

Wakīʿ, al-Firyābī, Ibn Abī Shaybah, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, Tammām al-Rāzī and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated. Al-Suyūṭī said, with a sound chain, from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding His saying ﴿to a high ground﴾, he said: "We were told that it is Damascus."

Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from ʿAbd Allāh ibn Salām the like of it, and Ibn Abī Ḥātim also narrated it from him. Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Umāmah, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar, and its chain is weak.

Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ṭabarānī in al-Awsaṭ, Ibn Mardawayh and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Murrah al-Nahzī, who said: I heard the Messenger of God (ﷺ) say: "The rabwah is al-Ramlah."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Al-Ṭabarānī, Ibn al-Sakan, Ibn Mandah, Abū Nuʿaym and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from al-Aqraʿ ibn Shufayy al-ʿAkkī, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), something similar.

Aḥmad, Muslim and others narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: The Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "O people, God is good and accepts only what is good, and God commanded the believers with what He commanded the messengers, so He said: ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things and do righteous deeds; indeed I am Knowing of what you do﴾ [al-Muʾminūn: 51], or He said: ﴿O you who have believed, eat of the good things with which We have provided you﴾ [al-Baqarah: 172]." Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās (p-986) regarding His saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾ (tatrā), he said: "They follow one another." In another wording he said: "Some of them upon the heels of others."

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Qatādah regarding ﴿And We made the son of Mary and his mother a sign﴾, he said: "She bore him without a father." Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from al-Rabīʿ ibn Anas regarding "āyah" that he said: "a lesson (ʿibrah)."

Ibn Jarīr and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Ibn ʿAbbās regarding ﴿And We gave them refuge on a high ground﴾, he said: "The rabwah is the level (mustawiyah) place, and the maʿīn is the flowing water, and it is the river of which God said: ﴿Your Lord has placed beneath you a stream﴾ [Maryam: 24]."

Ibn Abī Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from him regarding ﴿on a high ground﴾, he said: "It is the elevated place of the earth, and it is the best place for plants to grow." ﴿Of settled place (dhāt qarār)﴾: of fertility (khiṣb). And the maʿīn: the apparent (ẓāhir) water.

ʿAbd al-Razzāq, ʿAbd ibn Ḥumayd, Ibn Jarīr, Ibn Abī Ḥātim, al-Ḥākim in al-Kunā, and Ibn ʿAsākir narrated from Abū Hurayrah, who said: "It is al-Ramlah in Palestine." Ibn Mardawayh narrated from his hadith traced to the Prophet (ﷺ). Then he mentioned a man who prolongs the journey, disheveled and dusty, whose food is unlawful, whose drink is unlawful, whose clothing is unlawful, and who is nourished with the unlawful, raising his hands to the sky: "O Lord, O Lord!" How then is he to be answered?

Saʿīd ibn Manṣūr narrated from Ḥafṣ al-Fazārī regarding His saying ﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾, he said: "That is ʿĪsā ibn Maryam, who ate from the spinning of his mother." ʿAbdān narrated it in al-Ṣaḥābah from Ḥafṣ, traced to the Prophet (ﷺ), and it is mursal, because Ḥafṣ is a Tābiʿī.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 42–56 (part 1 of 2):**

(p-984)
Regarding His words: ﴿Then We brought into being after them other generations﴾, meaning after their destruction. It is said that they were the people of Salih, Lot, and Shu'ayb, as their stories occur in this order in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Hud. It is also said that they were the Children of Israel. The *qurun* (generations) are the nations. Perhaps the reason for the plural *qurun* here, while the singular was used shortly before, is that here He intends multiple nations, whereas there He intended a single nation.

Then Glorified is He, demonstrating His perfect knowledge and power concerning His servants, said: ﴿No nation can outstrip its term, nor can they delay﴾, meaning that no group gathered in a generation can advance its appointed time of destruction that was written for it, nor can it be delayed from it. A similar statement is His Exalted words: ﴿So when their term comes, they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they hasten it﴾ [al-A'raf: 34].

Then Glorified is He explained that after these generations His messengers came in succession, and that the situation of their nations was one of uniform denial of them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Our messengers in succession﴾. The clause is conjoined to the preceding clause, meaning that the sending of each messenger came after the emergence of the generation to which he was sent, not that the sending of all the messengers came after the emergence of all those generations together. The meaning of *tatra* (in succession) is that they came one after another, following one another, from *witr* (singleness). Al-Asma'i said: "I made my books follow one another (*watarta kutubi*): I made some of them follow others, except that between each one and the next there was an interval." Others said: *mutawatira* means consecutive without any interval.

Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Amr (Abu 'Amr) read *tatra* with tanwin (nunation), as a verbal noun. Al-Nahhas said: "On this basis, *tatra* may also be read with a kasra on the first *ta'*, since the meaning of *thumma arsalna* is *watarna* (We made them successive). It may also be in the position of a circumstantial (*hal*) clause, meaning *mutawatirin* (in succession)."

﴿Every time a messenger came to a nation, they denied him﴾. This sentence is a resumptive (*isti'naf*) clause, explaining the coming of each messenger to his nation, with the meaning of "coming" being delivery of the message. ﴿So We caused them to follow one another﴾, meaning in destruction, through the punishment that befell them. ﴿And We made them into tales﴾. *Ahadith* is the plural of *uhdutha*, which is what people speak of, like *a'ajib* (marvels), the plural of *u'juba*, which is what people marvel at.

Al-Akhfash said: "It is only said 'We made them tales' (*ahadith*) in regard to evil, not in regard to good, just as one says, 'So-and-so became a tale' (*hadith*), meaning a lesson, and as He, Glorified, said in another verse: ﴿So We made them tales and scattered them completely﴾ [Saba': 19]."

I say: This universal rule is not accepted, for one may say, "So-and-so became a good tale (*hadith hasan*)," and from this is the statement of Ibn Duraid in his *maqsura*:
"A man is but a tale after him,
so be a good tale for those who narrate."

﴿So away with a people who do not believe﴾. Here He described them with unbelief, while earlier He described them with wrongdoing (*zulm*). This is either because each of the two descriptions was issued by each of the two groups, or because these people only committed the bare act of not confirming, whereas those others added to it those vile statements, which are among the most severe and grievous forms of wrongdoing.

Then Glorified is He related what took place between Pharaoh and his people when Musa and Harun were sent to them, saying: ﴿Then We sent Musa and his brother Harun with Our signs﴾. These are the nine signs mentioned previously more than once. It is not correct to count the splitting of the sea among them here, because what is meant are the signs that they denied and disdained. By *sultan mubin* (a clear authority) is meant the evident, manifest proof. It is said that these are the nine signs themselves, and the conjunction is of the kind of:
"To the king, the lord, and the son of the brave one."
It is also said that He meant the staff, since it is the mother of the signs, and so this is of the kind of the conjunction of Gabriel with the angels. It is also said that by "signs" is meant what they had, and by "clear authority" the evident proofs, namely the nine signs.

By *mala'* (chiefs) in His words ﴿to Pharaoh and his chiefs﴾ is meant their nobles, as has been explained before more than once. ﴿But they were arrogant﴾, meaning they sought haughtiness and affected it, so they did not submit to the truth. ﴿And they were a haughty people﴾, overpowering people through oppression and injustice, dominating them, exalting themselves out of pride, obstinacy and rebellion.

The clause ﴿So they said, "Shall we believe two men like ourselves?"﴾ is conjoined to the clause "they were arrogant," with what lies between them being a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraḍ*). The interrogation is for denial, meaning: how can we confirm one who is like us in humanness? *Bashar* (human) is applied to the singular, as in His words ﴿a perfect human (*basharan sawiyyan*)﴾ [Maryam: 17], and it is also applied to the plural, as in His words ﴿if you see any human (*al-bashar*) at all﴾. So its dual here is according to the first meaning. He used the singular *mithl* (like) because it has the force of a verbal noun. The meaning of ﴿and their people are worshippers of us﴾ is that they are obedient to them, submitting to what they command them, like the submission of slaves. Al-Mubarrad said: "*Abid* (worshipper) means the obedient, the humbled." Abu 'Ubayda said: "The Arabs call everyone who submits to a king a worshipper of him." It is also said that it is possible he claimed divinity and called people to worship him, and they obeyed him. The *lam* in *lana* (to us) is connected to *abidun* (worshippers), placed before it for the sake of the rhyme-endings (*fawasil*), and the clause is circumstantial.

﴿So they denied them both﴾, meaning they persisted in denying them. ﴿So they were among those destroyed﴾ by drowning in the sea.

Then Glorified is He related what happened to the people of Musa after the destruction of their enemy, saying: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book﴾, meaning the Torah. Musa was singled out for mention because the Torah was revealed to him on the mountain, and Harun was his deputy among his people. ﴿That perhaps they might be guided﴾, meaning that perhaps the people of Musa would be guided by it to the truth and act upon the laws within it. Thus Glorified is He made Musa's receipt of it a giving to his people, since although it was revealed to Musa, it was for guiding his people. It is also said that there is an omitted *mudaf* (genitive construction), and the *mudaf ilayh* (the second term) was put in its place, meaning: "We gave the people of Musa the Book." It is also said that the pronoun in *la'allahum* (perhaps they) refers to Pharaoh and his chiefs, but this is an error, because Musa was not given the Torah except after the destruction of Pharaoh and his people, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿And We indeed gave Musa the Book after We had destroyed the former generations﴾ [al-Qasas: 43].

(p-985)
Then Glorified is He alluded briefly to the story of 'Isa, saying: ﴿And We made the son of Maryam and his mother a sign﴾, meaning a sign indicating the greatness of Our power and the wondrous nature of Our making. The discussion of this has already been presented at the end of Surat al-Anbiya' in the exegesis of His words: ﴿And We made her and her son a sign for the worlds﴾ [al-Anbiya': 91]. The meaning of His words ﴿and We sheltered them on a high ground﴾ is: to an elevated place, meaning We made them take refuge in it.

It is said that it is the land of Damascus, and this was said by 'Abdullah ibn Salam, Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab and Muqatil. It is also said that it is Bayt al-Maqdis (Jerusalem), as said by Qatada and Ka'b. It is also said that it is the land of Palestine, as said by al-Suddi. ﴿A place of settlement﴾, meaning a place of stability upon which its inhabitants settle, ﴿and running water (*ma'in*)﴾, meaning flowing water.

Al-Zajjaj said: "It is water flowing in springs, so the *mim* in this case is an augmentative, like its augmentation in *manba'* (source)." It is also said that *ma'in* is *fa'il* in the sense of *maf'ul* (passive). 'Ali ibn Sulayman al-Akhfash said: "The meaning of water when it flows is *ma'in* and *mamun*." Ibn al-A'rabi said likewise. It is also said that it is derived from *ma'un* (help, benefit), which is benefit, and Al-Farra' said the same as al-Zajjaj.

﴿O messengers, eat of the good things﴾. Al-Zajjaj said: "This address is to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), and the plural indicates that all the messengers were commanded likewise." It is also said that this address was made to every prophet, because this is their way, which they should follow, so the meaning is: "And We said, O messengers," addressing each one individually, due to the difference of their times. Ibn Jarir said that the address was to 'Isa.

Al-Farra' said: "It is like saying to one man, 'Stop from us.'" The *tayyibat* (good things) are what is found agreeable and pleasant. It is also said that they are the lawful, and it is also said that they are what combines the two descriptions mentioned.

Then, after commanding them to eat of the good things, He commanded them to do righteous deeds, saying: ﴿And do righteous deeds﴾, meaning a righteous deed, which is what conforms to the Law. Then He gave the reason for this command by His words: ﴿Indeed I am All-Knowing of what you do﴾, nothing of it being hidden from Me, and I will recompense you according to your deeds: if good, then good, and if evil, then evil.

﴿And indeed this community of yours is one community﴾. This is part of what was addressed to the prophets. The meaning is: this is your religion and your law, O messengers, a single religion and a unified law, comprising one principle, which is the greatest thing God sent His prophets with and revealed His books concerning: calling all the prophets to the worship of God, without partner.

It is also said that the meaning is: this which has been mentioned is your religion and your creed, so adhere to it, taking *ummah* here to mean religion, as in His words: ﴿Indeed we found our fathers following a religion (*ummah*)﴾ [al-Zukhruf: 22]. From this is the statement of al-Nabigha:
"I swore, and I left you no doubt,
and does one who follows a religion (*ummah*) sin while being obedient?"

*Inna* is read with a kasra, as a resumptive clause confirming what preceded it, and it is read with a fatha and doubled *nun*.

Al-Khalil said: "It is in the position of an accusative, since the governing preposition has been removed, meaning: I know that this is your religion, which I commanded you to believe in."

Al-Farra' said: "*Inna* is connected to a hidden verb, and its estimate is: 'And know that this is your community.'" Sibawayh said: "It is connected to *ittaqun* (fear Me), and the estimate is: 'So fear Me, because your community is one community.'" The *fa'* in *fattaqun* is for the ordering of the command to fear God upon what precedes it, namely that He is your Lord, exclusively possessing lordship. That is: do not do what would make punishment incumbent upon you from Me, by associating others with Me, or by opposing what I have commanded you or forbidden you.

Then Glorified is He mentioned what the nations did in opposing what the messengers commanded them, saying: ﴿But they cut their affair among themselves into sects (*zuburan*)﴾. The *fa'* indicates the ordering of their disobedience upon what preceded of the command to fear God. The pronoun refers to what the word "community" indicates, and the meaning is that they made their religion, despite its unity, into scattered and divergent pieces.

Al-Mubarrad said: "*Zuburan* means factions and divergent pieces; its singular is *zabur*, which is a faction and a group. Similar is *zubra*, whose plural is *zubur*." So Glorified is He described the nations as having differed. One faction followed the Torah, one the Psalms (*Zabur*), and one the Gospel, and then they distorted and altered, and one faction of polytheists followed what their fathers had laid down for them of error.

*Zuburan* is read with a damma on the *ba'*, as the plural of *zabur*, and it is read with a fatha, meaning pieces like pieces of iron. ﴿Each faction rejoicing in what they have﴾, meaning each group of these divergent people rejoices in what they possess, namely the religion they have, that is, they are pleased with it.

﴿So leave them in their confusion for a time﴾, meaning leave them in their ignorance, for they are not fit for guidance, and do not let your breast be constricted by the delay of the punishment from them, for everything has its time. Glorified is He likened what they are in of ignorance to water that overwhelms whoever enters it. *Ghamra* originally means that which covers and overtops you, and its origin is concealment. *Ghamr* is abundant water, because it covers the earth. *Ghamr al-ridа'* (the abundance of the cloak) is that which embraces people with gifts, and *ghamr* is said of resentment. What is meant here is confusion, heedlessness and error. The verse comes as a threat to them, not as a command to the Prophet (ﷺ) to refrain from them. *Hatta hin* (until a time) means until the time of their punishment by killing arrives, or until they die in disbelief and are punished in the Fire.

﴿Do they think that what We extend to them of wealth and children﴾, meaning: do they think that what We give them in this world of wealth and children, which We hasten to them in that wherein is their good and honour, [is ...]? The interrogative particle is for denial, and the answer to this is implied, indicated by His words: ﴿Nay, they do not perceive﴾, since it is conjoined to an implied clause to which the discourse extends, meaning: "Certainly not, We do not do that; rather, they do not perceive anything at all, like the beasts that do not understand or reason." For what We have bestowed upon them of blessings and what We have extended to them of good things is only a gradual leading on for them, so that they may increase in sin, as He, Glorified, said: ﴿We only give them respite so that they may increase in sin﴾ [Al 'Imran: 178].

Al-Zajjaj said: The meaning is "We hasten for them with it into good things," so "with it" (bihi) is omitted, and the "mā" in innamā is a relative pronoun (mawsūlah), and the linking element (al-rābiṭ) is this omitted word.

Al-Kisā'ī said: Here innamā (inna-mā) is a single particle, so it does not need an estimated linking element.

It was said that it is permissible to pause (waqf) on "banīn" (sons). It was also said that it is not good, because yaḥsabūna (they think) requires two objects, and the completion of the two objects is "in the good things." Ibn al-Anbārī said: This is an error, because mā is a kāffah (a particle that "restrains" inna from governing, i.e., it is not a relative pronoun).
