The meaning is: you will not be protected from Our punishment, and your lamentation will not benefit you.

It has been said that the meaning is: no help will reach you from Our side that would prevent you from the punishment that has overtaken you.

Then He, glory be to Him, enumerated their ugly deeds against them as rebuke, saying: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels﴾. That is, in the world, and they are the verses of the Qur'an. ﴿You turned back on your heels﴾ means you went backward behind you. The root of *al-nukūs* is to return backward, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"They claim they are on the paths of truth, while we are those who turned back on our heels."*

Here it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for turning away from the truth. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib read *ʿalā adbārikum* (on your backs) in place of *ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn*, with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*. The phrase *ʿalā aʿqābikum* is connected to *tankiṣūn*, or is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from the subject of *tankiṣūn*.

﴿Acting arrogantly by it﴾. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Sacred House (*al-bayt al-ʿatīq*). It has been said that it refers to the Sacred Precinct (*al-ḥaram*). What permitted the pronoun before mention is their well-known arrogance concerning it and their boasting of its guardianship and service to it. They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Sacred Precinct and its servants." To this view the majority of the exegetes went. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The meaning is that hearing it produces in them arrogance and insolence, so they do not believe in it. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is a good view."

(p-988) Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is preferable, and he clarified it with what we have mentioned."

According to the first view, *bihi* is connected to *mustakbirīn* (arrogant). According to the second view, it is connected to *sāmiran* (talking at night), because they used to gather around the House at night conversing, and most of their conversation was mention of the Qur'an and slander against it. *Al-sāmir* is like *al-ḥāḍir* in its use for a group.

Al-Wahidi said: "*Al-sāmir* is the group who converse at night, that is, they talk." It is permissible to connect it to *tahjurūn* (you talk nonsense). *Al-hajr* with a *fatḥah* means raving, that is, you rave concerning the Qur'an. It is also permissible that it derives from *al-hujr* with a *ḍammah*, which means obscenity.

Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywah read *summaran* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn* and a *fatḥah* on the *mīm* with shadda. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Abu Raja' read *samaran*, and this reading is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The accusative of *sāmiran* is a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of *tankiṣūn*, or from the pronoun in *mustakbirīn*. It has been said that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that came in the form of the active participle, as one says *qawmun sāmir* (a talking people). From this is the verse of the poet:

*"As if there had not been between al-Ḥajun and al-Ṣafa any companion, and no one had talked in Makkah at night."*

Al-Raghib said: "It is said *sāmir* and *summār*, and *sumr* and *sāmirūn*."

The majority read *tahjurūn* with a *fatḥah* on the upper *tā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *jīm*. Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *jīm*, from *ahjara*, meaning: he spoke obscenely in his speech. Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Nahik read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, a *fatḥah* on the *hā'*, and a shadda on the *kasrah* of the *jīm*, as the present tense of *hajjara*. Ibn Abi ʿAsim read it like the majority, except that it is with the lower *yā'*, and in it there is an *iltifāt* (shift from direct address to third-person reference).

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya (in *Na't al-Khā'ifīn*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (in *al-Shu'ab*) narrated from 'Ā'ishah, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, regarding the saying of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the man who steals, commits fornication, and drinks wine, and yet fears Allah?' He said, 'No, rather it is the man who fasts, gives charity, and prays, and yet fears that Allah will not accept it from him.'"

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Anbari (in *al-Masahif*, the codices of the Qur'an), Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'O Messenger of Allah,' and he mentioned something similar."

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "They give what they have been given."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾, that he said: "They act while fearful."

al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "The zakah (obligatory alms)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ā'ishah concerning (And those who give what they give), that she said: "They are those who fear Allah and obey Him."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'For this verse to be as I recite it would be dearer to me than red camels.' Ibn 'Abbas said to her, 'What is it?' She said, '(Those who give what they give).'" We have already mentioned its recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) and its meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from her, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited (Those who give what they give) *maqsuran* (with the initial long vowel shortened, i.e., without the madd), from *al-maji'* (the coming).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umar that he asked 'Ā'ishah: "How did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾?" She said, "Which of the two do you prefer?" I said, "By the One in whose hand is my soul, one of them is dearer to me than this world and everything in it combined." She said, "Which one?" I said, "﴿And those who give what they give﴾." She said, "I testify that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it that way, and that is how it was revealed, but *al-hijā'* (the orthography, i.e., the written form) is a letter (a variant of spelling)." Its chain contains Isma'il ibn 'Ali, who is weak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Those hasten toward the good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾, that he said: "Happiness from Allah preceded them."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾, that by *al-ghamrah* (confusion) he meant disbelief and doubt. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾, he said: "Evil deeds other than shirk (associating partners with Allah)." ﴿They will be doing them﴾, he said: "They must do them."

al-Nasa'i narrated from him concerning ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾, that he said: "They are the people of Badr." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿Then, when they cry out﴾, that he said: "They cry for help." And concerning His saying, ﴿You used to turn back on your heels﴾, he said: "You would turn away." And concerning His saying, ﴿Conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, he said: "They would gather around the House (the Ka'bah) at night and say *hujr* (abuse, nonsense)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, concerning ﴿conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, that he said: "The Quraysh used to sit in circles, talking around the House."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, and said: 'The polytheists would abuse the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with speech in their evening gatherings.'"

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Evening conversation was only disliked when this verse was revealed: ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 57–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, negated true goods from the disbelievers who lived in luxury, He followed that with mention of those who deserve goods, both in this world and the next. He described them with four attributes. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive of the fear of their Lord﴾. *Al-Ishfaq* (apprehension) means fear. You say, "I am *mushfiq* (apprehensive) of this matter," meaning: I fear it.

It has been said that *al-ishfaq* is the same as *al-khashyah* (awe, dread), so on the surface the verse is repetitive.

It has been answered by taking *al-khashyah* to mean the punishment: that is, they fear the punishment of their Lord. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

It has also been answered by taking *al-ishfaq* to mean what results from it, which is persistence in obedience. The meaning would then be: those who, out of fear of their Lord, are persistent in obeying Him.

It has also been answered that *al-ishfaq* is the perfection of fear, so there is no repetition. It has also been said that it is repetition for emphasis.

The second attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. It has been said that the signs here are the revealed ones (*al-tanziliyyah*), and it has been said that they are the created ones (*al-takwiniyyah*), and it has been said that they are both together. It has been said that belief in them does not mean merely affirming that they are evidences and that what they signify is true.

The third attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who do not associate partners with their Lord﴾, that is, they abandon association (*shirk*) completely, outwardly and inwardly.

The fourth attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord﴾. That is, they give what they give while their hearts are fearful on account of that giving, thinking that it will not save them from the punishment of Allah. The clause ﴿while their hearts are fearful﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while their hearts are in a state of extreme fear.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord. The cause of the trembling is that they fear their giving will not be accepted in the required manner, not merely their return to Him, glory be to Him."

It has also been said that the meaning is: whoever believes in the return to recompense and reckoning, and knows that the one who recompenses and reckons is the Lord from whom nothing is hidden, will not be free of trembling.

ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi read *ya'tūna mā ataw* (they do what they did) with a short alif, from *al-ityān* (coming/doing).

Al-Farra' said: "Even if this reading is sound, it does not contradict the reading of the majority, because some Arabs always keep the alif in the hamza in all cases."

Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning of this reading is: they do what they did."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "They compete for them." It has been said: "They race for them." It is also read *yusrīʿūna* (they hasten).

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾: the *lām* (in *lahā*) is for emphasis (*lil-taqwiyah*). The meaning is: they are foremost in reaching them. It has been said that the *lām* carries the sense of *ilā* (to), as in His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], meaning: inspired to it. Sibawayh cited the verse of the poet:

*"Turn aside from the people of Yamamah, O youth, and what you intended from them is other than yourself."*

meaning: toward your other. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the sense is: they are foremost over people for their sake.

Then, when the discussion turned to the deeds of the obligated, He mentioned two rulings concerning them. The first is His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity﴾. *Al-wus'* is capacity, and the explanation of this was given earlier at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. There are two views on interpreting *al-wus'*. The first is that it is capacity, as the lexicographers explained it. The second is that it is less than capacity; this is the view of Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The Mu'tazilah said: since *al-wus'* is so named because the act of its doer is spacious for him and does not constrain him, whoever cannot sit should pray by gesture, and whoever cannot fast should break the fast.

This sentence is a new independent clause (*mustaʾnafah*), urging the pursuit of acts of obedience that lead to honor, which were mentioned in describing the foremost, by explaining how easy they are and that they do not exceed the limit of capacity and ability. It also shows that this is Allah's custom with His servants in imposing obligations. The clause ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth﴾ completes what precedes it, negating obligation beyond capacity. The Book here means the records of deeds: that is, with Us is a Book in which the deeds of every obligated person have been recorded as they are. The meaning of ﴿speaks with truth﴾ is that the truth that corresponds to reality is made manifest through it, without addition or deficiency. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿This is Our Book; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾. In this there is a warning to the disobedient and reassurance to the obedient against injustice and oppression.

It has been said that the Book here means the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), since everything is written in it.

It has been said that the Book here means the Qur'an, but the first view is preferable.

The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ explains what precedes it, namely His bounty and justice in recompensing His servants: they will not be wronged by a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

Ibn Abi ʿAsim read it like the majority, except that it is with the lower *yā'*, and in it there is an *iltifāt* (shift from direct address to third-person reference).

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya (in *Na't al-Khā'ifīn*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (in *al-Shu'ab*) narrated from 'Ā'ishah, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, regarding the saying of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the man who steals, commits fornication, and drinks wine, and yet fears Allah?' He said, 'No, rather it is the man who fasts, gives charity, and prays, and yet fears that Allah will not accept it from him.'"

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Anbari (in *al-Masahif*, the codices of the Qur'an), Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'O Messenger of Allah,' and he mentioned something similar."

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "They give what they have been given."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾, that he said: "They act while fearful."

al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "The zakah (obligatory alms)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ā'ishah concerning (And those who give what they give), that she said: "They are those who fear Allah and obey Him."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'For this verse to be as I recite it would be dearer to me than red camels.' Ibn 'Abbas said to her, 'What is it?' She said, '(Those who give what they give).'" We have already mentioned its recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) and its meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from her, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited (Those who give what they give) *maqsuran* (with the initial long vowel shortened, i.e., without the madd), from *al-maji'* (the coming).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umar that he asked 'Ā'ishah: "How did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾?" She said, "Which of the two do you prefer?" I said, "By the One in whose hand is my soul, one of them is dearer to me than this world and everything in it combined." She said, "Which one?" I said, "﴿And those who give what they give﴾." She said, "I testify that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it that way, and that is how it was revealed, but *al-hijā'* (the orthography, i.e., the written form) is a letter (a variant of spelling)." Its chain contains Isma'il ibn 'Ali, who is weak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Those hasten toward the good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾, that he said: "Happiness from Allah preceded them."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾, that by *al-ghamrah* (confusion) he meant disbelief and doubt. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾, he said: "Evil deeds other than shirk (associating partners with Allah)." ﴿They will be doing them﴾, he said: "They must do them."

al-Nasa'i narrated from him concerning ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾, that he said: "They are the people of Badr." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿Then, when they cry out﴾, that he said: "They cry for help." And concerning His saying, ﴿You used to turn back on your heels﴾, he said: "You would turn away." And concerning His saying, ﴿Conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, he said: "They would gather around the House (the Ka'bah) at night and say *hujr* (abuse, nonsense)."

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Evening conversation was only disliked when this verse was revealed: ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 57–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, negated true goods from the disbelievers who lived in luxury, He followed that with mention of those who deserve goods, both in this world and the next. He described them with four attributes. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive of the fear of their Lord﴾. *Al-Ishfaq* (apprehension) means fear. You say, "I am *mushfiq* (apprehensive) of this matter," meaning: I fear it.

It has been said that *al-ishfaq* is the same as *al-khashyah* (awe, dread), so on the surface the verse is repetitive.

It has been answered by taking *al-khashyah* to mean the punishment: that is, they fear the punishment of their Lord. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

It has also been answered by taking *al-ishfaq* to mean what results from it, which is persistence in obedience. The meaning would then be: those who, out of fear of their Lord, are persistent in obeying Him.

It has also been answered that *al-ishfaq* is the perfection of fear, so there is no repetition. It has also been said that it is repetition for emphasis.

The second attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. It has been said that the signs here are the revealed ones (*al-tanziliyyah*), and it has been said that they are the created ones (*al-takwiniyyah*), and it has been said that they are both together. It has been said that belief in them does not mean merely affirming that they are evidences and that what they signify is true.

The third attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who do not associate partners with their Lord﴾, that is, they abandon association (*shirk*) completely, outwardly and inwardly.

The fourth attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord﴾. That is, they give what they give while their hearts are fearful on account of that giving, thinking that it will not save them from the punishment of Allah. The clause ﴿while their hearts are fearful﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while their hearts are in a state of extreme fear.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord. The cause of the trembling is that they fear their giving will not be accepted in the required manner, not merely their return to Him, glory be to Him."

It has also been said that the meaning is: whoever believes in the return to recompense and reckoning, and knows that the one who recompenses and reckons is the Lord from whom nothing is hidden, will not be free of trembling.

ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi read *ya'tūna mā ataw* (they do what they did) with a short alif, from *al-ityān* (coming/doing).

Al-Farra' said: "Even if this reading is sound, it does not contradict the reading of the majority, because some Arabs always keep the alif in the hamza in all cases."

Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning of this reading is: they do what they did."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "They compete for them." It has been said: "They race for them." It is also read *yusrīʿūna* (they hasten).

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾: the *lām* (in *lahā*) is for emphasis (*lil-taqwiyah*). The meaning is: they are foremost in reaching them. It has been said that the *lām* carries the sense of *ilā* (to), as in His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], meaning: inspired to it. Sibawayh cited the verse of the poet:

*"Turn aside from the people of Yamamah, O youth, and what you intended from them is other than yourself."*

meaning: toward your other. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the sense is: they are foremost over people for their sake.

Then, when the discussion turned to the deeds of the obligated, He mentioned two rulings concerning them. The first is His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity﴾. *Al-wus'* is capacity, and the explanation of this was given earlier at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. There are two views on interpreting *al-wus'*. The first is that it is capacity, as the lexicographers explained it. The second is that it is less than capacity; this is the view of Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The Mu'tazilah said: since *al-wus'* is so named because the act of its doer is spacious for him and does not constrain him, whoever cannot sit should pray by gesture, and whoever cannot fast should break the fast.

This sentence is a new independent clause (*mustaʾnafah*), urging the pursuit of acts of obedience that lead to honor, which were mentioned in describing the foremost, by explaining how easy they are and that they do not exceed the limit of capacity and ability. It also shows that this is Allah's custom with His servants in imposing obligations. The clause ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth﴾ completes what precedes it, negating obligation beyond capacity. The Book here means the records of deeds: that is, with Us is a Book in which the deeds of every obligated person have been recorded as they are. The meaning of ﴿speaks with truth﴾ is that the truth that corresponds to reality is made manifest through it, without addition or deficiency. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿This is Our Book; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾. In this there is a warning to the disobedient and reassurance to the obedient against injustice and oppression.

It has been said that the Book here means the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), since everything is written in it.

It has been said that the Book here means the Qur'an, but the first view is preferable.

In this verse there is a comparison of the Book to one from whom clear speech issues by his tongue, since the Book expresses what is in it just as a truthful speaker does. The phrase ﴿with truth﴾ is connected to *yantiqu* (speaks), or to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: it speaks while combined with truth. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ explains what precedes it, namely His bounty and justice in recompensing His servants: they will not be wronged by a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

Then He turned away from this and said: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers. That is: rather, the hearts of the disbelievers are in an overwhelming confusion concerning this Book which speaks with truth, or concerning the matter upon which the believers are. It is said: *ghamarahu al-ma'* (the water overwhelmed him) when it covered him, and *nahr ghamr* (a deep river) is one that covers whoever enters it. What is meant here is covering, heedlessness, or bewilderment and blindness. The discussion of *al-ghamrah* was given shortly before.

﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾. Qatadah and Mujahid said: that is, they have sins which they must commit apart from the truth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that they have evil deeds which they have not yet done, apart from what they are upon, which they must do, and by which they will enter the Fire. So the demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers either to the deeds of the believers or to the deeds of the disbelievers. That is: they have deeds beyond the deeds of the believers which Allah mentioned, or beyond the deeds of the disbelievers mentioned earlier, namely that their hearts are in great heedlessness of what has been mentioned. These are the varieties of their disbelief and disobedience, among which is what will come later of their slander against the Qur'an.

Al-Wahidi said: "The consensus of the exegetes and the scholars of meanings is that this is a report about what they will do of their evil deeds, which were written against them, and which they must do. The clause ﴿they are doing them﴾ confirms what precedes it, meaning: it is obligatory upon them to do them, and so they will enter the Fire because of what was previously decreed for them of wretchedness, and there is no escape for them from that."

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to describing the disbelievers and said: ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾. The particle *ḥattā* (until) here is the one after which speech begins, and the speech is the conditional clause mentioned. This clause explains what precedes it. The pronoun in *mutrafīhim* (their affluent ones) refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier. The meaning of *al-mutrafīn* (the affluent) is those among them who lived in luxury, namely those whom Allah provided for with the wealth and children mentioned earlier, or the meaning is their leaders. The punishment means their punishment by the sword on the day of Badr, or by hunger, through the supplication of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him and his family), when he said: "O Allah, make Your foot heavy upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Yusuf."

It has been said that the punishment means the punishment of the Hereafter. This is preferred because what issues from them of *al-ju'ar* (crying out) occurs at the punishment of the Hereafter, since it is seeking help from Allah, and such a thing did not occur from them on the day of Badr or in the years of hunger. It is answered that *al-ju'ar* in the language means shouting and screaming. Al-Jawhari said: "*Al-ju'ar* is like *al-khuwar* (bellowing); it is said: *ja'ara al-thawr* (the bull bellowed), meaning it cried out." This has occurred from them, and from their families and children, when they were punished by the sword on the day of Badr, and by hunger in the years of hunger. The *ju'ar* here is not restricted to the crying out that is supplication, so as to complete what that speaker mentioned.

The clause ﴿when they are crying out﴾ is the answer to the condition, and *idhā* here is the sudden *idhā* (*idhā al-fujā'iyyah*). The meaning is: until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, they cry out with screaming.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed that they will be told at that time, as a rebuke: ﴿Do not cry out today﴾. The speech is implicitly introduced by a verb of saying, and the sentence is directed to rebuke them, make them despair, and cut off their hopes. Allah specified the affluent ones, although the punishment reaches all of them, both affluent and non-affluent, to show that after the blessing they had been in, they became in a state contrary to and opposite to it, moving from complete ease to pure wretchedness. *Al-yawm* (today) is singled out for mention to intensify the horror. The clause ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾ gives the reason for the prohibition against crying out. The meaning is: you will not be protected from Our punishment, and your lamentation will not benefit you.

It has been said that the meaning is: no help will reach you from Our side that would prevent you from the punishment that has overtaken you.

Then He, glory be to Him, enumerated their ugly deeds against them as rebuke, saying: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels﴾. That is, in the world, and they are the verses of the Qur'an. ﴿You turned back on your heels﴾ means you went backward behind you. The root of *al-nukūs* is to return backward, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"They claim they are on the paths of truth, while we are those who turned back on our heels."*

Here it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for turning away from the truth. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib read *ʿalā adbārikum* (on your backs) in place of *ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn*, with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*. The phrase *ʿalā aʿqābikum* is connected to *tankiṣūn*, or is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from the subject of *tankiṣūn*.

﴿Acting arrogantly by it﴾. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Sacred House (*al-bayt al-ʿatīq*). It has been said that it refers to the Sacred Precinct (*al-ḥaram*). What permitted the pronoun before mention is their well-known arrogance concerning it and their boasting of its guardianship and service to it. They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Sacred Precinct and its servants." To this view the majority of the exegetes went. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The meaning is that hearing it produces in them arrogance and insolence, so they do not believe in it. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is a good view."

(p-988) Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is preferable, and he clarified it with what we have mentioned."

According to the first view, *bihi* is connected to *mustakbirīn* (arrogant). According to the second view, it is connected to *sāmiran* (talking at night), because they used to gather around the House at night conversing, and most of their conversation was mention of the Qur'an and slander against it. *Al-sāmir* is like *al-ḥāḍir* in its use for a group.

Al-Wahidi said: "*Al-sāmir* is the group who converse at night, that is, they talk." It is permissible to connect it to *tahjurūn* (you talk nonsense). *Al-hajr* with a *fatḥah* means raving, that is, you rave concerning the Qur'an. It is also permissible that it derives from *al-hujr* with a *ḍammah*, which means obscenity.

Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywah read *summaran* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn* and a *fatḥah* on the *mīm* with shadda. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Abu Raja' read *samaran*, and this reading is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The accusative of *sāmiran* is a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of *tankiṣūn*, or from the pronoun in *mustakbirīn*. It has been said that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that came in the form of the active participle, as one says *qawmun sāmir* (a talking people). From this is the verse of the poet:

*"As if there had not been between al-Ḥajun and al-Ṣafa any companion, and no one had talked in Makkah at night."*

Al-Raghib said: "It is said *sāmir* and *summār*, and *sumr* and *sāmirūn*."

The majority read *tahjurūn* with a *fatḥah* on the upper *tā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *jīm*. Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *jīm*, from *ahjara*, meaning: he spoke obscenely in his speech. Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Nahik read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, a *fatḥah* on the *hā'*, and a shadda on the *kasrah* of the *jīm*, as the present tense of *hajjara*. The fourth attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord﴾. That is, they give what they give while their hearts are fearful on account of that giving, thinking that it will not save them from the punishment of Allah. The clause ﴿while their hearts are fearful﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while their hearts are in a state of extreme fear.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord. The cause of the trembling is that they fear their giving will not be accepted in the required manner, not merely their return to Him, glory be to Him."

It has also been said that the meaning is: whoever believes in the return to recompense and reckoning, and knows that the one who recompenses and reckons is the Lord from whom nothing is hidden, will not be free of trembling.

ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi read *ya'tūna mā ataw* (they do what they did) with a short alif, from *al-ityān* (coming/doing).

Al-Farra' said: "Even if this reading is sound, it does not contradict the reading of the majority, because some Arabs always keep the alif in the hamza in all cases."

Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning of this reading is: they do what they did."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "They compete for them." It has been said: "They race for them." It is also read *yusrīʿūna* (they hasten).

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾: the *lām* (in *lahā*) is for emphasis (*lil-taqwiyah*). The meaning is: they are foremost in reaching them. It has been said that the *lām* carries the sense of *ilā* (to), as in His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], meaning: inspired to it. Sibawayh cited the verse of the poet:

meaning: toward your other. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the sense is: they are foremost over people for their sake.

Then, when the discussion turned to the deeds of the obligated, He mentioned two rulings concerning them. The first is His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity﴾. *Al-wus'* is capacity, and the explanation of this was given earlier at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. The second is that it is less than capacity; this is the view of Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The meaning of ﴿speaks with truth﴾ is that the truth that corresponds to reality is made manifest through it, without addition or deficiency. In this there is a warning to the disobedient and reassurance to the obedient against injustice and oppression.

It has been said that the Book here means the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), since everything is written in it.

It has been said that the Book here means the Qur'an, but the first view is preferable.

The phrase ﴿with truth﴾ is connected to *yantiqu* (speaks), or to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: it speaks while combined with truth. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ explains what precedes it, namely His bounty and justice in recompensing His servants: they will not be wronged by a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

Then He turned away from this and said: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers. That is: rather, the hearts of the disbelievers are in an overwhelming confusion concerning this Book which speaks with truth, or concerning the matter upon which the believers are. It is said: *ghamarahu al-ma'* (the water overwhelmed him) when it covered him, and *nahr ghamr* (a deep river) is one that covers whoever enters it. What is meant here is covering, heedlessness, or bewilderment and blindness. The discussion of *al-ghamrah* was given shortly before.

﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾. Qatadah and Mujahid said: that is, they have sins which they must commit apart from the truth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that they have evil deeds which they have not yet done, apart from what they are upon, which they must do, and by which they will enter the Fire. So the demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers either to the deeds of the believers or to the deeds of the disbelievers. That is: they have deeds beyond the deeds of the believers which Allah mentioned, or beyond the deeds of the disbelievers mentioned earlier, namely that their hearts are in great heedlessness of what has been mentioned. These are the varieties of their disbelief and disobedience, among which is what will come later of their slander against the Qur'an.

Al-Wahidi said: "The consensus of the exegetes and the scholars of meanings is that this is a report about what they will do of their evil deeds, which were written against them, and which they must do. The clause ﴿they are doing them﴾ confirms what precedes it, meaning: it is obligatory upon them to do them, and so they will enter the Fire because of what was previously decreed for them of wretchedness, and there is no escape for them from that."

Then He, glory be to Him, returned to describing the disbelievers and said: ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾. The particle *ḥattā* (until) here is the one after which speech begins, and the speech is the conditional clause mentioned. This clause explains what precedes it. The pronoun in *mutrafīhim* (their affluent ones) refers to the disbelievers mentioned earlier. The meaning of *al-mutrafīn* (the affluent) is those among them who lived in luxury, namely those whom Allah provided for with the wealth and children mentioned earlier, or the meaning is their leaders. The punishment means their punishment by the sword on the day of Badr, or by hunger, through the supplication of the Prophet (peace and blessings be upon him and his family), when he said: "O Allah, make Your foot heavy upon Mudar, and make for them years like the years of Yusuf."

It has been said that the punishment means the punishment of the Hereafter. This is preferred because what issues from them of *al-ju'ar* (crying out) occurs at the punishment of the Hereafter, since it is seeking help from Allah, and such a thing did not occur from them on the day of Badr or in the years of hunger. It is answered that *al-ju'ar* in the language means shouting and screaming. Al-Jawhari said: "*Al-ju'ar* is like *al-khuwar* (bellowing); it is said: *ja'ara al-thawr* (the bull bellowed), meaning it cried out." This has occurred from them, and from their families and children, when they were punished by the sword on the day of Badr, and by hunger in the years of hunger. The *ju'ar* here is not restricted to the crying out that is supplication, so as to complete what that speaker mentioned.

The clause ﴿when they are crying out﴾ is the answer to the condition, and *idhā* here is the sudden *idhā* (*idhā al-fujā'iyyah*). The meaning is: until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment, they cry out with screaming.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed that they will be told at that time, as a rebuke: ﴿Do not cry out today﴾. The speech is implicitly introduced by a verb of saying, and the sentence is directed to rebuke them, make them despair, and cut off their hopes. Allah specified the affluent ones, although the punishment reaches all of them, both affluent and non-affluent, to show that after the blessing they had been in, they became in a state contrary to and opposite to it, moving from complete ease to pure wretchedness. *Al-yawm* (today) is singled out for mention to intensify the horror. The clause ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾ gives the reason for the prohibition against crying out. The meaning is: you will not be protected from Our punishment, and your lamentation will not benefit you.

It has been said that the meaning is: no help will reach you from Our side that would prevent you from the punishment that has overtaken you.

That is, in the world, and they are the verses of the Qur'an. ﴿You turned back on your heels﴾ means you went backward behind you. The root of *al-nukūs* is to return backward, and from this is the verse of the poet:

*"They claim they are on the paths of truth, while we are those who turned back on our heels."*

Here it is a metaphor (*isti'arah*) for turning away from the truth. ʿAli ibn Abi Talib read *ʿalā adbārikum* (on your backs) in place of *ʿalā aʿqābikum tankiṣūn*, with a *ḍammah* on the *kāf*. The phrase *ʿalā aʿqābikum* is connected to *tankiṣūn*, or is connected to an omitted element that functions as a circumstantial clause from the subject of *tankiṣūn*.

﴿Acting arrogantly by it﴾. The pronoun in *bihi* refers to the Sacred House (*al-bayt al-ʿatīq*). It has been said that it refers to the Sacred Precinct (*al-ḥaram*). What permitted the pronoun before mention is their well-known arrogance concerning it and their boasting of its guardianship and service to it. They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Sacred Precinct and its servants." To this view the majority of the exegetes went. It has been said that the pronoun refers to the Qur'an. The meaning is that hearing it produces in them arrogance and insolence, so they do not believe in it. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is a good view."

(p-988) Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is preferable, and he clarified it with what we have mentioned."

According to the first view, *bihi* is connected to *mustakbirīn* (arrogant). According to the second view, it is connected to *sāmiran* (talking at night), because they used to gather around the House at night conversing, and most of their conversation was mention of the Qur'an and slander against it. *Al-sāmir* is like *al-ḥāḍir* in its use for a group.

Al-Wahidi said: "*Al-sāmir* is the group who converse at night, that is, they talk." It is permissible to connect it to *tahjurūn* (you talk nonsense). *Al-hajr* with a *fatḥah* means raving, that is, you rave concerning the Qur'an. It is also permissible that it derives from *al-hujr* with a *ḍammah*, which means obscenity.

Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywah read *summaran* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn* and a *fatḥah* on the *mīm* with shadda. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Abu Raja' read *samaran*, and this reading is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The accusative of *sāmiran* is a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of *tankiṣūn*, or from the pronoun in *mustakbirīn*. It has been said that it is a verbal noun (*maṣdar*) that came in the form of the active participle, as one says *qawmun sāmir* (a talking people). From this is the verse of the poet:

*"As if there had not been between al-Ḥajun and al-Ṣafa any companion, and no one had talked in Makkah at night."*

Al-Raghib said: "It is said *sāmir* and *summār*, and *sumr* and *sāmirūn*."

The majority read *tahjurūn* with a *fatḥah* on the upper *tā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *jīm*. Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *jīm*, from *ahjara*, meaning: he spoke obscenely in his speech. Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Nahik read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, a *fatḥah* on the *hā'*, and a shadda on the *kasrah* of the *jīm*, as the present tense of *hajjara*. Ibn Abi ʿAsim read it like the majority, except that it is with the lower *yā'*, and in it there is an *iltifāt* (shift from direct address to third-person reference).

Al-Firyabi, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, Ibn Majah, and Ibn Abi al-Dunya (in *Na't al-Khā'ifīn*), Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi (in *al-Shu'ab*) narrated from 'Ā'ishah, who said: "I said, 'O Messenger of Allah, regarding the saying of Allah, ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful﴾, is it the man who steals, commits fornication, and drinks wine, and yet fears Allah?' He said, 'No, rather it is the man who fasts, gives charity, and prays, and yet fears that Allah will not accept it from him.'"

Ibn Abi al-Dunya, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Anbari (in *al-Masahif*, the codices of the Qur'an), Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'O Messenger of Allah,' and he mentioned something similar."

'Abd al-Razzaq narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "They give what they have been given."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿and their hearts are fearful﴾, that he said: "They act while fearful."

al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "The zakah (obligatory alms)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ā'ishah concerning (And those who give what they give), that she said: "They are those who fear Allah and obey Him."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'For this verse to be as I recite it would be dearer to me than red camels.' Ibn 'Abbas said to her, 'What is it?' She said, '(Those who give what they give).'" We have already mentioned its recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) and its meaning.

Sa'id ibn Mansur and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from her, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he recited (Those who give what they give) *maqsuran* (with the initial long vowel shortened, i.e., without the madd), from *al-maji'* (the coming).

Sa'id ibn Mansur, Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his *Tarikh*, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Anbari in *al-Masahif*, al-Daraqutni in *al-Afrad*, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from 'Ubayd ibn 'Umar that he asked 'Ā'ishah: "How did the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recite this verse, ﴿And those who give what they give﴾?" She said, "Which of the two do you prefer?" I said, "By the One in whose hand is my soul, one of them is dearer to me than this world and everything in it combined." She said, "Which one?" I said, "﴿And those who give what they give﴾." She said, "I testify that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite it that way, and that is how it was revealed, but *al-hijā'* (the orthography, i.e., the written form) is a letter (a variant of spelling)." Its chain contains Isma'il ibn 'Ali, who is weak.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Those hasten toward the good deeds, and they are foremost in them﴾, that he said: "Happiness from Allah preceded them."

'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying, ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾, that by *al-ghamrah* (confusion) he meant disbelief and doubt. ﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾, he said: "Evil deeds other than shirk (associating partners with Allah)." ﴿They will be doing them﴾, he said: "They must do them."

al-Nasa'i narrated from him concerning ﴿Until when We seize their affluent ones with punishment﴾, that he said: "They are the people of Badr." Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him concerning His saying, ﴿Then, when they cry out﴾, that he said: "They cry for help." And concerning His saying, ﴿You used to turn back on your heels﴾, he said: "You would turn away." And concerning His saying, ﴿Conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, he said: "They would gather around the House (the Ka'bah) at night and say *hujr* (abuse, nonsense)."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn Abi Hatim also narrated from him, concerning ﴿conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, that he said: "The Quraysh used to sit in circles, talking around the House."

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from him: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to recite ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾, and said: 'The polytheists would abuse the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) with speech in their evening gatherings.'"

al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Evening conversation was only disliked when this verse was revealed: ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾."

Then Allah, glory be to Him, informed that they will be told at that time, as a rebuke: ﴿Do not cry out today﴾. The speech is implicitly introduced by a verb of saying, and the sentence is directed to rebuke them, make them despair, and cut off their hopes. The clause ﴿Indeed, you will not be helped by Us﴾ gives the reason for the prohibition against crying out. The meaning is: you will not be protected from Our punishment, and your lamentation will not benefit you.

It has been said that the meaning is: no help will reach you from Our side that would prevent you from the punishment that has overtaken you.

Then He, glory be to Him, enumerated their ugly deeds against them as rebuke, saying: ﴿My verses were recited to you, but you turned back on your heels﴾. What permitted the pronoun before mention is their well-known arrogance concerning it and their boasting of its guardianship and service to it. They used to say: "No one will prevail over us, for we are the people of the Sacred Precinct and its servants." To this view the majority of the exegetes went. Ibn ʿAtiyyah said: "This is a good view."

(p-988) Al-Nahhas said: "The first view is preferable, and he clarified it with what we have mentioned."

According to the first view, *bihi* is connected to *mustakbirīn* (arrogant). Al-Wahidi said: "*Al-sāmir* is the group who converse at night, that is, they talk." It is permissible to connect it to *tahjurūn* (you talk nonsense). *Al-hajr* with a *fatḥah* means raving, that is, you rave concerning the Qur'an. It is also permissible that it derives from *al-hujr* with a *ḍammah*, which means obscenity.

Ibn Masʿud, Ibn ʿAbbas, Ibn ʿUmar and Abu Haywah read *summaran* with a *ḍammah* on the *sīn* and a *fatḥah* on the *mīm* with shadda. Zayd ibn ʿAli and Abu Raja' read *samaran*, and this reading is reported from Ibn ʿAbbas. The accusative of *sāmiran* is a circumstantial clause, either from the subject of *tankiṣūn*, or from the pronoun in *mustakbirīn*. *"As if there had not been between al-Ḥajun and al-Ṣafa any companion, and no one had talked in Makkah at night."*

Al-Raghib said: "It is said *sāmir* and *summār*, and *sumr* and *sāmirūn*."

The majority read *tahjurūn* with a *fatḥah* on the upper *tā'* and a *ḍammah* on the *jīm*. Nafiʿ and Ibn Muhaysin read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'* and a *kasrah* on the *jīm*, from *ahjara*, meaning: he spoke obscenely in his speech. Zayd ibn ʿAli, Ibn Muhaysin and Abu Nahik read it with a *ḍammah* on the *tā'*, a *fatḥah* on the *hā'*, and a shadda on the *kasrah* of the *jīm*, as the present tense of *hajjara*. He said, 'No, rather it is the man who fasts, gives charity, and prays, and yet fears that Allah will not accept it from him.'"

al-Firyabi and Ibn Jarir narrated from Ibn 'Umar concerning ﴿And those who give what they give﴾, that he said: "The zakah (obligatory alms)."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from 'Ā'ishah concerning (And those who give what they give), that she said: "They are those who fear Allah and obey Him."

'Abd ibn Humayd narrated from Ibn Abi Mulaykah, who said: "'Ā'ishah said, 'For this verse to be as I recite it would be dearer to me than red camels.' Ibn 'Abbas said to her, 'What is it?' She said, '(Those who give what they give).'" We have already mentioned its recitation (qira'ah, a variant reading) and its meaning.

She said, "Which of the two do you prefer?" I said, "By the One in whose hand is my soul, one of them is dearer to me than this world and everything in it combined." She said, "Which one?" I said, "﴿And those who give what they give﴾." al-Nasa'i, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Evening conversation was only disliked when this verse was revealed: ﴿Arrogant about it, conversing at night, talking nonsense﴾."

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 57–67 (part 1 of 2):

When Allah, glory be to Him, negated true goods from the disbelievers who lived in luxury, He followed that with mention of those who deserve goods, both in this world and the next. He described them with four attributes. The first is His saying: ﴿Indeed, those who are apprehensive of the fear of their Lord﴾. *Al-Ishfaq* (apprehension) means fear. You say, "I am *mushfiq* (apprehensive) of this matter," meaning: I fear it.

It has been said that *al-ishfaq* is the same as *al-khashyah* (awe, dread), so on the surface the verse is repetitive.

It has been answered by taking *al-khashyah* to mean the punishment: that is, they fear the punishment of their Lord. This is the view of al-Kalbi and Muqatil.

It has also been answered by taking *al-ishfaq* to mean what results from it, which is persistence in obedience. The meaning would then be: those who, out of fear of their Lord, are persistent in obeying Him.

It has also been answered that *al-ishfaq* is the perfection of fear, so there is no repetition. It has also been said that it is repetition for emphasis.

The second attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who believe in the signs of their Lord﴾. It has been said that the signs here are the revealed ones (*al-tanziliyyah*), and it has been said that they are the created ones (*al-takwiniyyah*), and it has been said that they are both together. It has been said that belief in them does not mean merely affirming that they are evidences and that what they signify is true.

The third attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who do not associate partners with their Lord﴾, that is, they abandon association (*shirk*) completely, outwardly and inwardly.

The fourth attribute is His saying: ﴿And those who give what they give while their hearts are fearful, because they will return to their Lord﴾. That is, they give what they give while their hearts are fearful on account of that giving, thinking that it will not save them from the punishment of Allah. The clause ﴿while their hearts are fearful﴾ is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: while their hearts are in a state of extreme fear.

Al-Zajjaj said: "Their hearts are fearful because they will return to their Lord. The cause of the trembling is that they fear their giving will not be accepted in the required manner, not merely their return to Him, glory be to Him."

It has also been said that the meaning is: whoever believes in the return to recompense and reckoning, and knows that the one who recompenses and reckons is the Lord from whom nothing is hidden, will not be free of trembling.

ʿĀʾishah, Ibn ʿAbbas and al-Nakhaʿi read *ya'tūna mā ataw* (they do what they did) with a short alif, from *al-ityān* (coming/doing).

Al-Farra' said: "Even if this reading is sound, it does not contradict the reading of the majority, because some Arabs always keep the alif in the hamza in all cases."

Al-Nahhas said: "The meaning of this reading is: they do what they did."

The demonstrative in His saying ﴿those﴾ refers to those characterized by these attributes. The meaning of ﴿they hasten to good deeds﴾ is that they hasten toward them. Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: "They compete for them." It has been said: "They race for them." It is also read *yusrīʿūna* (they hasten).

﴿And they are foremost in them﴾: the *lām* (in *lahā*) is for emphasis (*lil-taqwiyah*). The meaning is: they are foremost in reaching them. It has been said that the *lām* carries the sense of *ilā* (to), as in His saying: ﴿because your Lord has inspired it﴾ [al-Zalzalah: 5], meaning: inspired to it. Sibawayh cited the verse of the poet:

*"Turn aside from the people of Yamamah, O youth, and what you intended from them is other than yourself."*

meaning: toward your other. It has been said that the object is omitted, and the sense is: they are foremost over people for their sake.

Then, when the discussion turned to the deeds of the obligated, He mentioned two rulings concerning them. The first is His saying: ﴿And We do not burden any soul except within its capacity﴾. *Al-wus'* is capacity, and the explanation of this was given earlier at the end of Surah al-Baqarah. There are two views on interpreting *al-wus'*. The first is that it is capacity, as the lexicographers explained it. The second is that it is less than capacity; this is the view of Muqatil, al-Dahhak and al-Kalbi.

The Mu'tazilah said: since *al-wus'* is so named because the act of its doer is spacious for him and does not constrain him, whoever cannot sit should pray by gesture, and whoever cannot fast should break the fast.

This sentence is a new independent clause (*mustaʾnafah*), urging the pursuit of acts of obedience that lead to honor, which were mentioned in describing the foremost, by explaining how easy they are and that they do not exceed the limit of capacity and ability. It also shows that this is Allah's custom with His servants in imposing obligations. The clause ﴿And with Us is a Book that speaks with truth﴾ completes what precedes it, negating obligation beyond capacity. The Book here means the records of deeds: that is, with Us is a Book in which the deeds of every obligated person have been recorded as they are. The meaning of ﴿speaks with truth﴾ is that the truth that corresponds to reality is made manifest through it, without addition or deficiency. A similar verse is His saying, glory be to Him: ﴿This is Our Book; it speaks against you with truth. Indeed, We were having copied what you used to do﴾. In this there is a warning to the disobedient and reassurance to the obedient against injustice and oppression.

It has been said that the Book here means the Preserved Tablet (*al-lawh al-mahfuz*), since everything is written in it.

It has been said that the Book here means the Qur'an, but the first view is preferable.

In this verse there is a comparison of the Book to one from whom clear speech issues by his tongue, since the Book expresses what is in it just as a truthful speaker does. The phrase ﴿with truth﴾ is connected to *yantiqu* (speaks), or to an omitted element functioning as a circumstantial clause from its subject, meaning: it speaks while combined with truth. The clause ﴿and they will not be wronged﴾ explains what precedes it, namely His bounty and justice in recompensing His servants: they will not be wronged by a reduction of reward or an increase in punishment. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿And they will find what they did present, and your Lord does not wrong anyone﴾.

Then He turned away from this and said: ﴿Rather, their hearts are in confusion about this﴾. The pronoun refers to the disbelievers. That is: rather, the hearts of the disbelievers are in an overwhelming confusion concerning this Book which speaks with truth, or concerning the matter upon which the believers are. It is said: *ghamarahu al-ma'* (the water overwhelmed him) when it covered him, and *nahr ghamr* (a deep river) is one that covers whoever enters it. What is meant here is covering, heedlessness, or bewilderment and blindness. The discussion of *al-ghamrah* was given shortly before.

﴿And they have deeds other than that﴾. Qatadah and Mujahid said: that is, they have sins which they must commit apart from the truth. Al-Hasan and Ibn Zayd said: the meaning is that they have evil deeds which they have not yet done, apart from what they are upon, which they must do, and by which they will enter the Fire. So the demonstrative in His saying ﴿that﴾ refers either to the deeds of the believers or to the deeds of the disbelievers. That is: they have deeds beyond the deeds of the believers which Allah mentioned, or beyond the deeds of the disbelievers mentioned earlier, namely that their hearts are in great heedlessness of what has been mentioned. These are the varieties of their disbelief and disobedience, among which is what will come later of their slander against the Qur'an.

Al-Wahidi said: "The consensus of the exegetes and the scholars of meanings is that this is a report about what they will do of their evil deeds, which were written against them, and which they must do. The clause ﴿they are doing them﴾ confirms what precedes it, meaning: it is obligatory upon them to do them, and so they will enter the Fire because of what was previously decreed for them of wretchedness, and there is no escape for them from that."
