Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, that he said: it has already passed; it was the Day of Badr.

(p-989) His saying: ﴿Do they not ponder over the Word?﴾ Allah, glory be to Him, explains that the cause of their rushing into disbelief is one of these four matters. The first is their failure to ponder the Qur'an. Had they reflected on its meanings, its truthfulness would have become clear to them, and they would have believed in it and in what it contains. The hamza is for rebuke (*al-hamza lil-inkar*), and the fa' is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause, meaning: they did what they did, and so they did not ponder. By "the Word" is meant the Qur'an. Similar is ﴿Then do they not ponder the Qur'an?﴾

The second is His saying: ﴿Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ Here *am* is the disjunctive *am* (*am al-munqati'a*), meaning: rather, there has come to them from the Book what did not come to their forefathers of old. This was the reason for their rejection of the Qur'an. The intended point is to establish that no messenger came to their forefathers of old, and therefore they denied it. Similar is His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾. It has also been said that messengers did come to their ancient forefathers, sent by Allah to them, as is Allah's custom, glory be to Him, in sending messengers to His servants; so these people knew this, so how could they deny this Qur'an? It has also been said that the meaning is: or has there come to them, of security from the punishment of Allah, what did not come to their forefathers of old, such as Isma'il and those after him.

The third is His saying: ﴿Or they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him?﴾ In this there is a shift (*idrab*) and transition from the rebuke mentioned earlier to a rebuke on another basis, meaning: rather, did they not know him for his trustworthiness and truthfulness, and yet deny him? It is known that they did indeed know him for that.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿Or they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ This too is a transition from one rebuke to another, meaning: rather, do they say that there is *jinnah* in him, that is, madness? Yet they knew that he was the most sound of intellect among people, but he came with what opposed their desires, so they repelled him and denied him out of partisanship and zealotry.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from all of that and said: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claimed regarding the Qur'an and the Messenger; rather, he has brought them the truth intermingled with the truth. The truth is the upright religion. ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾, because of what they were created with of partisanship, deviation from what is right, and distance from the truth; therefore they disliked this clear and manifest truth. The apparent sense of the wording is that the least of them did not dislike the truth, but they did not openly profess faith out of fear of those who disliked it.

The clause ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʼnafa*), brought to explain that if the truth had come according to what they desire and wish, that would have entailed great corruption and the complete breakdown of the order of the world. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted.﴾ Abu Salih, Ibn Juraij, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: the truth is Allah, and the meaning is: if He had made for Himself a partner, as they wish, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that by "the truth" is meant the Qur'an, that is: if the Qur'an had descended with what they love of polytheism, the order of the world would have been corrupted.

It has also been said that the meaning is: and if the truth were what they say, namely the unity of gods alongside Allah, the gods would have disagreed. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. The majority went to the first view, but this is refuted by the fact that the intended meaning there is Allah, glory be to Him. Therefore it is better to interpret "the truth" here and there as the sound truth of the pure religion from the law of Allah. The meaning is: if the truth had come following their desires, agreeing with their corrupt aims, corruption would have occurred. By His saying "and whoever is in them" is meant whoever is in the heavens and the earth among the creatures.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿and what is between them﴾. The cause of corruption among the accountable children of Adam is evident, namely their sins, among which is the desire that opposes the truth. As for the corruption of others besides them, it is by way of following, since they are for the most part governed by those of intellect; so when these became corrupt, the others became corrupt.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned that the descent of the Qur'an upon them is part of the truth, so He said: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾. By "reminder" here is meant the Qur'an, that is: with the Book which is their pride and honor. Similar is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. The meaning is: rather, We have brought them their pride and honor, which it was incumbent upon them to accept and to turn toward.

Qatadah said: the meaning is "with their reminder," in which is mentioned their reward and punishment.

It has also been said: the meaning is: with the reminder of what they need of matters of religion.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿ataytuhum﴾ with the *ta'* of the first person (I brought them).

Abu Haywa and al-Jahdari read ﴿atayta-hum﴾ with the *ta'* of address, that is: you (O Muhammad) brought them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿bi-dhikraahum﴾, and Qatadah read ﴿nudhakkiruhum﴾ with the *nun* and the doubling from *tadhkir* (reminding). In this reading the clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It has also been said: the reminder is admonition and warning. ﴿So they are averse to their reminder﴾, that is: they, because of what they did of arrogance and recoiling from this reminder specific to them, are averse, not turning to it in any state. In this construction there is an indication that their aversion is specific to that, not extending beyond it to anything else.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that the call of His Prophet (ﷺ) is not mixed with worldly greed, so He said: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am*, and the meaning: or do they claim that you ask them for a payment that you take from the message? *Kharj* is wage and reward. So they abandoned faith in you and in what you brought because of that, although they know that you did not ask them that nor did you seek it from them. ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾, that is, the provision of your Lord which He gives you in this world, and His reward which He will give you in the Hereafter, is better for you than what is mentioned.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿am tas'aluhum kharajan﴾. The rest read *kharjan*. All of them read ﴿fa-kharaju rabbika﴾ except Ibn 'Amir and Abu Haywa, who read ﴿fa-kharaja﴾ without the *alif*. *Al-kharj* is that which stands opposite to *al-dakhl* (income); it is said of everything you send out to another *kharj*. *Al-kharaj* is mostly used for the tax on land. al-Mubarrad said: *al-kharj* is the verbal noun, and *al-kharaj* is the noun. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the difference between *al-kharj* and *al-kharaj*, and he said: *al-kharaj* is what is obligatory upon you, and *al-kharj* is what you give voluntarily. It is narrated from him that he said: *al-kharj* is from people's necks, and *al-kharaj* is from land. ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. This sentence confirms what precedes it, that the payment of Allah is good.

(p-990) Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established for His Messenger the clear proofs that necessitate acceptance of what he brought and negated the opposites of that, He said: ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾, that is, to a clear way which the intellects attest is straight, not crooked. *Al-sirat* in the language means the road, so religion is called a road because it leads to Him.

Then He described them as being contrary to that, saying: ﴿And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ It is said: *nakaba 'an al-tariq yankubu nukuban*, when one turns away from the road and inclines to another. *Al-nukub* and *al-nakb* mean deviation and inclination. From it is *al-nakba'* (the north-east wind) for the wind between two winds, named so for its deviation from the directions. *'An al-sirat* is connected to *nakibun*. The meaning: those described as not believing in the Hereafter are certainly turning away from that path, or from the kind of path.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they persist in disbelief and never return from it in any state, so He said: ﴿Even if We had shown them mercy and removed what harm is upon them﴾, that is, of famine and drought, ﴿they would persist in their transgression﴾, that is: they would continue in their transgression and misguidance, ﴿wandering blindly, hesitating, and stumbling about.﴾ The root of *lajaj* is persistence in obstinacy, and from it is *al-lujjah* (with a fatha) for the repeated sound, and *lujjat al-bahr* is the repeated movement of its waves, and *lujjat al-layl* is the repetition of its darkness.

It has also been said: the meaning is: if We returned them to the world and did not admit them to the Fire, and tested them, they would persist in their transgression.

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾ is a resumptive clause, brought to confirm what precedes. As for *al-'adhab* (the punishment), it has been said it is the hunger that struck them in the years of drought; it has been said: sickness; it has been said: the fighting on the day of Badr, which al-Zajjaj chose; it has been said: death; it has been said: the intended is those among the earlier nations whom punishment reached. ﴿Yet they did not submit to their Lord﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves or become meek, but remained in their rebellion against Allah and their immersion in His disobediences. ﴿Nor did they supplicate﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves before Allah in hardships when they befell them, nor did they call upon Him to remove that.

﴿Until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾. It has been said this is the punishment of the Hereafter; it has been said: their slaughter by the sword on the day of Badr; it has been said: the famine that struck them; it has been said: the conquest of Makkah. ﴿Then they will be in despair therein﴾, that is: bewildered, not knowing what to do. *Al-ibsal* is bewilderment and despair of every good.

al-Sulami read ﴿mublasun﴾ with a fatha on the *lam*, from *ablasa-hu*, meaning: he caused him to enter into despair. This has been discussed in al-An'am.

﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾. He reminded them with some of the blessings He gave them, namely the blessing of hearing, sight and hearts, so that these faculties with them might hear admonitions, look at lessons, and reflect with their hearts. But they did not benefit from any of that because of their persistence in disbelief and distance from the truth, and they did not thank Him for it. Therefore He said: ﴿Little are you grateful.﴾ That is, a little, insignificant thanks, not considered in relation to those magnificent blessings. It has also been said: the meaning is that they do not thank Him at all, not that they have a little thanks, as one says of an ingrate: how little is his thanks, meaning he does not thank. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their hearts did not avail them anything﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26].

﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾, that is, He scattered you in it as seeds are scattered to grow; its verification has preceded. ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾, that is, you will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.

﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death﴾ by way of exclusive and sole authority. In this is a reminder of the blessing of life and an explanation of the transition from it to the Abode of the Hereafter. ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day.﴾ al-Farra' said: He is the One who made them differ, following each other and differing in darkness and brightness. It has been said: their alternation is the shortening of one and the lengthening of the other. It has been said: their recurrence, day after day and night after night. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, understanding the reality of His power and reflecting upon that.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they have no doubt in denying resurrection except clinging to the rope of blind imitation, based on mere improbability, so He said: ﴿Rather, they say the like of what the former ones said﴾, that is, their forefathers and those who agreed with them in their religion.

Then He explained what the former ones said, so He said: ﴿They say, "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ This is mere improbability, in which they attached themselves to no kind of doubt.

Then they completed that statement with their saying: ﴿We and our forefathers have indeed been promised this before﴾, that is: this resurrection was promised to us, and it was promised to our forefathers who came before us, yet we did not believe it, just as those before us did not believe it. Then they declared denial outright and fled to mere false assertion, saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former ones﴾, that is: this is nothing but the lies of the former ones, which they inscribed in books. *Asatir* is the plural of *usturah*, like *uhdutha*. *Al-asatir* are falsehoods, nonsense and lies.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih, regarding His saying: ﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ he said: they recognized him, but they envied him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾, he said: the truth is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, he said: We have made it clear to them. And they narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿Are deviating from the path﴾, he said: from the truth, swerving away.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, I implore you by God and by the ties of kinship, for we have eaten the *'ilhiz* (a food made of camel's blood mixed with hair or wool)', that is, the wool mixed with blood." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾

The origin of this report is in the two *Sahihs*: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh when they refused to accept Islam, saying: 'O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Joseph'," and the hadith continues.

Ibn Jarir, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, when he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), embraced Islam while he was a captive, and he was released. He then joined the people of al-Yamamah and cut off the supply of grain from al-Yamamah to the people of Makkah, until Quraysh ate the *'ilhiz*. Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He replied: "Yes." He said: "Then you have killed the fathers by the sword and the sons by hunger." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾, the verse.

Al-'Askari in *al-Mawa'iz* related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying: ﴿Yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate﴾, that he said: they did not humble themselves in supplication and did not submit. ﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾, that is, He scattered you in it as seeds are scattered to grow; its verification has preceded. ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾, that is, you will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.

﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death﴾ by way of exclusive and sole authority. In this is a reminder of the blessing of life and an explanation of the transition from it to the Abode of the Hereafter. ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day.﴾ al-Farra' said: He is the One who made them differ, following each other and differing in darkness and brightness. It has been said: their alternation is the shortening of one and the lengthening of the other. It has been said: their recurrence, day after day and night after night. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, understanding the reality of His power and reflecting upon that.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they have no doubt in denying resurrection except clinging to the rope of blind imitation, based on mere improbability, so He said: ﴿Rather, they say the like of what the former ones said﴾, that is, their forefathers and those who agreed with them in their religion.

Then He explained what the former ones said, so He said: ﴿They say, "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ This is mere improbability, in which they attached themselves to no kind of doubt.

Then they completed that statement with their saying: ﴿We and our forefathers have indeed been promised this before﴾, that is: this resurrection was promised to us, and it was promised to our forefathers who came before us, yet we did not believe it, just as those before us did not believe it. Then they declared denial outright and fled to mere false assertion, saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former ones﴾, that is: this is nothing but the lies of the former ones, which they inscribed in books. *Asatir* is the plural of *usturah*, like *uhdutha*. *Al-asatir* are falsehoods, nonsense and lies.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih, regarding His saying: ﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ he said: they recognized him, but they envied him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾, he said: the truth is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, he said: We have made it clear to them. And they narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿Are deviating from the path﴾, he said: from the truth, swerving away.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, I implore you by God and by the ties of kinship, for we have eaten the *'ilhiz* (a food made of camel's blood mixed with hair or wool)', that is, the wool mixed with blood." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾

The origin of this report is in the two *Sahihs*: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh when they refused to accept Islam, saying: 'O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Joseph'," and the hadith continues.

He then joined the people of al-Yamamah and cut off the supply of grain from al-Yamamah to the people of Makkah, until Quraysh ate the *'ilhiz*. Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He replied: "Yes." He said: "Then you have killed the fathers by the sword and the sons by hunger." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾, the verse.

Al-'Askari in *al-Mawa'iz* related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying: ﴿Yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate﴾, that he said: they did not humble themselves in supplication and did not submit. (p-٩٩١) Had they submitted to God, He would have answered them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, that he said: it has already passed; it was the Day of Badr.

(p-989) His saying: ﴿Do they not ponder over the Word?﴾ Allah, glory be to Him, explains that the cause of their rushing into disbelief is one of these four matters. The first is their failure to ponder the Qur'an. Had they reflected on its meanings, its truthfulness would have become clear to them, and they would have believed in it and in what it contains. The hamza is for rebuke (*al-hamza lil-inkar*), and the fa' is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause, meaning: they did what they did, and so they did not ponder. By "the Word" is meant the Qur'an. Similar is ﴿Then do they not ponder the Qur'an?﴾

The second is His saying: ﴿Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ Here *am* is the disjunctive *am* (*am al-munqati'a*), meaning: rather, there has come to them from the Book what did not come to their forefathers of old. This was the reason for their rejection of the Qur'an. The intended point is to establish that no messenger came to their forefathers of old, and therefore they denied it. Similar is His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾. It has also been said that messengers did come to their ancient forefathers, sent by Allah to them, as is Allah's custom, glory be to Him, in sending messengers to His servants; so these people knew this, so how could they deny this Qur'an? It has also been said that the meaning is: or has there come to them, of security from the punishment of Allah, what did not come to their forefathers of old, such as Isma'il and those after him.

The third is His saying: ﴿Or they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him?﴾ In this there is a shift (*idrab*) and transition from the rebuke mentioned earlier to a rebuke on another basis, meaning: rather, did they not know him for his trustworthiness and truthfulness, and yet deny him? It is known that they did indeed know him for that.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿Or they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ This too is a transition from one rebuke to another, meaning: rather, do they say that there is *jinnah* in him, that is, madness? Yet they knew that he was the most sound of intellect among people, but he came with what opposed their desires, so they repelled him and denied him out of partisanship and zealotry.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from all of that and said: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claimed regarding the Qur'an and the Messenger; rather, he has brought them the truth intermingled with the truth. The truth is the upright religion. ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾, because of what they were created with of partisanship, deviation from what is right, and distance from the truth; therefore they disliked this clear and manifest truth. The apparent sense of the wording is that the least of them did not dislike the truth, but they did not openly profess faith out of fear of those who disliked it.

The clause ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʼnafa*), brought to explain that if the truth had come according to what they desire and wish, that would have entailed great corruption and the complete breakdown of the order of the world. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted.﴾ Abu Salih, Ibn Juraij, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: the truth is Allah, and the meaning is: if He had made for Himself a partner, as they wish, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that by "the truth" is meant the Qur'an, that is: if the Qur'an had descended with what they love of polytheism, the order of the world would have been corrupted.

It has also been said that the meaning is: and if the truth were what they say, namely the unity of gods alongside Allah, the gods would have disagreed. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. The majority went to the first view, but this is refuted by the fact that the intended meaning there is Allah, glory be to Him. Therefore it is better to interpret "the truth" here and there as the sound truth of the pure religion from the law of Allah. The meaning is: if the truth had come following their desires, agreeing with their corrupt aims, corruption would have occurred. By His saying "and whoever is in them" is meant whoever is in the heavens and the earth among the creatures.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿and what is between them﴾. The cause of corruption among the accountable children of Adam is evident, namely their sins, among which is the desire that opposes the truth. As for the corruption of others besides them, it is by way of following, since they are for the most part governed by those of intellect; so when these became corrupt, the others became corrupt.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned that the descent of the Qur'an upon them is part of the truth, so He said: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾. By "reminder" here is meant the Qur'an, that is: with the Book which is their pride and honor. Similar is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. The meaning is: rather, We have brought them their pride and honor, which it was incumbent upon them to accept and to turn toward.

Qatadah said: the meaning is "with their reminder," in which is mentioned their reward and punishment.

It has also been said: the meaning is: with the reminder of what they need of matters of religion.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿ataytuhum﴾ with the *ta'* of the first person (I brought them).

Abu Haywa and al-Jahdari read ﴿atayta-hum﴾ with the *ta'* of address, that is: you (O Muhammad) brought them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿bi-dhikraahum﴾, and Qatadah read ﴿nudhakkiruhum﴾ with the *nun* and the doubling from *tadhkir* (reminding). In this reading the clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It has also been said: the reminder is admonition and warning. ﴿So they are averse to their reminder﴾, that is: they, because of what they did of arrogance and recoiling from this reminder specific to them, are averse, not turning to it in any state. In this construction there is an indication that their aversion is specific to that, not extending beyond it to anything else.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that the call of His Prophet (ﷺ) is not mixed with worldly greed, so He said: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am*, and the meaning: or do they claim that you ask them for a payment that you take from the message? *Kharj* is wage and reward. So they abandoned faith in you and in what you brought because of that, although they know that you did not ask them that nor did you seek it from them. ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾, that is, the provision of your Lord which He gives you in this world, and His reward which He will give you in the Hereafter, is better for you than what is mentioned.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, al-A'mash and Yahya ibn Wathhab read ﴿am tas'aluhum kharajan﴾. The rest read *kharjan*. It is narrated from him that he said: *al-kharj* is from people's necks, and *al-kharaj* is from land. ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. This sentence confirms what precedes it, that the payment of Allah is good.

(p-990) Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established for His Messenger the clear proofs that necessitate acceptance of what he brought and negated the opposites of that, He said: ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾, that is, to a clear way which the intellects attest is straight, not crooked. *Al-sirat* in the language means the road, so religion is called a road because it leads to Him.

Then He described them as being contrary to that, saying: ﴿And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ It is said: *nakaba 'an al-tariq yankubu nukuban*, when one turns away from the road and inclines to another. *Al-nukub* and *al-nakb* mean deviation and inclination. From it is *al-nakba'* (the north-east wind) for the wind between two winds, named so for its deviation from the directions. *'An al-sirat* is connected to *nakibun*. The meaning: those described as not believing in the Hereafter are certainly turning away from that path, or from the kind of path.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they persist in disbelief and never return from it in any state, so He said: ﴿Even if We had shown them mercy and removed what harm is upon them﴾, that is, of famine and drought, ﴿they would persist in their transgression﴾, that is: they would continue in their transgression and misguidance, ﴿wandering blindly, hesitating, and stumbling about.﴾ The root of *lajaj* is persistence in obstinacy, and from it is *al-lujjah* (with a fatha) for the repeated sound, and *lujjat al-bahr* is the repeated movement of its waves, and *lujjat al-layl* is the repetition of its darkness.

It has also been said: the meaning is: if We returned them to the world and did not admit them to the Fire, and tested them, they would persist in their transgression.

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾ is a resumptive clause, brought to confirm what precedes. As for *al-'adhab* (the punishment), it has been said it is the hunger that struck them in the years of drought; it has been said: sickness; it has been said: the fighting on the day of Badr, which al-Zajjaj chose; it has been said: death; it has been said: the intended is those among the earlier nations whom punishment reached. ﴿Yet they did not submit to their Lord﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves or become meek, but remained in their rebellion against Allah and their immersion in His disobediences. ﴿Nor did they supplicate﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves before Allah in hardships when they befell them, nor did they call upon Him to remove that.

﴿Until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾. It has been said this is the punishment of the Hereafter; it has been said: their slaughter by the sword on the day of Badr; it has been said: the famine that struck them; it has been said: the conquest of Makkah. ﴿Then they will be in despair therein﴾, that is: bewildered, not knowing what to do. *Al-ibsal* is bewilderment and despair of every good.

al-Sulami read ﴿mublasun﴾ with a fatha on the *lam*, from *ablasa-hu*, meaning: he caused him to enter into despair. This has been discussed in al-An'am.

﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾. He reminded them with some of the blessings He gave them, namely the blessing of hearing, sight and hearts, so that these faculties with them might hear admonitions, look at lessons, and reflect with their hearts. But they did not benefit from any of that because of their persistence in disbelief and distance from the truth, and they did not thank Him for it. Therefore He said: ﴿Little are you grateful.﴾ That is, a little, insignificant thanks, not considered in relation to those magnificent blessings. It has also been said: the meaning is that they do not thank Him at all, not that they have a little thanks, as one says of an ingrate: how little is his thanks, meaning he does not thank. All of them read ﴿fa-kharaju rabbika﴾ except Ibn 'Amir and Abu Haywa, who read ﴿fa-kharaja﴾ without the *alif*. *Al-kharj* is that which stands opposite to *al-dakhl* (income); it is said of everything you send out to another *kharj*. *Al-kharaj* is mostly used for the tax on land. al-Mubarrad said: *al-kharj* is the verbal noun, and *al-kharaj* is the noun. al-Nadr ibn Shumayl said: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' about the difference between *al-kharj* and *al-kharaj*, and he said: *al-kharaj* is what is obligatory upon you, and *al-kharj* is what you give voluntarily. It is narrated from him that he said: *al-kharj* is from people's necks, and *al-kharaj* is from land. ﴿And He is the best of providers﴾. This sentence confirms what precedes it, that the payment of Allah is good.

(p-990) Then, when Allah, glory be to Him, established for His Messenger the clear proofs that necessitate acceptance of what he brought and negated the opposites of that, He said: ﴿And indeed you call them to a straight path﴾, that is, to a clear way which the intellects attest is straight, not crooked. *Al-sirat* in the language means the road, so religion is called a road because it leads to Him.

Then He described them as being contrary to that, saying: ﴿And indeed those who do not believe in the Hereafter are deviating from the path.﴾ It is said: *nakaba 'an al-tariq yankubu nukuban*, when one turns away from the road and inclines to another. *Al-nukub* and *al-nakb* mean deviation and inclination. From it is *al-nakba'* (the north-east wind) for the wind between two winds, named so for its deviation from the directions. *'An al-sirat* is connected to *nakibun*. The meaning: those described as not believing in the Hereafter are certainly turning away from that path, or from the kind of path.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they persist in disbelief and never return from it in any state, so He said: ﴿Even if We had shown them mercy and removed what harm is upon them﴾, that is, of famine and drought, ﴿they would persist in their transgression﴾, that is: they would continue in their transgression and misguidance, ﴿wandering blindly, hesitating, and stumbling about.﴾ The root of *lajaj* is persistence in obstinacy, and from it is *al-lujjah* (with a fatha) for the repeated sound, and *lujjat al-bahr* is the repeated movement of its waves, and *lujjat al-layl* is the repetition of its darkness.

It has also been said: the meaning is: if We returned them to the world and did not admit them to the Fire, and tested them, they would persist in their transgression.

﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾ is a resumptive clause, brought to confirm what precedes. As for *al-'adhab* (the punishment), it has been said it is the hunger that struck them in the years of drought; it has been said: sickness; it has been said: the fighting on the day of Badr, which al-Zajjaj chose; it has been said: death; it has been said: the intended is those among the earlier nations whom punishment reached. ﴿Yet they did not submit to their Lord﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves or become meek, but remained in their rebellion against Allah and their immersion in His disobediences. ﴿Nor did they supplicate﴾, that is: they did not humble themselves before Allah in hardships when they befell them, nor did they call upon Him to remove that.

﴿Until when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾. It has been said this is the punishment of the Hereafter; it has been said: their slaughter by the sword on the day of Badr; it has been said: the famine that struck them; it has been said: the conquest of Makkah. ﴿Then they will be in despair therein﴾, that is: bewildered, not knowing what to do. *Al-ibsal* is bewilderment and despair of every good.

al-Sulami read ﴿mublasun﴾ with a fatha on the *lam*, from *ablasa-hu*, meaning: he caused him to enter into despair. This has been discussed in al-An'am.

﴿And it is He who produced for you hearing and sight﴾. He reminded them with some of the blessings He gave them, namely the blessing of hearing, sight and hearts, so that these faculties with them might hear admonitions, look at lessons, and reflect with their hearts. But they did not benefit from any of that because of their persistence in disbelief and distance from the truth, and they did not thank Him for it. Therefore He said: ﴿Little are you grateful.﴾ That is, a little, insignificant thanks, not considered in relation to those magnificent blessings. It has also been said: the meaning is that they do not thank Him at all, not that they have a little thanks, as one says of an ingrate: how little is his thanks, meaning he does not thank. A similar verse is His saying: ﴿Their hearing, their sight, and their hearts did not avail them anything﴾ [al-Ahqaf: 26].

﴿And it is He who multiplied you upon the earth﴾, that is, He scattered you in it as seeds are scattered to grow; its verification has preceded. ﴿And to Him you will be gathered﴾, that is, you will be assembled on the Day of Resurrection after your dispersal.

﴿And it is He who gives life and causes death﴾ by way of exclusive and sole authority. In this is a reminder of the blessing of life and an explanation of the transition from it to the Abode of the Hereafter. ﴿And to Him belongs the alternation of the night and the day.﴾ al-Farra' said: He is the One who made them differ, following each other and differing in darkness and brightness. It has been said: their alternation is the shortening of one and the lengthening of the other. It has been said: their recurrence, day after day and night after night. ﴿Will you not then reason?﴾, understanding the reality of His power and reflecting upon that.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that they have no doubt in denying resurrection except clinging to the rope of blind imitation, based on mere improbability, so He said: ﴿Rather, they say the like of what the former ones said﴾, that is, their forefathers and those who agreed with them in their religion.

Then He explained what the former ones said, so He said: ﴿They say, "When we are dead and have become dust and bones, shall we indeed be resurrected?"﴾ This is mere improbability, in which they attached themselves to no kind of doubt.

Then they completed that statement with their saying: ﴿We and our forefathers have indeed been promised this before﴾, that is: this resurrection was promised to us, and it was promised to our forefathers who came before us, yet we did not believe it, just as those before us did not believe it. Then they declared denial outright and fled to mere false assertion, saying: ﴿This is nothing but the fables of the former ones﴾, that is: this is nothing but the lies of the former ones, which they inscribed in books. *Asatir* is the plural of *usturah*, like *uhdutha*. *Al-asatir* are falsehoods, nonsense and lies.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Abu Salih, regarding His saying: ﴿Or did they not recognize their Messenger?﴾ he said: they recognized him, but they envied him.

Regarding His saying: ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾, he said: the truth is Allah, Mighty and Majestic.

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾, he said: We have made it clear to them. And they narrated from him regarding His saying: ﴿Are deviating from the path﴾, he said: from the truth, swerving away.

Al-Nasa'i, Ibn Jarir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim, who declared it sound, Ibn Mardawayh, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas, who said: "Abu Sufyan came to the Prophet (ﷺ) and said: 'O Muhammad, I implore you by God and by the ties of kinship, for we have eaten the *'ilhiz* (a food made of camel's blood mixed with hair or wool)', that is, the wool mixed with blood." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment, yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate.﴾

The origin of this report is in the two *Sahihs*: "The Messenger of God (ﷺ) invoked against Quraysh when they refused to accept Islam, saying: 'O God, help me against them with seven years like the seven years of Joseph'," and the hadith continues.

Ibn Jarir, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah*, and al-Bayhaqi in *al-Dala'il* related from Ibn 'Abbas that Ibn Uthal al-Hanafi, when he came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ), embraced Islam while he was a captive, and he was released. He then joined the people of al-Yamamah and cut off the supply of grain from al-Yamamah to the people of Makkah, until Quraysh ate the *'ilhiz*. Abu Sufyan came to the Messenger of God (ﷺ) and said: "Do you not claim that you were sent as a mercy to the worlds?" He replied: "Yes." He said: "Then you have killed the fathers by the sword and the sons by hunger." Then God revealed: ﴿And We had already seized them with punishment﴾, the verse.

Al-'Askari in *al-Mawa'iz* related from 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, regarding His saying: ﴿Yet they did not humble themselves before their Lord, nor did they supplicate﴾, that he said: they did not humble themselves in supplication and did not submit. (p-٩٩١) Had they submitted to God, He would have answered them.

Ibn Abi Shaybah, Ibn Jarir, and Ibn Mardawayh related from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying: ﴿Until, when We open upon them a gate of severe punishment﴾, that he said: it has already passed; it was the Day of Badr.

The first is their failure to ponder the Qur'an. Had they reflected on its meanings, its truthfulness would have become clear to them, and they would have believed in it and in what it contains. The hamza is for rebuke (*al-hamza lil-inkar*), and the fa' is for conjunction with an implied preceding clause, meaning: they did what they did, and so they did not ponder. By "the Word" is meant the Qur'an. Similar is ﴿Then do they not ponder the Qur'an?﴾

The second is His saying: ﴿Or has there come to them what did not come to their forefathers of old?﴾ Here *am* is the disjunctive *am* (*am al-munqati'a*), meaning: rather, there has come to them from the Book what did not come to their forefathers of old. This was the reason for their rejection of the Qur'an. The intended point is to establish that no messenger came to their forefathers of old, and therefore they denied it. Similar is His saying: ﴿So that you may warn a people whose forefathers were not warned﴾. It has also been said that messengers did come to their ancient forefathers, sent by Allah to them, as is Allah's custom, glory be to Him, in sending messengers to His servants; so these people knew this, so how could they deny this Qur'an? It has also been said that the meaning is: or has there come to them, of security from the punishment of Allah, what did not come to their forefathers of old, such as Isma'il and those after him.

The third is His saying: ﴿Or they did not recognize their Messenger, so they deny him?﴾ In this there is a shift (*idrab*) and transition from the rebuke mentioned earlier to a rebuke on another basis, meaning: rather, did they not know him for his trustworthiness and truthfulness, and yet deny him? It is known that they did indeed know him for that.

The fourth is His saying: ﴿Or they say, "There is madness in him"?﴾ This too is a transition from one rebuke to another, meaning: rather, do they say that there is *jinnah* in him, that is, madness? Yet they knew that he was the most sound of intellect among people, but he came with what opposed their desires, so they repelled him and denied him out of partisanship and zealotry.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, turned away from all of that and said: ﴿Rather, he has brought them the truth﴾, meaning: the matter is not as they claimed regarding the Qur'an and the Messenger; rather, he has brought them the truth intermingled with the truth. The truth is the upright religion. ﴿But most of them are averse to the truth﴾, because of what they were created with of partisanship, deviation from what is right, and distance from the truth; therefore they disliked this clear and manifest truth. The apparent sense of the wording is that the least of them did not dislike the truth, but they did not openly profess faith out of fear of those who disliked it.

The clause ﴿And if the truth had followed their desires﴾ is a resumptive clause (*jumla mustaʼnafa*), brought to explain that if the truth had come according to what they desire and wish, that would have entailed great corruption and the complete breakdown of the order of the world. This is the meaning of His saying: ﴿the heavens and the earth and whoever is in them would have been corrupted.﴾ Abu Salih, Ibn Juraij, Muqatil and al-Suddi said: the truth is Allah, and the meaning is: if He had made for Himself a partner, as they wish, the heavens and the earth would have been corrupted.

al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: it is possible that by "the truth" is meant the Qur'an, that is: if the Qur'an had descended with what they love of polytheism, the order of the world would have been corrupted.

It has also been said that the meaning is: and if the truth were what they say, namely the unity of gods alongside Allah, the gods would have disagreed. A similar statement is His saying: ﴿Had there been in them gods other than Allah, they would both have been corrupted﴾ [al-Anbiya': 22]. The majority went to the first view, but this is refuted by the fact that the intended meaning there is Allah, glory be to Him. Therefore it is better to interpret "the truth" here and there as the sound truth of the pure religion from the law of Allah. The meaning is: if the truth had come following their desires, agreeing with their corrupt aims, corruption would have occurred. By His saying "and whoever is in them" is meant whoever is in the heavens and the earth among the creatures.

Ibn Mas'ud read ﴿and what is between them﴾. The cause of corruption among the accountable children of Adam is evident, namely their sins, among which is the desire that opposes the truth. As for the corruption of others besides them, it is by way of following, since they are for the most part governed by those of intellect; so when these became corrupt, the others became corrupt.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, mentioned that the descent of the Qur'an upon them is part of the truth, so He said: ﴿Rather, We have brought them their reminder﴾. By "reminder" here is meant the Qur'an, that is: with the Book which is their pride and honor. Similar is His saying: ﴿And indeed it is a reminder for you and for your people﴾. The meaning is: rather, We have brought them their pride and honor, which it was incumbent upon them to accept and to turn toward.

Qatadah said: the meaning is "with their reminder," in which is mentioned their reward and punishment.

It has also been said: the meaning is: with the reminder of what they need of matters of religion.

Ibn Abi Ishaq and 'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿ataytuhum﴾ with the *ta'* of the first person (I brought them).

Abu Haywa and al-Jahdari read ﴿atayta-hum﴾ with the *ta'* of address, that is: you (O Muhammad) brought them.

'Isa ibn 'Umar read ﴿bi-dhikraahum﴾, and Qatadah read ﴿nudhakkiruhum﴾ with the *nun* and the doubling from *tadhkir* (reminding). In this reading the clause is in the place of an accusative as a circumstantial clause (*hal*). It has also been said: the reminder is admonition and warning. ﴿So they are averse to their reminder﴾, that is: they, because of what they did of arrogance and recoiling from this reminder specific to them, are averse, not turning to it in any state. In this construction there is an indication that their aversion is specific to that, not extending beyond it to anything else.

Then Allah, glory be to Him, explained that the call of His Prophet (ﷺ) is not mixed with worldly greed, so He said: ﴿Or do you ask them for a payment?﴾ *Am* here is the disjunctive *am*, and the meaning: or do they claim that you ask them for a payment that you take from the message? *Kharj* is wage and reward. So they abandoned faith in you and in what you brought because of that, although they know that you did not ask them that nor did you seek it from them. ﴿But the payment of your Lord is better﴾, that is, the provision of your Lord which He gives you in this world, and His reward which He will give you in the Hereafter, is better for you than what is mentioned.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 84–98:

God, glory be to Him, commanded His Prophet, may God bless him and his family and grant them peace, to ask the disbelievers about matters on which they have no excuse but to acknowledge them. Then He commanded him to reproach them after their acknowledgment and to rebuke them, so He said: ﴿Say: To whom belongs the earth and whoever is in it, if you know?﴾ That is, say, O Muhammad, this statement to the people of Makkah. What is meant by "whoever is in it" is all creation, and He expressed them with "whoever" (man) by way of giving precedence to the rational beings. ﴿If you know﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer to the conditional is omitted, meaning: if you know, then inform me. In this there is an allusion to their ignorance and their extreme dullness.

﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ That is, they must say this, because it is known by the immediate judgment of reason. Then God, glory be to Him, commanded him to say to them after their acknowledgment: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ as an encouragement for them to reflect and to consider and ponder deeply, for that leads them to follow the truth and abandon falsehood; for whoever was able to create initially is able to bring the dead back to life.

﴿Say: Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?﴾ They will say, "To God." He, glory be to Him, used the lam (to) in view of the meaning of the question, for your saying "whose is his lord" and "to whom does he belong" have one meaning, like your saying: "Whose is the lord of this house?" and it is said "Zayd," and it is said "to Zayd."

Abu 'Amr and the people of Iraq read (sa-yaqūlūna Allāh) without the lam, in view of the wording of the question, and this reading is clearer than the reading of the others with the lam. However, what supports the reading of the majority is that it is written in all the codices with the lam without an alif.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you know?﴾ ﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ with the lam, in view of the meaning of the question, as has passed.

The answer to the conditional is omitted, meaning: if you know, then inform me. In this there is an allusion to their ignorance and their extreme dullness.

﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ That is, they must say this, because it is known by the immediate judgment of reason. Then God, glory be to Him, commanded him to say to them after their acknowledgment: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ as an encouragement for them to reflect and to consider and ponder deeply, for that leads them to follow the truth and abandon falsehood; for whoever was able to create initially is able to bring the dead back to life.

﴿Say: Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?﴾ They will say, "To God." He, glory be to Him, used the lam (to) in view of the meaning of the question, for your saying "whose is his lord" and "to whom does he belong" have one meaning, like your saying: "Whose is the lord of this house?" and it is said "Zayd," and it is said "to Zayd."

Abu 'Amr and the people of Iraq read (sa-yaqūlūna Allāh) without the lam, in view of the wording of the question, and this reading is clearer than the reading of the others with the lam. However, what supports the reading of the majority is that it is written in all the codices with the lam without an alif.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you know?﴾ ﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ with the lam, in view of the meaning of the question, as has passed.

Abu 'Amr and the people of Iraq read it without the lam, in view of the wording of the question. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

When it is said, "Whose are the villages and the settlements, and the lord of the noble swift horses?" it is said, "To Khalid."

That is, to whom do the villages belong? Al-malakūt means the dominion, and the addition of the taa' is for emphasis, like jabarūt and rahabūt. The meaning of ﴿and He protects﴾ is that He rescues others when He wills and prevents them. ﴿And none can be protected against Him﴾ means that no one can prevent anyone from the punishment of God, nor is anyone able to help or rescue Him. It is said: "I protected so-and-so" when he sought refuge with you and you defended him, and "I protected against him" when I defended him from something.

﴿Say: Then how are you deluded?﴾ Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: that is, you are turned away from the truth and deceived. The meaning is: how is it imagined to you that the truth is falsehood and the sound is corrupt? The one who deceives them is Satan, or desire, or both.

Then God, glory be to Him, clarified that He had made the proof against them thorough, so He said: ﴿Rather, We have brought them the truth﴾ that is, the clear matter which deserves to be followed, ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ in what they attribute to God, glory be to Him, of offspring and partners.

Then He negated these two from Himself, saying: ﴿God has not taken any offspring, and there is not with Him any god.﴾ The "min" in both places is extra, for emphasis of the negation.

Then God, glory be to Him, clarified what the claim of the disbelievers necessitates together with the affirmation of a partner, so He said: ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech; its estimate is: and if there were with God gods, each god would have been independent with his creation, would have been self-sufficient in it, and his dominion would have been distinct from the dominion of the other, and there would have occurred among them contention, warfare, and mutual overpowering. ﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾ that is, the strong would have prevailed over the weak, subdued him and taken his dominion, as is the custom of kings among the children of Adam. This argument, just as it indicates the negation of a partner, also indicates the negation of offspring, because offspring would contend with its father for his dominion.

Then God, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of what they describe, so He said: ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾ that is, of partner and offspring, and the attribution of these to God, mighty and majestic.

Nafi', Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ('ālimu) in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is knowing.

The rest read it in the genitive, as an attribute of God or an apposition to Him.

The answer to the conditional is omitted, meaning: if you know, then inform me. In this there is an allusion to their ignorance and their extreme dullness.

﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ That is, they must say this, because it is known by the immediate judgment of reason. Then God, glory be to Him, commanded him to say to them after their acknowledgment: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ as an encouragement for them to reflect and to consider and ponder deeply, for that leads them to follow the truth and abandon falsehood; for whoever was able to create initially is able to bring the dead back to life.

He, glory be to Him, used the lam (to) in view of the meaning of the question, for your saying "whose is his lord" and "to whom does he belong" have one meaning, like your saying: "Whose is the lord of this house?" and it is said "Zayd," and it is said "to Zayd."

However, what supports the reading of the majority is that it is written in all the codices with the lam without an alif.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you know?﴾ ﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ with the lam, in view of the meaning of the question, as has passed.

When it is said, "Whose are the villages and the settlements, and the lord of the noble swift horses?" it is said, "To Khalid."

That is, to whom do the villages belong? Al-malakūt means the dominion, and the addition of the taa' is for emphasis, like jabarūt and rahabūt. The meaning of ﴿and He protects﴾ is that He rescues others when He wills and prevents them. ﴿And none can be protected against Him﴾ means that no one can prevent anyone from the punishment of God, nor is anyone able to help or rescue Him. It is said: "I protected so-and-so" when he sought refuge with you and you defended him, and "I protected against him" when I defended him from something.

Then He negated these two from Himself, saying: ﴿God has not taken any offspring, and there is not with Him any god.﴾ The "min" in both places is extra, for emphasis of the negation.

Then God, glory be to Him, clarified what the claim of the disbelievers necessitates together with the affirmation of a partner, so He said: ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech; its estimate is: and if there were with God gods, each god would have been independent with his creation, would have been self-sufficient in it, and his dominion would have been distinct from the dominion of the other, and there would have occurred among them contention, warfare, and mutual overpowering. ﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾ that is, the strong would have prevailed over the weak, subdued him and taken his dominion, as is the custom of kings among the children of Adam. The rest read it in the genitive, as an attribute of God or an apposition to Him.

What is meant by "whoever is in it" is all creation, and He expressed them with "whoever" (man) by way of giving precedence to the rational beings. ﴿If you know﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer to the conditional is omitted, meaning: if you know, then inform me. In this there is an allusion to their ignorance and their extreme dullness.

﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ That is, they must say this, because it is known by the immediate judgment of reason. Then God, glory be to Him, commanded him to say to them after their acknowledgment: ﴿Will you not then remember?﴾ as an encouragement for them to reflect and to consider and ponder deeply, for that leads them to follow the truth and abandon falsehood; for whoever was able to create initially is able to bring the dead back to life.

﴿Say: Whose is the Lord of the seven heavens and the Lord of the Great Throne?﴾ They will say, "To God." He, glory be to Him, used the lam (to) in view of the meaning of the question, for your saying "whose is his lord" and "to whom does he belong" have one meaning, like your saying: "Whose is the lord of this house?" and it is said "Zayd," and it is said "to Zayd."

Abu 'Amr and the people of Iraq read (sa-yaqūlūna Allāh) without the lam, in view of the wording of the question, and this reading is clearer than the reading of the others with the lam. However, what supports the reading of the majority is that it is written in all the codices with the lam without an alif.

Likewise in His saying: ﴿Say: In whose hand is the dominion of all things, and He protects while none can be protected against Him, if you know?﴾ ﴿They will say, "To God."﴾ with the lam, in view of the meaning of the question, as has passed.

Abu 'Amr and the people of Iraq read it without the lam, in view of the wording of the question. A similar example is the saying of the poet:

When it is said, "Whose are the villages and the settlements, and the lord of the noble swift horses?" it is said, "To Khalid."

That is, to whom do the villages belong? Al-malakūt means the dominion, and the addition of the taa' is for emphasis, like jabarūt and rahabūt. The meaning of ﴿and He protects﴾ is that He rescues others when He wills and prevents them. ﴿And none can be protected against Him﴾ means that no one can prevent anyone from the punishment of God, nor is anyone able to help or rescue Him. It is said: "I protected so-and-so" when he sought refuge with you and you defended him, and "I protected against him" when I defended him from something.

﴿Say: Then how are you deluded?﴾ Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: that is, you are turned away from the truth and deceived. The meaning is: how is it imagined to you that the truth is falsehood and the sound is corrupt? The one who deceives them is Satan, or desire, or both.

Then God, glory be to Him, clarified that He had made the proof against them thorough, so He said: ﴿Rather, We have brought them the truth﴾ that is, the clear matter which deserves to be followed, ﴿and indeed they are liars﴾ in what they attribute to God, glory be to Him, of offspring and partners.

Then He negated these two from Himself, saying: ﴿God has not taken any offspring, and there is not with Him any god.﴾ The "min" in both places is extra, for emphasis of the negation.

Then God, glory be to Him, clarified what the claim of the disbelievers necessitates together with the affirmation of a partner, so He said: ﴿Otherwise, each god would have taken away what he created﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech; its estimate is: and if there were with God gods, each god would have been independent with his creation, would have been self-sufficient in it, and his dominion would have been distinct from the dominion of the other, and there would have occurred among them contention, warfare, and mutual overpowering. ﴿And some of them would have overcome others﴾ that is, the strong would have prevailed over the weak, subdued him and taken his dominion, as is the custom of kings among the children of Adam. In that case, that weak, vanquished one does not deserve to be a god. When it is established that sharing in that is impossible, and that it is not carried out except by one, it is determined that this one is God, glory be to Him. This argument, just as it indicates the negation of a partner, also indicates the negation of offspring, because offspring would contend with its father for his dominion.

Then God, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of what they describe, so He said: ﴿Glory be to God above what they describe﴾ that is, of partner and offspring, and the attribution of these to God, mighty and majestic.

﴿Knower of the unseen and the witnessed﴾ that is, He is specialized in knowledge of the unseen and the witnessed; as for others, even if they know the witnessed, they do not know the unseen.

Nafi', Abu Bakr, Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read ('ālimu) in the nominative, as the predicate of an omitted subject, meaning: He is knowing.

The rest read it in the genitive, as an attribute of God or an apposition to Him.

It is narrated from Ya'qub that he would read in the genitive when continuing and in the nominative when beginning. ﴿Exalted is God above what they associate﴾ is conjoined to the meaning of what preceded, as if He said: the Knower of the unseen, so exalted; like your saying: "Zayd is brave, so his rank is great," that is, he was brave and so became great. Or it may be by supposing a verb of saying, meaning: I say, exalted is God. The meaning is that He, glory be to Him, is exalted above having any partner in dominion.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 1 of 2):**

.

*Ḥattā* here is the *ibtidā'iyyah* (the "inceptive" *ḥattā*, which introduces a new sentence), and it is followed by a conditional clause. It is nonetheless a *ghāyah* (terminal limit) for what precedes it, and it is connected to His words "they are liars" (*la-kādhibūn*). It has also been said that it is connected to *yaṣifūn* ("they describe"). By "the coming of death" is meant the coming of its signs. ﴿He says, "My Lord, send me back."﴾ That is, the one to whom death has come says this out of regret and grief over what he neglected. "My Lord, send me back" means: return me to the world. He said *irji'ūnī* with the plural pronoun to honour the one addressed.

It has also been said that it is an emphatic repetition of the verb, meaning "send me back, send me back, send me back." A parallel is His words ﴿Cast, cast into Hell﴾ (Q. 50:24). Al-Māzinī said: its meaning is "cast, cast." The same has been said of the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

> *Qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa-manzili*
> ("Halt, let us weep for the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling")

From this is also the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:

> *Yā ḥarasī, iḍribā 'unuqahu*
> ("O my guards, strike his neck")

And from it is the saying of the poet:

> *Wa-law shi'tu ḥarramtu al-nisā'a siwākum*
> ("Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you")

And the saying of another:

> *Alā fārḥamūnī yā ilāha Muḥammadin*
> ("Ah, have mercy upon me, O God of Muhammad")

It has also been said that when they cried out to God, the one among them said "My Lord." Then he returned to addressing the angels and said: ﴿"Send me back, that I may do righteousness."﴾ That is, that I may do righteous deeds in the world if I am returned to it: faith and what follows from it of good works. When he wished to return in order to act, God answered him with His words: ﴿By no means! It is only a word he speaks.﴾ So He brought the particle of repulsion and rebuke (*kallā*). The pronoun in *innahā* ("indeed it") refers to his words "My Lord, send me back." That is: this word is indeed what he says, without doubt, and the matter is not as he supposes, that he will be granted a return to the world. Or the meaning is: even if he were granted that, he would not fulfil it, as in His words ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden﴾ (Q. 6:28). It has also been said that the pronoun in *qā'iluhā* ("its speaker") refers to God, meaning: there is no breach in His report, and He has informed us that He does not delay a soul when its term comes.

﴿And before them is a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾: that is, behind them and before them. The *barzakh* is the partition between two things, as stated by al-Jawharī.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: it is a barrier between death and resurrection.

Al-Kalbī said: it is the term between the two blasts, and between them is forty years.

Al-Suddī said: it is the term, and ﴿until the day they are raised﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾: it has been said this is the first blast, and it has been said it is the second. The latter is preferred. It is the blast that occurs between the raising and the rising. It has also been said that the meaning is: when He blows into the bodies their spirits, taking *al-ṣuwar* as the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), not the horn. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḥasan, *al-ṣuwari* with a fatḥah on the *wāw* and a ḍammah on the *ṣād*, as the plural of *ṣūrah*. Abū Razīn read it with a fatḥah on the *ṣād* and the *wāw*.

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the *ṣād* and a sukūn on the *wāw*, meaning the horn into which one blows.

﴿So there will be no kinship among them that day﴾: that is, they will not boast of their lineages or mention them, because of the bewilderment and astonishment they are in. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾: that is, one will not ask another, for they will then have a preoccupation that absorbs them. From this is His saying: ﴿On the day a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons﴾ (Q. 80:34–36), and His saying: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask of his intimate friend﴾ (Q. 70:10). This is not contradicted by another verse, His saying: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ (Q. 37:27). That is to be understood as referring to the differing standing-places on the Day of Resurrection: the affirmation applies to some of them, and the negation to others, as we have established in the parallels of this matter, which is affirmed at one time and negated at another.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: that is, whose weighed deeds (*mawzūnātuhu*) of righteous works are heavy. ﴿Those are the successful﴾: that is, the ones who attain their beloved aims, who are saved from the things they feared.

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾: these are his righteous deeds. ﴿Those are they who have lost their souls﴾: that is, they wasted and abandoned what would have benefited them. ﴿In Hell they will abide eternally﴾. This is a *badal* (substitute) for the relative clause's connection, or a second predicate of the demonstrative *ulā'ika*. The discussion of this verse has already been given in full, so we will not repeat it.

The clause ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*). It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or it may be a further predicate of *ulā'ika*. *Al-laf'* is burning: one says *lafathathu al-nār* ("the fire scorched him") when it burns him, and *laftuhu bi-al-sayf* ("I struck him with the sword") when one strikes him. He singled out the faces because they are the noblest of the limbs.

﴿And they therein are grimacing﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. *Al-kālih* is one whose lips have drawn back and whose teeth are exposed, as stated by al-Zajjāj. One says *dahrun kālih*, meaning a severe age.

The lexicographers said: *al-kulūḥ* is a gathering together in frowning.

The clause ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ is governed by an implied verb of saying: that is, it will be said to them, as rebuke and reproach: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿So you used to deny them﴾.

The clause ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, an answer to an implied question: that is, our pleasures and our desires overcame us. That was called wretchedness (*shiqwah*) because it ends in misery.

Abū 'Amr and 'Āṣim, the people of Madina, read *shiqwatunā*; the rest read *shaqāwatunā*. This reading is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ūd and al-Ḥasan.

﴿And we were a people who had gone astray﴾: that is, because of that, for they strayed from the truth through that wretchedness.

Then they asked for what they would not be granted, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we return to what we were upon of disbelief and unbelief, then indeed we are wrongdoers to ourselves by returning to that. God answered them with His words: ﴿He said, "Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ That is, remain in Hell. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-khasʾ* is removal with something disliked. Al-Zajjāj said: go away with the going away of wrath, and be removed as a dog is removed.

The meaning according to this is: be removed into Hell, as one says to a dog *ikhsa'* ("begone"), that is, go away. *Khasa'tu al-kalb khasʾan* means I drove the dog off. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ about bringing you out of the Fire and returning you to the world, or about lifting the punishment from you. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not speak to Me at all.

Then He gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said﴾, and they are the believers. It has been said they are the Companions, ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ The majority read *innahu kāna farīqun* with a kasrah on *inna*, as a resumptive explanatory clause. Ubayy read it with a fatḥah.

﴿And you took them in mockery﴾ (*sikhriyyan*). Nāfi', Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *sīn* with a ḍammah. The rest read it with a kasrah. Abū 'Amr distinguished between them: he made the kasrah refer to ridicule (*al-huzuw*), and the ḍammah to subjugation (*al-sukhriyyah*).

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' do not know this distinction. Al-Tha'labī related from al-Kisā'ī that the kasrah means mockery and derision in speech, and the ḍammah means making subservient and deeming remote in deed.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾: that is, you took them for mockery to this extent, for they forgot the remembrance of God because of their great preoccupation with ridicule. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ in the world. The meaning is: until you forgot My remembrance by your preoccupation with mockery and laughter. He attributed this to His servants, the believers, because they were the cause.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, confirming what came before. The *bā'* in *bi-mā ṣabarū* ("for what they endured") indicates causation.

﴿That they are the ones who are successful﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *hamzah* with a kasrah as a new sentence. The rest read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because they are the successful ones." It may also be in the accusative as the second object of the verb.

﴿He said, "How long did you remain on earth, counting years?"﴾ The speaker is God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is a reminder to them: how long did they remain? When they asked to return to the world, after He had informed them that this would not happen, as in His saying "be silent in it." The earth meant is the earth to which they asked to return. It is possible the question concerns the whole of what they remained in life and in the graves. It has also been said that it is a question about the duration of their stay in the graves, because of the phrase "on earth," not "upon the earth." This has been refuted by a parallel like His words ﴿and do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ (Q. 7:56, 85). The accusative of *ʿadada sinīn* is as a specification (*tamyīz*), because of the vagueness in *kam*. *Sinīn* with a fatḥah on the *nūn* is taken as the plural *nūn*. Some Arabs put it in the genitive and give it tanwīn.

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ They underestimated the duration of their stay because of the severe punishment they were in.

It has been said that the punishment was lifted from them between the two blasts, so they forgot the punishment they had been in in their graves. It has also been said that God caused them to forget the punishment they had been in from the first blast to the second.

Then, when they realised what had befallen them of forgetfulness, because of the great terror they were in, they referred the matter to others and said: ﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, those who are capable of knowing the number. They are the angels, because they are the guardians who know the deeds and lifespans of the servants. It has also been said that the meaning is: ask those who reckon, the people who know reckoning among mankind.

Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "How long did you remain on earth?"﴾ in the imperative. The meaning: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers. Or it is an imperative to the angel to question them. Or the implied sense is: say, "How long did you remain?" The speech is thus given the form of a command to one person while the meaning is a group.

The rest read ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ taking the speaker to be God, the Mighty and Majestic, or the angel.

﴿He said, "You remained but a little, if only you had known."﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "If you remained but a little"﴾ as in the first verse. The rest read *qāla* ("he said") as a report. The two readings have already been explained. The meaning: you did not remain on earth except a brief stay, ﴿if only you had known﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer is omitted: if you had known, you would have known today the brevity of your stay on earth or in the graves or in both. All of that is brief in comparison with their staying.

Then He, glory be to Him, increased their rebuke and said: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain?﴾ The *hamzah* is for rebuke and affirmation, and the *fā'* is for coordination with an implied element, as explained elsewhere: that is, did you not know anything, so that you supposed? *ʿAbathan* in the accusative is either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*): playing about; or as a cause: for play.

Sībawayh and Quṭrub said the first; Abū 'Ubayda said the second.

He also said: it may be accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The clause ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ is coordinated with *annamā khalaqnākum ʿabatan* ("that We created you in vain"). *Al-ʿabath* in the lexicon is play: one says *ʿabatha yaʿbathu ʿabatan*, so he is *ʿābith*, meaning playing. Its root is from the phrase *ʿabathtu al-aqiṭ*, "I mixed the dried curd." The meaning: did you suppose that Our creating you was for neglect, as cattle are created, with no reward and no punishment, and that you would not return to Us in resurrection and rising, so that We would recompense you for your deeds?

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *turjaʿūn* with a fatḥah on the initial *tā'* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, in the active voice. The rest read it in the passive voice.

It has been said that ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ may be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, in the sense: that We created you for play and for not being returned.

Then He, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of imperfection and said: ﴿So exalted is God﴾: that is, He is far removed from having children and partners, or from creating anything in vain, or from all of that. He is the King who alone rightly possesses sovereignty absolutely, the Truth in all His acts and words. ﴿There is no deity but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾. How then could He not be God and Lord of what is beneath the Noble Throne among created beings? The description of the Throne as *al-karīm* ("noble") is because mercy and goodness descend from it, or with regard to the one who sits upon it, as one says *bayt karīm* ("a noble house") when its occupants are noble.

Abū Ja'far, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ismā'īl and Abān ibn Tha'lab read *al-karīmu* in the nominative, as an epithet of *Rabb* ("Lord"). The rest read it in the genitive, as an epithet of *al-ʿarsh* ("the Throne").

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 2 of 2):

Then He refuted what the people of polytheism held, rebuking and reproaching them, and said: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him alongside Allah or worshipping him alone. The clause ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb) as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah) of the word ilāhan (إلهًا, "a god"). It is a necessary qualifier (ṣifah lāzimah), brought for emphasis, like His saying ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. Al-burhān (البُرْهان) means the clear argument and the evident proof. The answer to the conditional clause (sharṭ) is His saying: ﴿then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾. The clause "for which he has no proof" is an interjected clause (mu‘taridah) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of good from him, so Allah will reward him."
