The meaning: did you suppose that Our creating you was for neglect, as cattle are created, with no reward and no punishment, and that you would not return to Us in resurrection and rising, so that We would recompense you for your deeds?

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *turjaʿūn* with a fatḥah on the initial *tā'* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, in the active voice. The rest read it in the passive voice.

It has been said that ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ may be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, in the sense: that We created you for play and for not being returned.

Then He, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of imperfection and said: ﴿So exalted is God﴾: that is, He is far removed from having children and partners, or from creating anything in vain, or from all of that. He is the King who alone rightly possesses sovereignty absolutely, the Truth in all His acts and words. ﴿There is no deity but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾. How then could He not be God and Lord of what is beneath the Noble Throne among created beings? The description of the Throne as *al-karīm* ("noble") is because mercy and goodness descend from it, or with regard to the one who sits upon it, as one says *bayt karīm* ("a noble house") when its occupants are noble.

Abū Ja'far, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ismā'īl and Abān ibn Tha'lab read *al-karīmu* in the nominative, as an epithet of *Rabb* ("Lord"). The rest read it in the genitive, as an epithet of *al-ʿarsh* ("the Throne").

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 2 of 2):

Then He refuted what the people of polytheism held, rebuking and reproaching them, and said: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him alongside Allah or worshipping him alone. The clause ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb) as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah) of the word ilāhan (إلهًا, "a god"). It is a necessary qualifier (ṣifah lāzimah), brought for emphasis, like His saying ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. Al-burhān (البُرْهان) means the clear argument and the evident proof. The answer to the conditional clause (sharṭ) is His saying: ﴿then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾. The clause "for which he has no proof" is an interjected clause (mu‘taridah) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of good from him, so Allah will reward him." It was also said that the response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, with the response particle (fā’ al-jazā’) omitted, as in the poet's words:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them.*

﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatadah read *innа* (أنَّ) with a fatḥah, as a causal clause (ta‘līl, "giving a reason"). The rest read it with a kasrah, as a new independent sentence (isti’nāf, "resumption"). Al-Hasan also read *lā yufliḥu* (لا يُفْلِحُ) with a fatḥah on the yā' and the lām, as the present tense of *falaḥa*, with the same meaning as *aflaḥa*.

Then He concluded this surah by teaching His Messenger (ﷺ) to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, so He said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ He, glorified is He, commanded him to seek forgiveness so that his community would follow him. It was also said: He commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community. The explanation of His being the most merciful of the merciful has already been given. The connection of this with what precedes it is that when He, glorified is He, described the conditions of the disbelievers, He commanded (the Prophet) to turn exclusively to Him and to seek refuge in His forgiveness and mercy.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the disbeliever is placed in his grave and sees his seat in the Fire, he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ — 'I will repent and do righteous deeds.' Then it is said to him: 'You have been given a life long enough for what you were given.' His grave then constricts upon him, and he becomes like one being stung, writhing and screaming, while the snakes and scorpions of the earth swarm upon him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "They claimed that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Aishah: 'When the believer sees the angels, they say: "We will send you back to the world." He says: "To the house of worries and sorrows? Rather, send me forward to Allah." As for the disbelievers, they say to him: "We will send you back," and he says: "My Lord, send me back ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾."'" This is a mursal report (one whose chain lacks a companion).

Al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death approaches a person, everything that prevents him from the truth is gathered for him and placed before his eyes. At that moment he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back, so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind.﴾"

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds﴾: he said, "I will say: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Aishah, who said: "Woe to the people of sins from the people of the graves. Black snakes enter upon them in their graves: a snake at his head and a snake at his feet, pinching him until they meet in his middle. That is the punishment in the barzakh (intermediate state) of which Allah said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾: he said, "When the Trumpet is blown, no one will remain alive except Allah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he was asked about His saying ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾ and His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27; al-Tur: 25]. He said: "These are different stations. As for the station in which there is no kinship between them and they do not ask one another, it is at the first blast (al-ṣa‘qah al-ūlā), when there is no kinship between them, for they will be struck down. But when the final blast comes, they will be standing and asking one another."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, also related from him that he was asked about the two verses. He said: "As for His saying ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾, this is at the first blast, when nothing remains upon the earth. As for His saying ﴿So some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 50], this is when they have entered Paradise, and some of them turn to others, asking one another."

Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will gather the first and the last." In another wording: "On the Day of Resurrection, a servant or a maidservant will be taken by the hand before the heads of the first and the last, then a herald will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come and take his right.'"

In another wording: "Whoever has a grievance, let him come and take his right. By Allah, a man will rejoice that he has a right against his father, his son, or his wife, even if she is small. The proof of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾"

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, kinship is cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship, my cause (sabab) and my in-law relation (ṣihr)."

Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym, al-Hakim and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every cause and every kinship will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my cause and my kinship."

Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every kinship and in-law relation will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship and my in-law relation."

Ahmad related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say from the pulpit: "What is the matter with men who say that the kinship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will not benefit his people? Indeed, by Allah, my kinship is connected in this world and the Hereafter, and I, O people, am your forerunner (faraṭ)."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: he said, "It blows upon them."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in *Sifat al-Nar* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying: "﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: it scorches them with one scorching, and their flesh slides off their heels."

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: "It scorched them with one scorching, leaving no flesh on a bone without throwing it off their heels."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Sifat al-Nar*, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn Mardawayh related concerning His saying ﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾: "The Fire disfigures them, so that the upper lip is drawn up until it reaches the middle of the head, and the lower lip hangs down until it strikes the navel."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse: "The grimace of a cooked head: their teeth show and their lips are drawn back."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿kāliḥūn﴾ (grimacing): "Frowning."

Many well-known reports have come concerning the description of the people of the Fire, what they will say, and what will be said to them.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wa'l-Laylah*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related "from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited into the ear of a afflicted person ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ until he completed the surah, and he was healed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'With what did you recite into his ear?' He informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if a man with certainty recited it over a mountain, it would move.'"

Ibn al-Sunni, Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* related, and al-Suyuti said with a good chain, through the route of Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a military expedition and commanded us to say, when we reached evening and morning: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ We recited it, and we gained booty and were safe." End of quotation.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 1 of 2):**

.

*Ḥattā* here is the *ibtidā'iyyah* (the "inceptive" *ḥattā*, which introduces a new sentence), and it is followed by a conditional clause. It is nonetheless a *ghāyah* (terminal limit) for what precedes it, and it is connected to His words "they are liars" (*la-kādhibūn*). It has also been said that it is connected to *yaṣifūn* ("they describe"). By "the coming of death" is meant the coming of its signs. ﴿He says, "My Lord, send me back."﴾ That is, the one to whom death has come says this out of regret and grief over what he neglected. "My Lord, send me back" means: return me to the world. He said *irji'ūnī* with the plural pronoun to honour the one addressed.

It has also been said that it is an emphatic repetition of the verb, meaning "send me back, send me back, send me back." A parallel is His words ﴿Cast, cast into Hell﴾ (Q. 50:24). Al-Māzinī said: its meaning is "cast, cast." The same has been said of the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

> *Qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa-manzili*
> ("Halt, let us weep for the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling")

From this is also the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:

> *Yā ḥarasī, iḍribā 'unuqahu*
> ("O my guards, strike his neck")

And from it is the saying of the poet:

> *Wa-law shi'tu ḥarramtu al-nisā'a siwākum*
> ("Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you")

And the saying of another:

> *Alā fārḥamūnī yā ilāha Muḥammadin*
> ("Ah, have mercy upon me, O God of Muhammad")

It has also been said that when they cried out to God, the one among them said "My Lord." Then he returned to addressing the angels and said: ﴿"Send me back, that I may do righteousness."﴾ That is, that I may do righteous deeds in the world if I am returned to it: faith and what follows from it of good works. When he wished to return in order to act, God answered him with His words: ﴿By no means! It is only a word he speaks.﴾ So He brought the particle of repulsion and rebuke (*kallā*). The pronoun in *innahā* ("indeed it") refers to his words "My Lord, send me back." That is: this word is indeed what he says, without doubt, and the matter is not as he supposes, that he will be granted a return to the world. Or the meaning is: even if he were granted that, he would not fulfil it, as in His words ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden﴾ (Q. 6:28). It has also been said that the pronoun in *qā'iluhā* ("its speaker") refers to God, meaning: there is no breach in His report, and He has informed us that He does not delay a soul when its term comes.

﴿And before them is a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾: that is, behind them and before them. The *barzakh* is the partition between two things, as stated by al-Jawharī.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: it is a barrier between death and resurrection.

Al-Kalbī said: it is the term between the two blasts, and between them is forty years.

Al-Suddī said: it is the term, and ﴿until the day they are raised﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾: it has been said this is the first blast, and it has been said it is the second. The latter is preferred. It is the blast that occurs between the raising and the rising. It has also been said that the meaning is: when He blows into the bodies their spirits, taking *al-ṣuwar* as the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), not the horn. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḥasan, *al-ṣuwari* with a fatḥah on the *wāw* and a ḍammah on the *ṣād*, as the plural of *ṣūrah*. Abū Razīn read it with a fatḥah on the *ṣād* and the *wāw*.

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the *ṣād* and a sukūn on the *wāw*, meaning the horn into which one blows.

﴿So there will be no kinship among them that day﴾: that is, they will not boast of their lineages or mention them, because of the bewilderment and astonishment they are in. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾: that is, one will not ask another, for they will then have a preoccupation that absorbs them. From this is His saying: ﴿On the day a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons﴾ (Q. 80:34–36), and His saying: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask of his intimate friend﴾ (Q. 70:10). This is not contradicted by another verse, His saying: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ (Q. 37:27). That is to be understood as referring to the differing standing-places on the Day of Resurrection: the affirmation applies to some of them, and the negation to others, as we have established in the parallels of this matter, which is affirmed at one time and negated at another.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: that is, whose weighed deeds (*mawzūnātuhu*) of righteous works are heavy. ﴿Those are the successful﴾: that is, the ones who attain their beloved aims, who are saved from the things they feared.

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾: these are his righteous deeds. ﴿Those are they who have lost their souls﴾: that is, they wasted and abandoned what would have benefited them. ﴿In Hell they will abide eternally﴾. This is a *badal* (substitute) for the relative clause's connection, or a second predicate of the demonstrative *ulā'ika*. The discussion of this verse has already been given in full, so we will not repeat it.

The clause ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*). It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or it may be a further predicate of *ulā'ika*. *Al-laf'* is burning: one says *lafathathu al-nār* ("the fire scorched him") when it burns him, and *laftuhu bi-al-sayf* ("I struck him with the sword") when one strikes him. He singled out the faces because they are the noblest of the limbs.

﴿And they therein are grimacing﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. *Al-kālih* is one whose lips have drawn back and whose teeth are exposed, as stated by al-Zajjāj. One says *dahrun kālih*, meaning a severe age.

The lexicographers said: *al-kulūḥ* is a gathering together in frowning.

The clause ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ is governed by an implied verb of saying: that is, it will be said to them, as rebuke and reproach: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿So you used to deny them﴾.

The clause ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, an answer to an implied question: that is, our pleasures and our desires overcame us. That was called wretchedness (*shiqwah*) because it ends in misery.

Abū 'Amr and 'Āṣim, the people of Madina, read *shiqwatunā*; the rest read *shaqāwatunā*. This reading is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ūd and al-Ḥasan.

﴿And we were a people who had gone astray﴾: that is, because of that, for they strayed from the truth through that wretchedness.

Then they asked for what they would not be granted, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we return to what we were upon of disbelief and unbelief, then indeed we are wrongdoers to ourselves by returning to that. God answered them with His words: ﴿He said, "Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ That is, remain in Hell. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-khasʾ* is removal with something disliked. Al-Zajjāj said: go away with the going away of wrath, and be removed as a dog is removed.

The meaning according to this is: be removed into Hell, as one says to a dog *ikhsa'* ("begone"), that is, go away. *Khasa'tu al-kalb khasʾan* means I drove the dog off. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ about bringing you out of the Fire and returning you to the world, or about lifting the punishment from you. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not speak to Me at all.

Then He gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said﴾, and they are the believers. It has been said they are the Companions, ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ The majority read *innahu kāna farīqun* with a kasrah on *inna*, as a resumptive explanatory clause. Ubayy read it with a fatḥah.

﴿And you took them in mockery﴾ (*sikhriyyan*). Nāfi', Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *sīn* with a ḍammah. The rest read it with a kasrah. Abū 'Amr distinguished between them: he made the kasrah refer to ridicule (*al-huzuw*), and the ḍammah to subjugation (*al-sukhriyyah*).

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' do not know this distinction. Al-Tha'labī related from al-Kisā'ī that the kasrah means mockery and derision in speech, and the ḍammah means making subservient and deeming remote in deed.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾: that is, you took them for mockery to this extent, for they forgot the remembrance of God because of their great preoccupation with ridicule. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ in the world. The meaning is: until you forgot My remembrance by your preoccupation with mockery and laughter. He attributed this to His servants, the believers, because they were the cause.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, confirming what came before. The *bā'* in *bi-mā ṣabarū* ("for what they endured") indicates causation.

﴿That they are the ones who are successful﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *hamzah* with a kasrah as a new sentence. The rest read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because they are the successful ones." It may also be in the accusative as the second object of the verb.

﴿He said, "How long did you remain on earth, counting years?"﴾ The speaker is God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is a reminder to them: how long did they remain? When they asked to return to the world, after He had informed them that this would not happen, as in His saying "be silent in it." The earth meant is the earth to which they asked to return. It is possible the question concerns the whole of what they remained in life and in the graves. It has also been said that it is a question about the duration of their stay in the graves, because of the phrase "on earth," not "upon the earth." This has been refuted by a parallel like His words ﴿and do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ (Q. 7:56, 85). The accusative of *ʿadada sinīn* is as a specification (*tamyīz*), because of the vagueness in *kam*. *Sinīn* with a fatḥah on the *nūn* is taken as the plural *nūn*. Some Arabs put it in the genitive and give it tanwīn.

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ They underestimated the duration of their stay because of the severe punishment they were in.

It has been said that the punishment was lifted from them between the two blasts, so they forgot the punishment they had been in in their graves. It has also been said that God caused them to forget the punishment they had been in from the first blast to the second.

Then, when they realised what had befallen them of forgetfulness, because of the great terror they were in, they referred the matter to others and said: ﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, those who are capable of knowing the number. They are the angels, because they are the guardians who know the deeds and lifespans of the servants. It has also been said that the meaning is: ask those who reckon, the people who know reckoning among mankind.

Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "How long did you remain on earth?"﴾ in the imperative. The meaning: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers. Or it is an imperative to the angel to question them. Or the implied sense is: say, "How long did you remain?" The speech is thus given the form of a command to one person while the meaning is a group.

The rest read ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ taking the speaker to be God, the Mighty and Majestic, or the angel.

﴿He said, "You remained but a little, if only you had known."﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "If you remained but a little"﴾ as in the first verse. The rest read *qāla* ("he said") as a report. The two readings have already been explained. The meaning: you did not remain on earth except a brief stay, ﴿if only you had known﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer is omitted: if you had known, you would have known today the brevity of your stay on earth or in the graves or in both. All of that is brief in comparison with their staying.

Then He, glory be to Him, increased their rebuke and said: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain?﴾ The *hamzah* is for rebuke and affirmation, and the *fā'* is for coordination with an implied element, as explained elsewhere: that is, did you not know anything, so that you supposed? *ʿAbathan* in the accusative is either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*): playing about; or as a cause: for play.

Sībawayh and Quṭrub said the first; Abū 'Ubayda said the second.

He also said: it may be accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The clause ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ is coordinated with *annamā khalaqnākum ʿabatan* ("that We created you in vain"). *Al-ʿabath* in the lexicon is play: one says *ʿabatha yaʿbathu ʿabatan*, so he is *ʿābith*, meaning playing. Its root is from the phrase *ʿabathtu al-aqiṭ*, "I mixed the dried curd." The meaning: did you suppose that Our creating you was for neglect, as cattle are created, with no reward and no punishment, and that you would not return to Us in resurrection and rising, so that We would recompense you for your deeds?

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *turjaʿūn* with a fatḥah on the initial *tā'* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, in the active voice. The rest read it in the passive voice.

It has been said that ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ may be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, in the sense: that We created you for play and for not being returned.

Then He, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of imperfection and said: ﴿So exalted is God﴾: that is, He is far removed from having children and partners, or from creating anything in vain, or from all of that. He is the King who alone rightly possesses sovereignty absolutely, the Truth in all His acts and words. ﴿There is no deity but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾. How then could He not be God and Lord of what is beneath the Noble Throne among created beings? The description of the Throne as *al-karīm* ("noble") is because mercy and goodness descend from it, or with regard to the one who sits upon it, as one says *bayt karīm* ("a noble house") when its occupants are noble.

Abū Ja'far, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ismā'īl and Abān ibn Tha'lab read *al-karīmu* in the nominative, as an epithet of *Rabb* ("Lord"). The rest read it in the genitive, as an epithet of *al-ʿarsh* ("the Throne").

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 2 of 2):

Then He refuted what the people of polytheism held, rebuking and reproaching them, and said: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him alongside Allah or worshipping him alone. The clause ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb) as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah) of the word ilāhan (إلهًا, "a god"). It is a necessary qualifier (ṣifah lāzimah), brought for emphasis, like His saying ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. Al-burhān (البُرْهان) means the clear argument and the evident proof. The answer to the conditional clause (sharṭ) is His saying: ﴿then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾. The clause "for which he has no proof" is an interjected clause (mu‘taridah) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of good from him, so Allah will reward him." It was also said that the response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, with the response particle (fā’ al-jazā’) omitted, as in the poet's words:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them.*

﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatadah read *innа* (أنَّ) with a fatḥah, as a causal clause (ta‘līl, "giving a reason"). The rest read it with a kasrah, as a new independent sentence (isti’nāf, "resumption"). Al-Hasan also read *lā yufliḥu* (لا يُفْلِحُ) with a fatḥah on the yā' and the lām, as the present tense of *falaḥa*, with the same meaning as *aflaḥa*.

Then He concluded this surah by teaching His Messenger (ﷺ) to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, so He said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ He, glorified is He, commanded him to seek forgiveness so that his community would follow him. It was also said: He commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community. The explanation of His being the most merciful of the merciful has already been given. The connection of this with what precedes it is that when He, glorified is He, described the conditions of the disbelievers, He commanded (the Prophet) to turn exclusively to Him and to seek refuge in His forgiveness and mercy.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the disbeliever is placed in his grave and sees his seat in the Fire, he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ — 'I will repent and do righteous deeds.' Then it is said to him: 'You have been given a life long enough for what you were given.' His grave then constricts upon him, and he becomes like one being stung, writhing and screaming, while the snakes and scorpions of the earth swarm upon him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "They claimed that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Aishah: 'When the believer sees the angels, they say: "We will send you back to the world." He says: "To the house of worries and sorrows? Rather, send me forward to Allah." As for the disbelievers, they say to him: "We will send you back," and he says: "My Lord, send me back ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾."'" This is a mursal report (one whose chain lacks a companion).

Al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death approaches a person, everything that prevents him from the truth is gathered for him and placed before his eyes. At that moment he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back, so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind.﴾"

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds﴾: he said, "I will say: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Aishah, who said: "Woe to the people of sins from the people of the graves. Black snakes enter upon them in their graves: a snake at his head and a snake at his feet, pinching him until they meet in his middle. That is the punishment in the barzakh (intermediate state) of which Allah said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾: he said, "When the Trumpet is blown, no one will remain alive except Allah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he was asked about His saying ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾ and His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27; al-Tur: 25]. He said: "These are different stations. As for the station in which there is no kinship between them and they do not ask one another, it is at the first blast (al-ṣa‘qah al-ūlā), when there is no kinship between them, for they will be struck down. But when the final blast comes, they will be standing and asking one another."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, also related from him that he was asked about the two verses. He said: "As for His saying ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾, this is at the first blast, when nothing remains upon the earth. As for His saying ﴿So some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 50], this is when they have entered Paradise, and some of them turn to others, asking one another."

Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will gather the first and the last." In another wording: "On the Day of Resurrection, a servant or a maidservant will be taken by the hand before the heads of the first and the last, then a herald will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come and take his right.'"

In another wording: "Whoever has a grievance, let him come and take his right. By Allah, a man will rejoice that he has a right against his father, his son, or his wife, even if she is small. The proof of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾"

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, kinship is cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship, my cause (sabab) and my in-law relation (ṣihr)."

Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym, al-Hakim and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every cause and every kinship will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my cause and my kinship."

Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every kinship and in-law relation will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship and my in-law relation."

Ahmad related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say from the pulpit: "What is the matter with men who say that the kinship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will not benefit his people? Indeed, by Allah, my kinship is connected in this world and the Hereafter, and I, O people, am your forerunner (faraṭ)."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: he said, "It blows upon them."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in *Sifat al-Nar* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying: "﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: it scorches them with one scorching, and their flesh slides off their heels."

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: "It scorched them with one scorching, leaving no flesh on a bone without throwing it off their heels."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Sifat al-Nar*, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn Mardawayh related concerning His saying ﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾: "The Fire disfigures them, so that the upper lip is drawn up until it reaches the middle of the head, and the lower lip hangs down until it strikes the navel."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse: "The grimace of a cooked head: their teeth show and their lips are drawn back."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿kāliḥūn﴾ (grimacing): "Frowning."

Many well-known reports have come concerning the description of the people of the Fire, what they will say, and what will be said to them.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wa'l-Laylah*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related "from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited into the ear of a afflicted person ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ until he completed the surah, and he was healed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'With what did you recite into his ear?' He informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if a man with certainty recited it over a mountain, it would move.'"

Ibn al-Sunni, Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* related, and al-Suyuti said with a good chain, through the route of Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a military expedition and commanded us to say, when we reached evening and morning: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ We recited it, and we gained booty and were safe." End of quotation.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 1 of 2):**

.

*Ḥattā* here is the *ibtidā'iyyah* (the "inceptive" *ḥattā*, which introduces a new sentence), and it is followed by a conditional clause. It is nonetheless a *ghāyah* (terminal limit) for what precedes it, and it is connected to His words "they are liars" (*la-kādhibūn*). It has also been said that it is connected to *yaṣifūn* ("they describe"). By "the coming of death" is meant the coming of its signs. ﴿He says, "My Lord, send me back."﴾ That is, the one to whom death has come says this out of regret and grief over what he neglected. "My Lord, send me back" means: return me to the world. He said *irji'ūnī* with the plural pronoun to honour the one addressed.

It has also been said that it is an emphatic repetition of the verb, meaning "send me back, send me back, send me back." A parallel is His words ﴿Cast, cast into Hell﴾ (Q. 50:24). Al-Māzinī said: its meaning is "cast, cast." The same has been said of the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

> *Qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa-manzili*
> ("Halt, let us weep for the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling")

From this is also the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:

> *Yā ḥarasī, iḍribā 'unuqahu*
> ("O my guards, strike his neck")

And from it is the saying of the poet:

> *Wa-law shi'tu ḥarramtu al-nisā'a siwākum*
> ("Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you")

And the saying of another:

> *Alā fārḥamūnī yā ilāha Muḥammadin*
> ("Ah, have mercy upon me, O God of Muhammad")

It has also been said that when they cried out to God, the one among them said "My Lord." Then he returned to addressing the angels and said: ﴿"Send me back, that I may do righteousness."﴾ That is, that I may do righteous deeds in the world if I am returned to it: faith and what follows from it of good works. When he wished to return in order to act, God answered him with His words: ﴿By no means! It is only a word he speaks.﴾ So He brought the particle of repulsion and rebuke (*kallā*). The pronoun in *innahā* ("indeed it") refers to his words "My Lord, send me back." That is: this word is indeed what he says, without doubt, and the matter is not as he supposes, that he will be granted a return to the world. Or the meaning is: even if he were granted that, he would not fulfil it, as in His words ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden﴾ (Q. 6:28). It has also been said that the pronoun in *qā'iluhā* ("its speaker") refers to God, meaning: there is no breach in His report, and He has informed us that He does not delay a soul when its term comes.

﴿And before them is a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾: that is, behind them and before them. The *barzakh* is the partition between two things, as stated by al-Jawharī.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: it is a barrier between death and resurrection.

Al-Kalbī said: it is the term between the two blasts, and between them is forty years.

Al-Suddī said: it is the term, and ﴿until the day they are raised﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾: it has been said this is the first blast, and it has been said it is the second. The latter is preferred. It is the blast that occurs between the raising and the rising. It has also been said that the meaning is: when He blows into the bodies their spirits, taking *al-ṣuwar* as the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), not the horn. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḥasan, *al-ṣuwari* with a fatḥah on the *wāw* and a ḍammah on the *ṣād*, as the plural of *ṣūrah*. Abū Razīn read it with a fatḥah on the *ṣād* and the *wāw*.

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the *ṣād* and a sukūn on the *wāw*, meaning the horn into which one blows.

﴿So there will be no kinship among them that day﴾: that is, they will not boast of their lineages or mention them, because of the bewilderment and astonishment they are in. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾: that is, one will not ask another, for they will then have a preoccupation that absorbs them. From this is His saying: ﴿On the day a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons﴾ (Q. 80:34–36), and His saying: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask of his intimate friend﴾ (Q. 70:10). This is not contradicted by another verse, His saying: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ (Q. 37:27). That is to be understood as referring to the differing standing-places on the Day of Resurrection: the affirmation applies to some of them, and the negation to others, as we have established in the parallels of this matter, which is affirmed at one time and negated at another.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: that is, whose weighed deeds (*mawzūnātuhu*) of righteous works are heavy. ﴿Those are the successful﴾: that is, the ones who attain their beloved aims, who are saved from the things they feared.

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾: these are his righteous deeds. ﴿Those are they who have lost their souls﴾: that is, they wasted and abandoned what would have benefited them. ﴿In Hell they will abide eternally﴾. This is a *badal* (substitute) for the relative clause's connection, or a second predicate of the demonstrative *ulā'ika*. The discussion of this verse has already been given in full, so we will not repeat it.

The clause ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*). It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or it may be a further predicate of *ulā'ika*. *Al-laf'* is burning: one says *lafathathu al-nār* ("the fire scorched him") when it burns him, and *laftuhu bi-al-sayf* ("I struck him with the sword") when one strikes him. He singled out the faces because they are the noblest of the limbs.

﴿And they therein are grimacing﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. *Al-kālih* is one whose lips have drawn back and whose teeth are exposed, as stated by al-Zajjāj. One says *dahrun kālih*, meaning a severe age.

The lexicographers said: *al-kulūḥ* is a gathering together in frowning.

The clause ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ is governed by an implied verb of saying: that is, it will be said to them, as rebuke and reproach: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿So you used to deny them﴾.

The clause ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, an answer to an implied question: that is, our pleasures and our desires overcame us. That was called wretchedness (*shiqwah*) because it ends in misery.

Abū 'Amr and 'Āṣim, the people of Madina, read *shiqwatunā*; the rest read *shaqāwatunā*. This reading is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ūd and al-Ḥasan.

﴿And we were a people who had gone astray﴾: that is, because of that, for they strayed from the truth through that wretchedness.

Then they asked for what they would not be granted, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we return to what we were upon of disbelief and unbelief, then indeed we are wrongdoers to ourselves by returning to that. God answered them with His words: ﴿He said, "Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ That is, remain in Hell. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-khasʾ* is removal with something disliked. Al-Zajjāj said: go away with the going away of wrath, and be removed as a dog is removed.

The meaning according to this is: be removed into Hell, as one says to a dog *ikhsa'* ("begone"), that is, go away. *Khasa'tu al-kalb khasʾan* means I drove the dog off. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ about bringing you out of the Fire and returning you to the world, or about lifting the punishment from you. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not speak to Me at all.

Then He gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said﴾, and they are the believers. It has been said they are the Companions, ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ The majority read *innahu kāna farīqun* with a kasrah on *inna*, as a resumptive explanatory clause. Ubayy read it with a fatḥah.

﴿And you took them in mockery﴾ (*sikhriyyan*). Nāfi', Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *sīn* with a ḍammah. The rest read it with a kasrah. Abū 'Amr distinguished between them: he made the kasrah refer to ridicule (*al-huzuw*), and the ḍammah to subjugation (*al-sukhriyyah*).

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' do not know this distinction. Al-Tha'labī related from al-Kisā'ī that the kasrah means mockery and derision in speech, and the ḍammah means making subservient and deeming remote in deed.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾: that is, you took them for mockery to this extent, for they forgot the remembrance of God because of their great preoccupation with ridicule. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ in the world. The meaning is: until you forgot My remembrance by your preoccupation with mockery and laughter. He attributed this to His servants, the believers, because they were the cause.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, confirming what came before. The *bā'* in *bi-mā ṣabarū* ("for what they endured") indicates causation.

﴿That they are the ones who are successful﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *hamzah* with a kasrah as a new sentence. The rest read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because they are the successful ones." It may also be in the accusative as the second object of the verb.

﴿He said, "How long did you remain on earth, counting years?"﴾ The speaker is God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is a reminder to them: how long did they remain? When they asked to return to the world, after He had informed them that this would not happen, as in His saying "be silent in it." The earth meant is the earth to which they asked to return. It is possible the question concerns the whole of what they remained in life and in the graves. It has also been said that it is a question about the duration of their stay in the graves, because of the phrase "on earth," not "upon the earth." This has been refuted by a parallel like His words ﴿and do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ (Q. 7:56, 85). The accusative of *ʿadada sinīn* is as a specification (*tamyīz*), because of the vagueness in *kam*. *Sinīn* with a fatḥah on the *nūn* is taken as the plural *nūn*. Some Arabs put it in the genitive and give it tanwīn.

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ They underestimated the duration of their stay because of the severe punishment they were in.

It has been said that the punishment was lifted from them between the two blasts, so they forgot the punishment they had been in in their graves. It has also been said that God caused them to forget the punishment they had been in from the first blast to the second.

Then, when they realised what had befallen them of forgetfulness, because of the great terror they were in, they referred the matter to others and said: ﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, those who are capable of knowing the number. They are the angels, because they are the guardians who know the deeds and lifespans of the servants. It has also been said that the meaning is: ask those who reckon, the people who know reckoning among mankind.

Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "How long did you remain on earth?"﴾ in the imperative. The meaning: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers. Or it is an imperative to the angel to question them. Or the implied sense is: say, "How long did you remain?" The speech is thus given the form of a command to one person while the meaning is a group.

The rest read ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ taking the speaker to be God, the Mighty and Majestic, or the angel.

﴿He said, "You remained but a little, if only you had known."﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "If you remained but a little"﴾ as in the first verse. The rest read *qāla* ("he said") as a report. The two readings have already been explained. The meaning: you did not remain on earth except a brief stay, ﴿if only you had known﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer is omitted: if you had known, you would have known today the brevity of your stay on earth or in the graves or in both. All of that is brief in comparison with their staying.

Then He, glory be to Him, increased their rebuke and said: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain?﴾ The *hamzah* is for rebuke and affirmation, and the *fā'* is for coordination with an implied element, as explained elsewhere: that is, did you not know anything, so that you supposed? *ʿAbathan* in the accusative is either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*): playing about; or as a cause: for play.

Sībawayh and Quṭrub said the first; Abū 'Ubayda said the second.

He also said: it may be accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The clause ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ is coordinated with *annamā khalaqnākum ʿabatan* ("that We created you in vain"). *Al-ʿabath* in the lexicon is play: one says *ʿabatha yaʿbathu ʿabatan*, so he is *ʿābith*, meaning playing. Its root is from the phrase *ʿabathtu al-aqiṭ*, "I mixed the dried curd." The meaning: did you suppose that Our creating you was for neglect, as cattle are created, with no reward and no punishment, and that you would not return to Us in resurrection and rising, so that We would recompense you for your deeds?

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *turjaʿūn* with a fatḥah on the initial *tā'* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, in the active voice. The rest read it in the passive voice.

It has been said that ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ may be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, in the sense: that We created you for play and for not being returned.

Then He, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of imperfection and said: ﴿So exalted is God﴾: that is, He is far removed from having children and partners, or from creating anything in vain, or from all of that. He is the King who alone rightly possesses sovereignty absolutely, the Truth in all His acts and words. ﴿There is no deity but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾. How then could He not be God and Lord of what is beneath the Noble Throne among created beings? The description of the Throne as *al-karīm* ("noble") is because mercy and goodness descend from it, or with regard to the one who sits upon it, as one says *bayt karīm* ("a noble house") when its occupants are noble.

Abū Ja'far, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ismā'īl and Abān ibn Tha'lab read *al-karīmu* in the nominative, as an epithet of *Rabb* ("Lord"). The rest read it in the genitive, as an epithet of *al-ʿarsh* ("the Throne").

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 2 of 2):

Then He refuted what the people of polytheism held, rebuking and reproaching them, and said: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him alongside Allah or worshipping him alone. The clause ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb) as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah) of the word ilāhan (إلهًا, "a god"). It is a necessary qualifier (ṣifah lāzimah), brought for emphasis, like His saying ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. Al-burhān (البُرْهان) means the clear argument and the evident proof. The answer to the conditional clause (sharṭ) is His saying: ﴿then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾. The clause "for which he has no proof" is an interjected clause (mu‘taridah) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of good from him, so Allah will reward him." It was also said that the response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, with the response particle (fā’ al-jazā’) omitted, as in the poet's words:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them.*

﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatadah read *innа* (أنَّ) with a fatḥah, as a causal clause (ta‘līl, "giving a reason"). The rest read it with a kasrah, as a new independent sentence (isti’nāf, "resumption"). Al-Hasan also read *lā yufliḥu* (لا يُفْلِحُ) with a fatḥah on the yā' and the lām, as the present tense of *falaḥa*, with the same meaning as *aflaḥa*.

Then He concluded this surah by teaching His Messenger (ﷺ) to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, so He said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ He, glorified is He, commanded him to seek forgiveness so that his community would follow him. It was also said: He commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community. The explanation of His being the most merciful of the merciful has already been given. The connection of this with what precedes it is that when He, glorified is He, described the conditions of the disbelievers, He commanded (the Prophet) to turn exclusively to Him and to seek refuge in His forgiveness and mercy.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the disbeliever is placed in his grave and sees his seat in the Fire, he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ — 'I will repent and do righteous deeds.' Then it is said to him: 'You have been given a life long enough for what you were given.' His grave then constricts upon him, and he becomes like one being stung, writhing and screaming, while the snakes and scorpions of the earth swarm upon him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "They claimed that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Aishah: 'When the believer sees the angels, they say: "We will send you back to the world." He says: "To the house of worries and sorrows? Rather, send me forward to Allah." As for the disbelievers, they say to him: "We will send you back," and he says: "My Lord, send me back ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾."'" This is a mursal report (one whose chain lacks a companion).

Al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death approaches a person, everything that prevents him from the truth is gathered for him and placed before his eyes. At that moment he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back, so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind.﴾"

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds﴾: he said, "I will say: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Aishah, who said: "Woe to the people of sins from the people of the graves. Black snakes enter upon them in their graves: a snake at his head and a snake at his feet, pinching him until they meet in his middle. That is the punishment in the barzakh (intermediate state) of which Allah said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾"

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying: ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾: he said, "When the Trumpet is blown, no one will remain alive except Allah."

Sa'id ibn Mansur, 'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from him that he was asked about His saying ﴿Then there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another﴾ and His saying ﴿And some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 27; al-Tur: 25]. He said: "These are different stations. As for the station in which there is no kinship between them and they do not ask one another, it is at the first blast (al-ṣa‘qah al-ūlā), when there is no kinship between them, for they will be struck down. But when the final blast comes, they will be standing and asking one another."

Ibn Jarir and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, also related from him that he was asked about the two verses. He said: "As for His saying ﴿nor will they ask one another﴾, this is at the first blast, when nothing remains upon the earth. As for His saying ﴿So some of them will turn to others, asking one another﴾ [al-Saffat: 50], this is when they have entered Paradise, and some of them turn to others, asking one another."

Ibn al-Mubarak in *al-Zuhd*, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "When the Day of Resurrection comes, Allah will gather the first and the last." In another wording: "On the Day of Resurrection, a servant or a maidservant will be taken by the hand before the heads of the first and the last, then a herald will call out: 'Behold, this is so-and-so son of so-and-so. Whoever has a right against him, let him come and take his right.'"

In another wording: "Whoever has a grievance, let him come and take his right. By Allah, a man will rejoice that he has a right against his father, his son, or his wife, even if she is small. The proof of this is in the Book of Allah: ﴿So when the Trumpet is blown, there will be no kinship between them that day, nor will they ask one another.﴾"

Ahmad, al-Tabarani, al-Hakim and al-Bayhaqi in his *Sunan* related from al-Miswar ibn Makhramah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed, kinship is cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship, my cause (sabab) and my in-law relation (ṣihr)."

Al-Bazzar, al-Tabarani, Abu Nu'aym, al-Hakim and al-Diya' in *al-Mukhtarah* related from 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Every cause and every kinship will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my cause and my kinship."

Ibn 'Asakir related from Ibn 'Umar, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Every kinship and in-law relation will be cut off on the Day of Resurrection except my kinship and my in-law relation."

Ahmad related from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say from the pulpit: "What is the matter with men who say that the kinship of the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) will not benefit his people? Indeed, by Allah, my kinship is connected in this world and the Hereafter, and I, O people, am your forerunner (faraṭ)."

Ibn Jarir related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: he said, "It blows upon them."

Ibn Mardawayh and al-Diya' in *Sifat al-Nar* related from Abu al-Darda', who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said concerning His saying: "﴿The Fire will scorch their faces﴾: it scorches them with one scorching, and their flesh slides off their heels."

Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse, who said: "It scorched them with one scorching, leaving no flesh on a bone without throwing it off their heels."

Ahmad, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Tirmidhi, who authenticated it, Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Sifat al-Nar*, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Hakim, who authenticated it, Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah*, and Ibn Mardawayh related concerning His saying ﴿and they therein are grimacing﴾: "The Fire disfigures them, so that the upper lip is drawn up until it reaches the middle of the head, and the lower lip hangs down until it strikes the navel."

'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, Ibn Abi Shaybah, Hannad, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, al-Tabarani and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, related from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse: "The grimace of a cooked head: their teeth show and their lips are drawn back."

Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Ibn 'Abbas concerning ﴿kāliḥūn﴾ (grimacing): "Frowning."

Many well-known reports have come concerning the description of the people of the Fire, what they will say, and what will be said to them.

Al-Hakim al-Tirmidhi, Abu Ya'la, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Ibn al-Sunni in *'Amal al-Yawm wa'l-Laylah*, Ibn Mardawayh and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Hilyah* related "from Ibn Mas'ud that he recited into the ear of a afflicted person ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain?﴾ until he completed the surah, and he was healed. The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'With what did you recite into his ear?' He informed him, and the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'By Him in whose hand is my soul, if a man with certainty recited it over a mountain, it would move.'"

Ibn al-Sunni, Ibn Mandah and Abu Nu'aym in *al-Ma'rifah* related, and al-Suyuti said with a good chain, through the route of Muhammad ibn Ibrahim al-Taymi from his father, who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) sent us on a military expedition and commanded us to say, when we reached evening and morning: ﴿Did you think that We created you in vain, and that you would not be returned to Us?﴾ We recited it, and we gained booty and were safe." End of quotation.

**Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 1 of 2):**

.

*Ḥattā* here is the *ibtidā'iyyah* (the "inceptive" *ḥattā*, which introduces a new sentence), and it is followed by a conditional clause. It is nonetheless a *ghāyah* (terminal limit) for what precedes it, and it is connected to His words "they are liars" (*la-kādhibūn*). It has also been said that it is connected to *yaṣifūn* ("they describe"). By "the coming of death" is meant the coming of its signs. ﴿He says, "My Lord, send me back."﴾ That is, the one to whom death has come says this out of regret and grief over what he neglected. "My Lord, send me back" means: return me to the world. He said *irji'ūnī* with the plural pronoun to honour the one addressed.

It has also been said that it is an emphatic repetition of the verb, meaning "send me back, send me back, send me back." A parallel is His words ﴿Cast, cast into Hell﴾ (Q. 50:24). Al-Māzinī said: its meaning is "cast, cast." The same has been said of the verse of Imru' al-Qays:

> *Qifā nabki min dhikrā ḥabībin wa-manzili*
> ("Halt, let us weep for the remembrance of a beloved and a dwelling")

From this is also the saying of al-Ḥajjāj:

> *Yā ḥarasī, iḍribā 'unuqahu*
> ("O my guards, strike his neck")

And from it is the saying of the poet:

> *Wa-law shi'tu ḥarramtu al-nisā'a siwākum*
> ("Had I wished, I would have forbidden women other than you")

And the saying of another:

> *Alā fārḥamūnī yā ilāha Muḥammadin*
> ("Ah, have mercy upon me, O God of Muhammad")

It has also been said that when they cried out to God, the one among them said "My Lord." Then he returned to addressing the angels and said: ﴿"Send me back, that I may do righteousness."﴾ That is, that I may do righteous deeds in the world if I am returned to it: faith and what follows from it of good works. When he wished to return in order to act, God answered him with His words: ﴿By no means! It is only a word he speaks.﴾ So He brought the particle of repulsion and rebuke (*kallā*). The pronoun in *innahā* ("indeed it") refers to his words "My Lord, send me back." That is: this word is indeed what he says, without doubt, and the matter is not as he supposes, that he will be granted a return to the world. Or the meaning is: even if he were granted that, he would not fulfil it, as in His words ﴿And had they been returned, they would have gone back to what they were forbidden﴾ (Q. 6:28). It has also been said that the pronoun in *qā'iluhā* ("its speaker") refers to God, meaning: there is no breach in His report, and He has informed us that He does not delay a soul when its term comes.

﴿And before them is a barrier (*barzakh*)﴾: that is, behind them and before them. The *barzakh* is the partition between two things, as stated by al-Jawharī.

The interpreters differed about the meaning of the verse. Al-Ḍaḥḥāk, Mujāhid and Ibn Zayd said: it is a barrier between death and resurrection.

Al-Kalbī said: it is the term between the two blasts, and between them is forty years.

Al-Suddī said: it is the term, and ﴿until the day they are raised﴾ is the Day of Resurrection.

﴿Then when the Trumpet is blown﴾: it has been said this is the first blast, and it has been said it is the second. The latter is preferred. It is the blast that occurs between the raising and the rising. It has also been said that the meaning is: when He blows into the bodies their spirits, taking *al-ṣuwar* as the plural of *ṣūrah* (form), not the horn. This is supported by the reading of Ibn 'Abbās and al-Ḥasan, *al-ṣuwari* with a fatḥah on the *wāw* and a ḍammah on the *ṣād*, as the plural of *ṣūrah*. Abū Razīn read it with a fatḥah on the *ṣād* and the *wāw*.

The rest read it with a ḍammah on the *ṣād* and a sukūn on the *wāw*, meaning the horn into which one blows.

﴿So there will be no kinship among them that day﴾: that is, they will not boast of their lineages or mention them, because of the bewilderment and astonishment they are in. ﴿Nor will they ask one another﴾: that is, one will not ask another, for they will then have a preoccupation that absorbs them. From this is His saying: ﴿On the day a man flees from his brother, his mother, his father, his companion and his sons﴾ (Q. 80:34–36), and His saying: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask of his intimate friend﴾ (Q. 70:10). This is not contradicted by another verse, His saying: ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning each other﴾ (Q. 37:27). That is to be understood as referring to the differing standing-places on the Day of Resurrection: the affirmation applies to some of them, and the negation to others, as we have established in the parallels of this matter, which is affirmed at one time and negated at another.

﴿Then whoever's scales are heavy﴾: that is, whose weighed deeds (*mawzūnātuhu*) of righteous works are heavy. ﴿Those are the successful﴾: that is, the ones who attain their beloved aims, who are saved from the things they feared.

﴿And whoever's scales are light﴾: these are his righteous deeds. ﴿Those are they who have lost their souls﴾: that is, they wasted and abandoned what would have benefited them. ﴿In Hell they will abide eternally﴾. This is a *badal* (substitute) for the relative clause's connection, or a second predicate of the demonstrative *ulā'ika*. The discussion of this verse has already been given in full, so we will not repeat it.

The clause ﴿The Fire scorches their faces﴾ is a new resumptive sentence (*mustaʾnafah*). It may also be in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*), or it may be a further predicate of *ulā'ika*. *Al-laf'* is burning: one says *lafathathu al-nār* ("the fire scorched him") when it burns him, and *laftuhu bi-al-sayf* ("I struck him with the sword") when one strikes him. He singled out the faces because they are the noblest of the limbs.

﴿And they therein are grimacing﴾: this clause is in the accusative position as a circumstantial clause. *Al-kālih* is one whose lips have drawn back and whose teeth are exposed, as stated by al-Zajjāj. One says *dahrun kālih*, meaning a severe age.

The lexicographers said: *al-kulūḥ* is a gathering together in frowning.

The clause ﴿Were not My verses recited to you?﴾ is governed by an implied verb of saying: that is, it will be said to them, as rebuke and reproach: "Were not My verses recited to you in the world?" ﴿So you used to deny them﴾.

The clause ﴿They will say, "Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us"﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, an answer to an implied question: that is, our pleasures and our desires overcame us. That was called wretchedness (*shiqwah*) because it ends in misery.

Abū 'Amr and 'Āṣim, the people of Madina, read *shiqwatunā*; the rest read *shaqāwatunā*. This reading is transmitted from Ibn Mas'ūd and al-Ḥasan.

﴿And we were a people who had gone astray﴾: that is, because of that, for they strayed from the truth through that wretchedness.

Then they asked for what they would not be granted, and they said: ﴿Our Lord, bring us out of it, and if we return, then indeed we are wrongdoers﴾: that is, if we return to what we were upon of disbelief and unbelief, then indeed we are wrongdoers to ourselves by returning to that. God answered them with His words: ﴿He said, "Be silent in it, and do not speak to Me."﴾ That is, remain in Hell. Al-Mubarrad said: *al-khasʾ* is removal with something disliked. Al-Zajjāj said: go away with the going away of wrath, and be removed as a dog is removed.

The meaning according to this is: be removed into Hell, as one says to a dog *ikhsa'* ("begone"), that is, go away. *Khasa'tu al-kalb khasʾan* means I drove the dog off. ﴿And do not speak to Me﴾ about bringing you out of the Fire and returning you to the world, or about lifting the punishment from you. It has also been said that the meaning is: do not speak to Me at all.

Then He gave the reason for this with His words: ﴿Indeed, there was a group of My servants who said﴾, and they are the believers. It has been said they are the Companions, ﴿"Our Lord, we have believed, so forgive us and have mercy upon us, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ The majority read *innahu kāna farīqun* with a kasrah on *inna*, as a resumptive explanatory clause. Ubayy read it with a fatḥah.

﴿And you took them in mockery﴾ (*sikhriyyan*). Nāfi', Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *sīn* with a ḍammah. The rest read it with a kasrah. Abū 'Amr distinguished between them: he made the kasrah refer to ridicule (*al-huzuw*), and the ḍammah to subjugation (*al-sukhriyyah*).

Al-Naḥḥās said: al-Khalīl, Sībawayh, al-Kisā'ī and al-Farrā' do not know this distinction. Al-Tha'labī related from al-Kisā'ī that the kasrah means mockery and derision in speech, and the ḍammah means making subservient and deeming remote in deed.

﴿Until they made you forget My remembrance﴾: that is, you took them for mockery to this extent, for they forgot the remembrance of God because of their great preoccupation with ridicule. ﴿And you used to laugh at them﴾ in the world. The meaning is: until you forgot My remembrance by your preoccupation with mockery and laughter. He attributed this to His servants, the believers, because they were the cause.

The clause ﴿Indeed, I have rewarded them today for what they endured﴾ is a new resumptive sentence, confirming what came before. The *bā'* in *bi-mā ṣabarū* ("for what they endured") indicates causation.

﴿That they are the ones who are successful﴾. Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read the *hamzah* with a kasrah as a new sentence. The rest read it with a fatḥah, meaning "because they are the successful ones." It may also be in the accusative as the second object of the verb.

﴿He said, "How long did you remain on earth, counting years?"﴾ The speaker is God, the Mighty and Majestic, and it is a reminder to them: how long did they remain? When they asked to return to the world, after He had informed them that this would not happen, as in His saying "be silent in it." The earth meant is the earth to which they asked to return. It is possible the question concerns the whole of what they remained in life and in the graves. It has also been said that it is a question about the duration of their stay in the graves, because of the phrase "on earth," not "upon the earth." This has been refuted by a parallel like His words ﴿and do not cause corruption on the earth﴾ (Q. 7:56, 85). The accusative of *ʿadada sinīn* is as a specification (*tamyīz*), because of the vagueness in *kam*. *Sinīn* with a fatḥah on the *nūn* is taken as the plural *nūn*. Some Arabs put it in the genitive and give it tanwīn.

﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day."﴾ They underestimated the duration of their stay because of the severe punishment they were in.

It has been said that the punishment was lifted from them between the two blasts, so they forgot the punishment they had been in in their graves. It has also been said that God caused them to forget the punishment they had been in from the first blast to the second.

Then, when they realised what had befallen them of forgetfulness, because of the great terror they were in, they referred the matter to others and said: ﴿So ask those who count.﴾ That is, those who are capable of knowing the number. They are the angels, because they are the guardians who know the deeds and lifespans of the servants. It has also been said that the meaning is: ask those who reckon, the people who know reckoning among mankind.

Ibn Kathīr, Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "How long did you remain on earth?"﴾ in the imperative. The meaning: say, O Muhammad, to the disbelievers. Or it is an imperative to the angel to question them. Or the implied sense is: say, "How long did you remain?" The speech is thus given the form of a command to one person while the meaning is a group.

The rest read ﴿He said, "How long did you remain?"﴾ taking the speaker to be God, the Mighty and Majestic, or the angel.

﴿He said, "You remained but a little, if only you had known."﴾ Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read ﴿Say, "If you remained but a little"﴾ as in the first verse. The rest read *qāla* ("he said") as a report. The two readings have already been explained. The meaning: you did not remain on earth except a brief stay, ﴿if only you had known﴾ anything of knowledge. The answer is omitted: if you had known, you would have known today the brevity of your stay on earth or in the graves or in both. All of that is brief in comparison with their staying.

Then He, glory be to Him, increased their rebuke and said: ﴿Did you suppose that We created you in vain?﴾ The *hamzah* is for rebuke and affirmation, and the *fā'* is for coordination with an implied element, as explained elsewhere: that is, did you not know anything, so that you supposed? *ʿAbathan* in the accusative is either as a circumstantial state (*ḥāl*): playing about; or as a cause: for play.

Sībawayh and Quṭrub said the first; Abū 'Ubayda said the second.

He also said: it may be accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*). The clause ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ is coordinated with *annamā khalaqnākum ʿabatan* ("that We created you in vain"). *Al-ʿabath* in the lexicon is play: one says *ʿabatha yaʿbathu ʿabatan*, so he is *ʿābith*, meaning playing. Its root is from the phrase *ʿabathtu al-aqiṭ*, "I mixed the dried curd." The meaning: did you suppose that Our creating you was for neglect, as cattle are created, with no reward and no punishment, and that you would not return to Us in resurrection and rising, so that We would recompense you for your deeds?

Ḥamzah and al-Kisā'ī read *turjaʿūn* with a fatḥah on the initial *tā'* and a kasrah on the *jīm*, in the active voice. The rest read it in the passive voice.

It has been said that ﴿and that you would not be returned to Us﴾ may be coordinated with *ʿabathan*, in the sense: that We created you for play and for not being returned.

Then He, glory be to Him, declared Himself free of imperfection and said: ﴿So exalted is God﴾: that is, He is far removed from having children and partners, or from creating anything in vain, or from all of that. He is the King who alone rightly possesses sovereignty absolutely, the Truth in all His acts and words. ﴿There is no deity but Him, Lord of the Noble Throne﴾. How then could He not be God and Lord of what is beneath the Noble Throne among created beings? The description of the Throne as *al-karīm* ("noble") is because mercy and goodness descend from it, or with regard to the one who sits upon it, as one says *bayt karīm* ("a noble house") when its occupants are noble.

Abū Ja'far, Ibn Muḥayṣin, Ismā'īl and Abān ibn Tha'lab read *al-karīmu* in the nominative, as an epithet of *Rabb* ("Lord"). The rest read it in the genitive, as an epithet of *al-ʿarsh* ("the Throne").

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 23, verses 99–118 (part 2 of 2):

Then He refuted what the people of polytheism held, rebuking and reproaching them, and said: ﴿And whoever calls upon another god along with Allah﴾, worshipping him alongside Allah or worshipping him alone. The clause ﴿for which he has no proof﴾ is in the accusative position (maḥall naṣb) as a descriptive qualifier (ṣifah) of the word ilāhan (إلهًا, "a god"). It is a necessary qualifier (ṣifah lāzimah), brought for emphasis, like His saying ﴿flies with its two wings﴾. Al-burhān (البُرْهان) means the clear argument and the evident proof. The answer to the conditional clause (sharṭ) is His saying: ﴿then his reckoning is only with his Lord﴾. The clause "for which he has no proof" is an interjected clause (mu‘taridah) between the conditional and its response, like your saying: "Whoever does good to Zayd, there is no one more deserving of good from him, so Allah will reward him." It was also said that the response of the conditional is His saying: ﴿for which he has no proof﴾, with the response particle (fā’ al-jazā’) omitted, as in the poet's words:

*Whoever does good deeds, Allah will reward them.*

﴿Indeed, the disbelievers will not succeed.﴾ Al-Hasan and Qatadah read *innа* (أنَّ) with a fatḥah, as a causal clause (ta‘līl, "giving a reason"). The rest read it with a kasrah, as a new independent sentence (isti’nāf, "resumption"). Al-Hasan also read *lā yufliḥu* (لا يُفْلِحُ) with a fatḥah on the yā' and the lām, as the present tense of *falaḥa*, with the same meaning as *aflaḥa*.

Then He concluded this surah by teaching His Messenger (ﷺ) to ask Him for forgiveness and mercy, so He said: ﴿And say: "My Lord, forgive and have mercy, and You are the best of the merciful."﴾ He, glorified is He, commanded him to seek forgiveness so that his community would follow him. It was also said: He commanded him to seek forgiveness for his community. The explanation of His being the most merciful of the merciful has already been given. The connection of this with what precedes it is that when He, glorified is He, described the conditions of the disbelievers, He commanded (the Prophet) to turn exclusively to Him and to seek refuge in His forgiveness and mercy.

Ibn Abi al-Dunya in *Dhikr al-Mawt* and Ibn Abi Hatim related from Abu Hurayrah, who said: "When the disbeliever is placed in his grave and sees his seat in the Fire, he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back﴾ — 'I will repent and do righteous deeds.' Then it is said to him: 'You have been given a life long enough for what you were given.' His grave then constricts upon him, and he becomes like one being stung, writhing and screaming, while the snakes and scorpions of the earth swarm upon him."

Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir related from Ibn Jurayj, who said: "They claimed that the Prophet (ﷺ) said to 'Aishah: 'When the believer sees the angels, they say: "We will send you back to the world." He says: "To the house of worries and sorrows? Rather, send me forward to Allah." As for the disbelievers, they say to him: "We will send you back," and he says: "My Lord, send me back ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind﴾."'" This is a mursal report (one whose chain lacks a companion).

Al-Daylami related from Jabir ibn 'Abd Allah, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "When death approaches a person, everything that prevents him from the truth is gathered for him and placed before his eyes. At that moment he says: ﴿My Lord, send me back, so that I may do righteous deeds in what I have left behind.﴾"

Al-Bayhaqi in *al-Asma' wa'l-Sifat* related through the route of 'Ikrimah from Ibn 'Abbas concerning His saying ﴿so that I may do righteous deeds﴾: he said, "I will say: There is no god but Allah."

Ibn Abi Hatim related from 'Aishah, who said: "Woe to the people of sins from the people of the graves. Black snakes enter upon them in their graves: a snake at his head and a snake at his feet, pinching him until they meet in his middle. That is the punishment in the barzakh (intermediate state) of which Allah said: ﴿And behind them is a barrier until the day they are resurrected.﴾"
